I wish Steam had a “Mixed” option instead of forcing either a positive or negative review.  I love Slay the Spire 2. I loved the first game, and I’ll probably keep playing this one for a long time. Several other reviews have already gone into detail about the game’s broader balance issues, so I won’t repeat all of that. Instead, I want to focus on what ultimately sours so many otherwise great runs for me: Aeonglass.  One of the best parts of Slay the Spire is letting the run evolve naturally. Sometimes the game practically tells you, “Congratulations, you’re an Exhaust build,” or “Here’s a pile of Ethereal synergy on Necrobinder, guess you’re learning that today!” Those are some of the most memorable and enjoyable runs because you’re adapting to what the game gives you instead of forcing a predetermined strategy.  The problem is that by Act 3 especially on A10 with two bosses, I feel like I have to build every run around the possibility of encountering Aeonglass. Instead of embracing the roguelike nature of the game, I’m constantly asking, “Will this deck even be allowed to beat Aeonglass?” That completely changes how I approach earlier acts.  This game is about playing cards, finding synergies, and occasionally discovering some ridiculous interaction that lets you break the game. Those moments are rare enough that they feel earned. Much more often, you’re piloting a deck that’s simply good enough to win. But then a single boss can completely invalidate the playstyle you’ve spent an entire run developing.  Aeonglass is the worst example of this. A boss that heavily punishes you for playing cards in a game fundamentally about playing cards already feels questionable. Pair that with enormous damage output and Artifact, and it stops feeling like a test of your deck and starts feeling like a deck check. Either you happened to build the “correct” kind of deck from Act 1, or your run is effectively over.  I don’t mind difficult bosses. I don’t even mind losing. What frustrates me is feeling like I’m being punished for engaging with the core roguelike philosophy of adapting to what the game gives me. Instead of experimenting, I feel incentivized to hedge against one specific encounter from the very beginning.  I still love this game. I think it has fantastic mechanics, interesting classes, and that same satisfying crescendo that makes the final act feel meaningful. But Aeonglass feels out of place, overtuned, and significantly less fun than the rest of the game. I hope it gets another balance pass, because right now it turns too many great runs into frustrating ones.

It feels to me like the people who made the game are not the ones patching it but that can't be right.   The patches are either good, very good or they see that it's bad and they revert or revise. Excellent, in fact that's so far above my expectations for patches I'm grateful just to read the notes.   What I mean is when the game first launched every character could go infinite rather easily using just cards. And the first patch thought that was black magic and banished or reworked almost every card that made energy. To the benefit of the game as you will see later.   The boss rewards that remove 4, or remove 2 every fire seemed like the perfect compliment to going infinite. Even Pandora's Box's transform all basics was out shined a bit by give all defends exhaust and permanent block every play. Those are still in the game as a vestige of the original intention, which clearly seemed to be support an infinite where your deck supplies the energy. Right?  The relics, baring Pendulum and the returning Abacus, seemed very ambivalent about infinites which I took as a suggestion of intent. You see in Spire 1, many infinites were facilitated by a singular relic, Sundial. But not just that, the interaction of Sundial with drawing from an empty draw pile gave more energy than intended. Unfortunately, I would have preferred if that was the dominant way to go infinite in this game, because that would be the only thing they have to change! Instead, when all the characters go infinite with multiple cards, multiple cards on each character have to be changed. Realistically it was a bit of a ripping of the band aid moment, but it had to happen. Repeatable energy gain from cards had to be harder to get.  Thus they have made a great leap forward on the energy generating cards giving infinite damage. Which let me see the real challenge undertaken by Spire 2.   You see there was this really obvious time where I could go infinite and didn't want to. Showing Slay the Spire to my friend for the first time. Multiplayer is the best addition to this game I possibly could have imagined, but it made me immediately see why this game doesn't want infinites. They are boring in multiplayer. My brother is a Magic player and I showed him the game a few weeks ago. Yesterday he went infinite on Ironclad against the Intangible boss. I went to get food, cleaned the kitchen a bit, came back, ate, talked for a while, looked up... its at 200 health. So infinites are still in the game, just not on demand like before. Remember how I didn't want to go infinite with my friend? That run got a little hard so I added two commons and an uncommon and went infinite in act 2. And to be fair to the Magic player and the current iteration of Spire he was trying real hard the whole run and got there by late act 3  Besides the cards that gain energy much is the same as it's always been. The patches have mostly been to empower some dormant enemies that have been studying our weaknesses. The Invincible Coral was a pushover and the Infested Prism easier than a hallway the first few times up the Spire. I'm glad they are worthy foes now. I do miss the idea of an overstated berserker enemy asking for a free hit every turn but I have every faith that will return.   I get it, I do. I cannot imagine balancing a game like this. They do, and they are doing a great job it's just a process. So trust the process. Patch by patch the cards are transitioning from infinites to reality, so I would recommend trying them out now, as they will only get better with time. Thank you for your game.   I like playing one of the new characters, Necrobinder. They were imo the most consistent at going infinite on release and seemed to be focused on that with about half their card pool. You still can go off pretty hard on a specific turn and the character is still enjoyable. The issue is that half the card pool doesn't work with the other half and you end up feeling like Defect 1.

I was so scared that I had changed, that the glut of roguelike deckbuilders spawned by this game's predecessor had made me grow tired of the genre and I wouldn't be able to enjoy this game in the same way that made STS1 one of my all-time favorites. It turns out Mega Crit is just that cracked, and since nobody else had been capable of making a roguelike deckbuilder that could touch STS1 in the seven years since its release, they decided they'd do it themselves.  This game is visibly incomplete, and it's still better than STS1, which is a complement of the highest order. Five well-balanced characters, two more than the first game ("well-balanced" being the keyword here—rest in piss, Watcher), the inclusion of Ancient relics, which are way more varied and interesting than STS1's default of "gain 1 energy per turn in exchange for X downside," and the range of enchantments and events make this game feel almost infinitely replayable. I hate early access in most cases, but having the game meaningfully change from week to week in response (in part) to the way you play it is genuinely so cool. Don't miss being along for the ride: you'll be missing out by waiting for full release.  (Also go play Library of Ruina—it's not a roguelike, but it's the only deckbuilder in the same league as STS.)

Is a Roguelike supposed to be choices or just gambling? This game feels more like gambling.  There is so little control over what you can do in your deckbuilding that it ends up feeling like 90% of your runs are just a waste of time. To top it off, there's very mild meta progression elements.   Is the game interesting? Sure. But once you've played all of the characters a few times, you realize just how oppressive most of the bosses are. The bosses completely restrict what builds actually function. I get that this is the core gameplay loop of a roguelike, but the problem is that you can strategize all you want, but if you don't get incredibly lucky with your deck build, you can demolish all normal and elite level combats and die in the first 2 turns on a boss. It's insane how big the difficulty spikes are and how little tools you have to deal with them. To give you an example, my friend and I got to the second boss (out of three total) on our first run. We got obliterated by an enemy called the Knowledge Demon that constantly restricts what you can do doing the fight (take extra damage every turn, or reduce your card draw/energy etc). Despite knowing this enemy was coming, we weren't able to beat him in the next 10 or so runs, until we finally got lucky and beat him with literally 1 HP remaining. We reached the final boss on that same run and it has just as many punishing mechanics as the second boss. It's simply not fun because you feel like all of your choices are being stripped away from you.   I wouldn't recommend this game because it doesn't feel like you have enough control over what you do. If you like gambling, you might love this game. If you want to play an actual game, I think it's debatable on how much this actually qualifies.

Great game, but be warned that it's difficult and often has an even frustration-to-fun to ratio. There's a big learning curve and no QoL to ameliorate it. The game hides a lot of information from you, and it expects that you will understand exactly why you died and how to avoid it next time. The cards are tricky to evaluate and sequence, and each character's card pool supports at least 3 distinct archetypes. To further complicate things, there are relics which grant passive abilities and once-per-combat abilities, as well as potions which grant one-time effects. The potions add a considerable element of resource management (you can only carry a fixed number which decreases on higher difficulties), since being too liberal or stingy with them will result in avoidable losses. The upside to all this variance and complexity is that every run feels fresh and allows for an almost infinite degree of skill expression.  Finally, three pieces of advice for new/inexperienced players: 1) You usually can't afford to skip cards in act 1 because every starter deck is awful. By the same logic, be judicious about what you take in acts 2 and 3 because you want your deck to start having some level of consistent synergy at this point, and taking unnecessary cards detracts from that.  2) While there is no built-in undo or retry, you can save scum if you misplayed and are going to die. Save and quit before ending your turn and you can start over at the beginning of the encounter. The game does not punish this in any way. You can do this as much as you want, but it does not change the RNG (i.e., you draw the same cards in the same order, enemies take the same actions, etc).  3) The Untapped overlay gives you helpful insight into which starting options at the beginning of each act give you the best odds of winning according to tons of collected playthrough data. It is free to download and unobtrusive. A lot of the seemingly good act 1 offers often have surprisingly high rates of early failure.

Slay the Spire 1 is one of the best, most beautifully designed games of all time. It is the very definition of the Deck Builder genre. Slay the Spire 2 is currently, at worst, as good as Slay the Spire 1 is as a finished game, while having more characters, better presentation, more narrative, and even Co-op. And it is still in Early Access. But don't let that Early Access label scare you, Slay the Spire 2 is more of a finished game in Early Access than most modern games are on their full release. It is not a "hey the game isn't finished yet but you can play part of it" Early Access, it is a "here is a full game's worth of content, but we are continuing to tweak it, add to it, and redesign parts of it until it is as close to perfect as possible" Early Access. I've played around 2000 hours total on Slay the Spire 1 across 4 platforms since I got it in Early Access and I currently have 116 hours in Slay the Spire 2 and I can assure you, Mega Crit knows what they're doing. [h1]The Ultimate Deck Builder[/h1]   [i]There will be a TL;DR at the end.[/i]   ~   I once called the original [i]Slay The Spire[/i] [b]”The Quintessential Card-Crawler”[/b] It’s an incredible game and sets the gold standard for deck builders out there. [b]Mega Crit[/b] did a phenomenal job making the world interesting, the combat addictive, and the experience approachable. I gave it an 8/10 because it is easily an all-time favorite of mine and an all-around [b]Great[/b] game from 2019.  There are some things that [b]2[/b] does better than [i]1[/i] by lightyears - but there are also massive blunders that [b]Mega Crit[/b] will either have to address in patches or, more realistically, we will have to cede as weevils in the otherwise bountiful harvest.  There lots of wonderful stuff this game has to offer over the original - the kind that you don’t notice too much, but miss dearly on a return visit. It all serves to highlight some of the [b]Great[/b] things that [b]STS2[/b] has to offer:  - Massive quality of life updates to the UI and general gamefeel. It is smoother in every way! - Higher quality art assets and more nuanced enemy types. - Little things like drawing on the map and cute sound effects. - It feels intuitive and challenging. - The [i]Watcher[/i] isn't here. Good riddance. - Tons and TONS of new synergy styles to build around with your deck! - The Necrobinder is an instant classic and everyone loves her. - Epochs reward players with lore and more content for completing challenges and milestones - It's a lot of the same quality gameplay that [i]STS[/i] fans are lovingly familiar with. - Incredible value for price!  The details are important. Some details solidify [b]2[/b] as an upgrade, but let’s go over some things for newcomers:  In [i]Deckbuilder[/i] games, players craft their deck. Each turn they pull a random selection from it and play with what they have. Knowing what cards give the best value, work best with others, and protect you from particular enemies is key! The ideal deck is one where there is [i]no fat[/i] and the only options are either the high-yield ones for the deck’s synergy, or supporting ones that keep you alive ; a refined machine that can deal with most situations reliably and safely.  The fight against RNG and drawing your "answers" is key. Sometimes you don't draw the answer and you lose. Sometimes you draw your answer too early and cannot use it, and then you lose. The aim is to know what your "answers" are and build a deck that supports them and increases their viability wherever they might be.  The thing that made [i]STS1[/i] so wonderful for many was its ability to appeal to the two core demographics of deck building: 1 - Leveraging quality strategies to build a deck with intent and foresight, being able to make a lean, focused deck to reliably tackle end-game threats. 2- Ascension 1 and just vibe while listening to a podcast or something to unwind.  This is the context that reveals why [b]2[/b] is under fire. Underneath all the shiny upgrades, new content, and fun times with friends - there is corruption flowing deeper than the Ironclad’s blood.  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3772556964 It's good because there's more! It's horrible because THERES MORE!!  In [b]STS2[/b] there is only [b]fatty[/b] decks.  There’s another reviewer that summed this up well: [quote=Random_Killer312]“What if we took one of the cleanest roguelike deck-builders ever made and patched it into a psychological endurance test for people who enjoy being audited by the IRS?”[/quote]  The new design direction that [b]Mega Crit[/b] is moving towards deviates painfully from the flow that made the original title a smashing success:  - Hyper Specific Enemy Needs. - Special card solutions to special problems. - Many build and item synergies fall apart without “keystone” pulls. - Enemy ramp and card control are punitive without "the right answers". - Some "rewards" are bad enough to end your run. - Deck bloat is unavoidable. - In spite of the new synergy types, there aren’t additional card rewards to choose from or ways to steer towards what you want. You're likely going to end up with a chimera deck of 4+ different builds that don't quite play nice together. - Enemy difficulty and intricacy promotes frantic solution seeking that is at odds with the shorter climb. - The climb is too short and either feels too simple (because you got all the synergies you needed to win) or hopeless (because there was no way that you could win) - Shops are less reliable - Co op is fun but only shines a spotlight on the game's strange idea of balance. - Devs are trying to clamp down on powerful synergies (such as infinites) while also making enemies more resilient. Building around specific "answers" is half the fun and rarely rewarding. - Still no true "endless" mode, which is sorely lacking from the first. How has this not been added? - Lots of outcry over the game from devoted fans who desperately want megacrit to move away from their current trajectory and course correct. - The Regent  [spoiler]There's also some drama around the game because some game award-winning political activist is in the credits. They don't really have any sway over the game's direction, so just ignore folks mentioning them.[/spoiler]  Sometimes it feels like they’re trying to ruin the experience. Where you used to be able to say “I’ll do a poison run” on [i]The Silent[/i] or “Let’s do a Lightning-Orb build” on [i]The Defect[/i] - here things often fall apart and leave you with the empty feeling of helplessness instead of determination.  So I went back to play the original [i]STS[/i] again. But that’s just it. It’s [i]Slay The Spire [b]1[/b][/i]  [b]Slay The Spire 2[/b] It's [i]better[/i] and [i][b]not[/b] better[/i] than one of the greatest things ever.  [i]Subnautica, Dragon Age, Hotline Miami, Halo, Fallout, The Forest, Slime Rancher[/i] - Many titles that exemplify that there’s no escaping what comes before in a franchise, but it's an important part of evaluating a sequel.  [b]STS2[/b] has some things that make it [i]better[/i] than [i]STS[/i] [b]STS2[/b] has some things that make it [b]worse[/b] than [i]STS[/i]  [b]STS2[/b] may or may not be remembered as the better experience to [i]STS[/i] depending on who you ask.  [b]STS2[/b] is, when compared to other games on the market, without a doubt, a [b]Great[/b] game. No always online connection, no microtransaction or battlepass system, no overpriced entry fee or predatory data harvesting. Even with all of its problems, it’s still one of the best deckbuilders ever made. You get hundreds of hours of content, mods, play with your friends, draw silly things as you climb, make great memories, and feel the thrill of making an unstoppable deck.  When you see folks give a thumbs up because they think that the pretty colors and numbers are fun, it's valid. When you see folks giving thumbs down and trying to get the attention of the devs to avoid tragedy, it's valid.  I hope the devs are listening to their community and moving away from the current design philosophies. I'm not going to give the game a thumbs down just to get their attention. I'm giving it a thumbs up for you. Yes [b]YOU[/b] who is reading this.  What the game creation wizards, political figures, and worldwide philosophers think isn't what matters. What matters is if this dorky gamer thinks this is worth [b]YOUR[/b] time. It's a good, cheap, fun, game that won't exploit you. It's worth your time, it’s worth your effort, it's worth your laughter, and it will be worth remembering.  ~   [h3]TL;DR[/h3] [b]8/10[/b] [i]Slay The Spire 2[/i] is a [b]Great[/b] game. In some ways it’s better than the original, in some ways it’s worse. In all ways it is a worthy successor and a quality experience to have in your [i]Steam[/i] library.

Slay the Spire 2 tickles my brains in ways that are almost dangerously good. It will eat your thoughts and your life. It took what worked in the first game and made it even more exciting and addicting.  What I like ========== * New Characters -- Necrobinder and Regent are actually fun! Regent took me a little while to figure out, but juggling stars and a huge sword pay off with some incredibly big hitting builds. And Necrobinder has a spooky skeleton hand, that's just fun.  * New Ancients -- The ancients for Act II and III could probably still use some additional passes, but they're already interesting spins. Goopy dragon guy can give me a piece of his flesh, while Vaaku will gladly take over my first turn and set me up for failure if I let him :)  * Incredibly Solid -- It's early access, but it's a good game from start to finish and feels largely well-balanced (with some tweaks here and there).  * Fairer than it looks -- Sure, there's RNG, but most runs are actually winnable. It really rewards planning and thinking about every decision and seeing how they pay off down the road. (Or you can be like me, just grab every card and hope for the best and declare yourself a genius if you win anyway)  What I don't like ============== * Some fights are just unfun -- I do not like the 3 body centipede in Act 2. And those stupid little scrolls that eat your max health in Act 3 bring out an audible groan from me. And for bosses, I just don't like Knowledge Demon. (The sand worm on the other hand? That's a fun gimmick and I'd love to see Spire do more fights like that)  * Some card interactions are unclear -- If you replay a X-cost card, does it use the same X energy from the first play or what you have now? When can an eternal curse be transformed to something that isn't a curse? Does a card being autoplayed count as "[you] playing a card"? These are all edge cases, but you basically have to play to figure it out.  What I'm meh about ===================  * There's now little stories and plot behind the characters -- It's interesting but fluff lore. I'm happy it's there for those who want it. I like that there's big gaps where I can just imagine why they're there.  If they ever go for a Spire 3, it will be hard to beat this one, but I trust in the devs that they've got the formula down great.

Early Access is a dirty word in 2026, but sometimes you have to make an exception.  I’ve got about 20 hours in so far, and while the "Mixed" review score on Steam right now is understandable given the server hiccups and some janky co-op lobbies, I think people are missing the forest for the trees. This isn't a cash-grab; it's a genuine evolution.  The Co-op Elephant in the Room Let's address the big change first: 4-player mode. I was skeptical—how do you translate a solitary card-slinging experience into a group activity? Surprisingly, it works. The new "Aura" cards that affect adjacent players and the "Combo Chain" system (where playing certain cards in sequence across teammates triggers bonus effects) add a layer of coordination I didn't know I needed. That said, the scaling is wonky. Playing solo feels crisp and punishing. Playing with three friends feels like the Spire is actively cheating; enemy health pools get so bloated that fights turn into 15-minute attrition slogs. The devs need to halve the HP scaling for 3-4 players, stat.  Who's In, Who's Out The Devs brought back the Ironclad, Silent, and Defect, but they aren't just copy-pastes. The Silent finally feels like a proper assassin instead of a poison-bot, and the Defect's new "Fission" orbs add some much-needed burst potential. The Watcher is MIA, and honestly? Good. She would have broken the co-op mode over her knee in two seconds.  For the newcomers: Necrobinder is a blast. She plays like a sacrificial necromancer—spending HP to summon temporary minions that soak damage. It's risky, rewarding, and fits the Spire's vibe perfectly. Regent, though... yikes. He revolves around "Royal Decrees" that buff your allies but require you to track turn-order and positioning. In theory, it's a brilliant support class. In practice, it feels like you're managing a stock portfolio while your friends are actually playing a game. He’s powerful, but I’d rather watch paint dry.  The Grind and The Glitches Let's be real: the balance is rough right now. Certain elite enemies in Act 2 are absolute run-enders, and one of the new relics literally crashes the game when combined with a specific Silent card. But here’s the thing—the developers have pushed three hotfixes in four days. They're listening. The foundation is rock-solid, and the new lore fragments you find between floors actually make me care about why the Spire exists, which the original never quite managed.  Final Takeaway Ignore the doom-posting. The final boss is overtuned, the multiplayer netcode can be spotty, and Regent needs a complete rework. But the core loop—that addictive "just one more run" dopamine hit—is absolutely intact.  If you loved the first game, this is a no-brainer. If you're new, wait two weeks for the first major patch. Either way, the Spire has grown, and I'm thrilled to be climbing it again—preferably with a buddy to share the pain.  Worth your money. Just don't bring Regent.

I would like to start out with saying that there are plenty of things that I really enjoy about this game. I also find there to be plenty things that are absolutely infuriating.   A particular gripe about the game that makes it borderline unenjoyable when playing solo. Seeded gameplay NEEDS to be removed. I'm tired of solo being impossible because I didn't CHOOSE the one card that was needed for the next 6 sequences of card rewards which would align with the win condition. Seeded card rewards and card draws defines the game outcome before it was ever even chosen. If I happen to choose what isn't the optimal choice, (of which is impossible to know without hindsight) then lose because of that, that is ridiculous. There is little to no player agency and it doesn't FEEL like a skilled game whatsoever. It doesn't matter if you know card combinations and pick accordingly, because rewards, relics, and fights are all chosen prior to start of the game, and will be shown in a particular order. The chance doesn't apply to you the moment a reward appears, it is determined prior to. The run is mathematically won or lost by the cards you decide to grab. I can reload the same game, and still draw the same cards in the exact same order. There is nothing random about this game whatsoever. Check out tckmn on YouTube, "winning STS2 A10 in 21 card plays". They can prepare a sequence of draws, relics, enemies, mystery rooms, card transformations, etc. to win the game with minimal card plays. The outcome will be the exact same with the exact same choices. There is no variance in the way the game is laid out. This SHOULDN'T be possible if player agency is to have any impact on the gameplay.   Something else to add: Winning in the game doesn't feel good. It feels cheesy. If I don't have a broken combo with cards (It's not a chance, it's do I or don't I) , then I am at a loss. When I win, I've rolled the nuts, and yet it was purely based on luck (or was it?). It doesn't FEEL good, it feels like I've just gotten by, by the luck of the draw. I'm never crawling past the finish line. It's a complete clap fiesta and the game is a breeze, or I'm not scaling enough due to the nature of card rewards and the propensity to play in a different manner each run (there are clear and obvious broken synergies which are borderline throwing a run by not grabbing them). There is a clear functionality between the cards, and yet it almost seems impossible to get the chance to try them all (as there's no reason to).  However, the games music, art style, animations, and everything improved upon from the first game are all a plus. These are all simple yet effective ways to keep a player on the game.  Now to the games biggest pro. Multiplayer. Despite the games design, multiplayer allows for at least one person to hopefully make the only correct choices to obtain the "broken" status. It is fun to have the reassurance that your run is not a loss due to being carried. There are also fun multiplayer cards/interactions which make the game feel more engaging. Who also doesn't like playing games with friends? That is a plus in it of itself.   I would like to add, that a single person usually carries our game. I find where myself or others fail to pick correctly, somebody else usually fills those shoes. Runs tend to be carried by an individual. Now despite enemies with boosted health stats, a single person (with the same base/upgraded cards as if it were a singleplayer game) can still solo the game. Now why is it that is even possible? The same broken deck that would wipe your solo run, could also solo mobs with 2x/3x/4x hp? Need I explain more on the games balance? Streamers and top players will build in a particular fashion because of the need to. This isn't a skill issue, this is a balance/agency problem. Clear and obvious card choices have been determined because the latter is clearly horrible and offers nothing to the player. All cards should have applicability and not just be an obvious skip.  Despite my obvious rage review, if the goal is to play with friends and just have a good time, stick to the daily's and A0. If the goal is to play by yourself and have a good time, you may find that. If you're like me, who finds the game to be unfair and out of the hands of the player, just play multiplayer. Buy it or don't. It seems if you're casual enough to just want to play, you'll enjoy it. If you're in the middle ground like me, who's of not a fan of losing every run uncontrollably, just play with friends. If you're a min/maxing sweat taking 45 second turns, you'll say just get good. There are too many thoughts on the game and not enough space to fill it. Enjoy at your own discretion.

At the moment I cannot recommend this game for anyone looking for a casual pastime. Slay the Spire 1 was not perfect, but I felt that it struck a fairly good balance - providing a reasonable challenge while still allowing you to skew your deck towards specialised builds, and most importantly it was possible to make the vast majority of builds 'work' against all bosses and elites (provided you were careful to round out your deck with a few utility cards).   The same cannot be said for Slay the Spire 2. There are countless negative reviews from players far more skilled than me about the neuances of the way in which certain bosses and elites make it completely impossible to win unless you were lucky enough (and I stress the word lucky here) to have been offered the required cards to protect against their specific gimmic. For example - if you dont happen to see any ways to remove cards from your deck, and dont have very high damage output, you will simply lose to any of the elites that put overwhelming numbers of debuff cards into your hand and deck. I would not have an issue with this if I had been offered the methods to counter it, which I had not taken, or if the elites that hard counter specific builds were a rare ocurrence (or they only appeared in the later floors to give you time to build up a defence). But they are frequent, they are varied in what they target (good luck guessing which ones to account for on any particular run), they come at you early in the run, and they are so targeted at a particular win condition that the game essentially punishes you for guessing wrong. It is not fun to lose when I dont have a sense that it was my fault.   From looking at the discourse around this game, it seems like the community has been divided between those looking for a casual, fun way to spend a few hours finding cool synergies, and those looking for a very precise, very challenging technical game requiring a deep understanding of the intricacies of card interactions and enemy turn orders. Trying to balance for both seems to have dragged the developers into the no mans land in the middle, where neither group are happy.   All of this is a long way of saying that I would not recommend purchasing the game as is.

This game is fun, and is more or less what you would be expecting from a deckbuilder rogue like. It is undeniably rough around the edges in several glaring ways, but that is to be expected with an early access game. The reason I am not recommending this game and joining the hate wagon, so to speak, is that 2 player coop remains completely and utterly unbalanced. And while I do respect that this game is in early access and thus deserves some leniency, I did pay for this game and I am entitled to publicly air my grievances rather than just shouting into the abyss of the in-game feedback menu.  	An example of the poor multiplayer balance is the Test Subject, an Act 3 boss, which has a phase where he gains strength whenever a player uses a skill card, just like the Gremlin Nob from the first game. This does not sound like a problem, until you discover that he gains this strength for everyone whenever anyone plays a skill. This creates a situation where players are forced to either ration their health for a few turns, paying an absolutely enormous quantity and likely tanking the rest of the fight, or a player sacrifices themselves so that the other can scale and hopefully have a shot at winning the fight. At face value, this simply is not enjoyable. I do not like having to inescapable pay half of my health to avoid sinking the team. There is no finesse, no skill, no complex decision making in the situation presented here.   	I would maybe be willing to bitterly accept this as “just a part of the game” or “multiplayer quirk” or whatever, but they recently changed an elite enemy called the Infested Prism to do the same thing as the Test Subject, except each player scales it individually, meaning they are free to play how they like without putting their teammates in jeopardy. Clearly, at some level, they understand that how the Test Subject scales is not healthy in multiplayer. Why else would they not have the Infested Prism function the same way? The whole situation is baffling to me honestly. It feels very demoralizing to fight your way through an A10 climb with your friend, only to lose at the very end to an enemy the developers refuse to balance.  	This game has a lot of potential and I urge the developers to not neglect coop. It should be viewed as a core part of the game and its balance should be of upmost priority.  	This review is negative, and I do stand by that. I do not recommend this game currently. However if you are looking for more Slay the Spire after playing the first game and only intend to climb solo than this game is probably for you.

I recommend the game, *but not in its current state for higher challenge players* I'll also preface this by saying I don't watch people play this game. That does nothing for me and I am comfortable speaking to my own experience compared to the first game (beat A20 on switch, all achievements)  and that of my friends, rather than "what defines the meta" or however people talk about this.   I know I could be way better. Just trying to speak to the experience of a casual player who maybe has 3 or 4 days a month to sit down and game for an evening.   Generally love this game and I recognize we are still in early access, but I have to call it soon after the recent waves of changes. I don't have time to keep adapting to card changes, making a pick and then realizing it is a completely different card, and elite and boss changes that feel like spaghetti stuck on a wall, but gradually sliding down to make room for less sticky spaghetti. I'm glad I supported the project and had a ton of fun at the initial release. I regret nothing, but I honestly just want people to wait until its done so they don't leave with a sour taste in their throats.   Generally I'm talking about A8-10 here, but it also extends to the game as a whole.  Not a fan of aeonglass. Not a fan of the demon dorito. Generally, there seems to be a hyperfixation on enemies that swing every turn, punishing skill card based decks to balance silent and necrobinder, but those decks adapt better. The regent and the defect can't as well, especially the defect in multiplayer.  Also not a fan of the curve in act 1. Still feels sad to see all the tools for an incredible build except 1, and then come across some of the higher difficulty fights in a chain, and watch a unique opportunity die. The filter could be shifted to act 3 floors, which is often a cakewalk by comparison until the boss.   It just generally feels like the game introduced more mechanics, and then punishes you for trying to explore ways to use new cards and systems a bit too quickly. It felt like there was more room to find your stride and discover synergies you hadn't considered and leverage them in the first game. In this game, and I recognize I am not the best of players, I often find an incredible build in the desperate attempt to not die, and then never see the exact combination of cards again after not pulling it off or getting the card I hoped for in time. Obviously I can adapt and play the tried and true methods, but I liked finding crazy ways to win in the first game. Feels like straying off the beaten path at all just doesn't work nearly as often.   It just occurred to me that you can check the win rates, so here are my takes on characters.   Ironclad feels solid, but I don't love builds that are just "Block, Swing, Repeat." I know there is much more nuance than that (I reached Ascension 10 as IC first try 6 weeks ago) but it feels less engaging than other characters with really nitty gritty card interactions. Also absolutely dominates with 4 vulnerable builds in MP.  Silent has always been the darling of the game. She has three archetypes with incredible synergy and great patch cards to solve problems in builds. If you commit to one and adopt aspects of another, you would almost always win (beat A10 here as well a month ago). That said, I think the devs got tired of hearing how easy she was by comparison (Same with Necrobinder) and overcorrected with silly bosses. Silent is currently lowest of all the win rates on A10. Not sure why they felt the need to giver her a dirt nap, but I'm sure she gets enough love that she will be exhumed shortly.   Regent is my personal favorite in this game. Feels like an oddball amalgam of colorless card creation, stars, minions, or swords. Overlap between build types is harder to incorporate than the Silent, but he clicked in my head (I got A10 here too about a week ago, again on my first try.)  the Necrobinder feels like it fully redefines the game. It is easy to build something that can cruise to the end of act 3 once you get the hang of souls (kinda RIP due to Aeonglass though), doom, ethereal, and Osty. Much like the Silent, the overlap between the archetypes feels very forgiving, and taking damage is often optional. I like having new players stick to Necro until they feel confident in enemy patterns. I don't think changing that would be good. I am fine accepting that the Necrobinder is just easiest for most. (Had a bad chain of luck, but still won after 3 attempts on A10 a few days ago)  My big gripe is the Defect. Completing A10 with him for me just felt soo much more like random chance with him. There are just too many subtypes with limited payoffs and interactions. All the cool synergies seem locked behind rare cards that entirely disappear behind Ascension 9-10's rare card filtration. With Status cards, Lightning, Ice, Dark, 0 Cost, Glass, and Energy subsets, it just feels like there are too many subsets within the class that DON'T have near the amount of synergy as the other classes, and despite consistently ranking lowest in success for multiplayer and single player, the development team seems content leaving my little robot to his namesake. I love that guy, and he was my favorite in the first game. Devs, don't be afraid to make him more supportive in multiplayer. Wouldn't hurt to add ice functionality to zero cost, or a bit more interaction with glass (There are only 3 glass orb cards and their damage is lackluster compared to lightning), or a bit more staying power to the focus cards. I wouldn't even be opposed to removing glass orbs entirely to smoothen out the odds by a small margin of finding cards for the other builds.   If you loved the first game, I'm confident the devs will eventually get this game to the same standard and beyond. It just doesn't feel that way now. I'm leaving this because it finally occurred to me that I wasn't having fun anymore. I don't particularly mind losing. I would say that overall the game is quite good. It is fun to discover and the coop mode is a most welcome addition. However I can't bring myself to put a positive review yet due to several reasons.  First, I think the balancing of the game is fragile compared to the first title. A lot more monsters just output insane dps in a sustained manner which is make you more vulnerable to unlucky draws, instead of relying on gimmicks. Conversely, a lot of monsters are just complete punching bags. This creates a frustrating dynamics where a player can completely dunk on a whole act just to get obliterated in two turns in a random fight.  Also, some of the more cheesy strats and exploits that made the game easier were nerfed heavily. Personally, I find it unnecessary and a bit sad. Cheesy strats are fun and one cannot really do it by accident. This is a single player game with a coop mode without matchmaking, so its not as if using an exploit will accidentally ruin someone else's enjoyment of the game. In my opinion, it is okay to embrace the fact that some builds and archetypes are (too) strong if it allows for more variety.   Lastly, on a smaller note, I wish the Mega Crit would not hire mendacious consultants that have such a disastrous influence on every project they are involved in.  When the official release happens, if I am happier with the balancing and overall state of the game, I'll gladly change this review to be positive.

Imagine building a deck that moves through ~90% of the game with no issues (and even taking minimal damage in what would be difficult scenarios), but getting steam rolled due to RNG (such as facing multiple turns of drawing all attacks in the enemy's large damage turn into a turn with all blocks during the enemy's setup turn) or just outrageous enemies (Aeonglass lol). To the point of the Aeonglass, I seriously don't understand how The Doormaker (post rework) was removed due to hitting a "complexity ceiling". Instead, they replace the doormaker with a boss that allows minimal interaction and counter play against most characters. The boss effectively funnels you into needing to play as The Silent or Ironclad as these both have exhaust or discard outlets to remove wither cards. Doing large damage, punishing through even the most block-heavy decks,  and having the mechanic is absurd. All in all, the pace of the game is so jacked up right now that I'm surprised that the developer has not acted on some common sentiment between 95,000+ negative reviews. An absolute masterpiece in the roguelike genre, even in the early access state it currently is in, it may as well be complete.  Truly a worthy sequel to it's already incredible predecessor.  The addition of multiplayer was unexpected, but overwhelmingly welcome.  The characters in the game provide a vast array of different playstyles, one will certainly be of your liking.  (My personal favorites are Ironclad and Regent.)  The build variation for each character is magnificent, many of the cards in these builds bleed into other builds and allow you to create off-kilter ones that can lead to some truly memorable runs.    Slay the Spire 2 is a difficult game.  It requires you to keep track of a lot of variables, use foresight to navigate properly and make decisions accordingly.  You will lose a lot while learning to play this game and even as a veteran.  However, with each run you will learn something about what you did wrong, how to combat certain enemies, how to prepare for those enemies and what synergies will work best for what is ahead of you.  Be patient, be mindful and sometimes... just get lucky!  I believe many of the gripes people have about this game boil down to one or two things.  First of all, people that cannot stand losing:  THIS GAME IS NOT FOR YOU.  Secondly, the game IS in early access.  The devs have been changing much about the game since it's release, some changes make the game harder, others make it easier.  Overall, I think the devs have done an outstanding job listening to player feedback, while adding changes of their own that benefit the balance testing.  In it's current state, the game is well balanced (even if it wasn't I would still love it, the game is too fun.).  It's a wonderful experience every time I sit down to play.  Sure, sometimes it can be frustrating, but the gameplay is so addicting and the promise of wacky or overpowered builds is too tempting to resist.  A true masterpiece in my book, 10/10.

The vastly increased build variety, more dynamic character mechanics, and meaningful card synergies make every run feel fresh, while moving away from infinite combo strategies encourages more interactive and thoughtful deck construction.  Combat remains brutally challenging, especially at Ascension 10, demanding careful planning, resource management, and a deep understanding of enemy patterns. Each character offers significantly more diverse archetypes than before, with viable strategies that reward experimentation rather than funneling players toward a handful of dominant builds.  However, the increased difficulty occasionally crosses the line into frustration. Certain Act 2 elites and several Act 3 bosses can feel disproportionately punishing, often requiring very specific deck answers rather than rewarding flexible play. The reduced availability of energy-generating relics also makes many runs feel overly constrained, limiting deck potential and forcing more conservative drafting than expected.  Despite these balance concerns, Slay the Spire 2 is an outstanding sequel that deepens an already exceptional formula through greater strategic depth, richer character design, and endless replayability.[/b] Slay the Spire 2 is an excellent successor to the first game, improving on it in nearly every way: [list]     [*] refreshing new characters and archetypes     [*] cool animations now     [*] multiplayer mode as a first-class citizen, with some very fun multiplayer-exclusive cards     [*] better modding [/list]  It's not perfect, and the devs would be the first to admit there's still a lot of refinement needed. The first game went through almost 2 years of fine tuning in early access, which is absolutely what made it so polished and replayable. But there are many more people playing STS2 now than were playing STS1 in its early access period, and quite a few of them do not have the patience for a game whose balance is still evolving.  At time of writing, the most notable issue is the Aeonglass boss, which is much more difficult to beat on high ascensions than the others. Worse than just being difficult, though, it restricts your deckbuilding decisions throughout the run so tightly that it [i]makes the game less fun[/i]. I think the devs made a pretty big misstep with this one, but I have total confidence that they will figure out how to fix it, retaining the best parts of the difficulty without killing deck variety.

Trying out different card combinations and seeing a build come together is still incredibly satisfying. Even when a run falls apart, I usually end up thinking about what I could have done differently instead of blaming the game.  One of my favourite additions is co-op. Being able to play with a friend adds a completely new way to enjoy the game, and it’s been a lot of fun figuring out strategies together. It keeps the same tactical feel as the single-player game but makes those big wins and terrible mistakes even more memorable.  It also plays really well on the Steam Deck, which makes it perfect for more casual gaming. Being able to pick it up for a quick run while relaxing at home or take it with you for a trip, like a long flight, makes it a game that’s really easy to keep coming back to.  The new characters, cards and enemies give you plenty to experiment with, and the updated graphics are a nice touch without losing the style that made the original so good.  The only slight criticism I have is that the enemy scaling in multiplayer feels like it needs a bit more balancing. Slay the Spire 2 was my first deckbuilder. I picked it up on a friend's recommendation about three months ago, and I have to admit—right from the start, the five distinct characters, the sheer variety of interesting cards, the deckbuilding process, and the way you utilize and respond to different mechanics all blew me away. I'd heard about Slay the Spire's renowned number balancing and mechanical design long before I ever played, and when I finally did, it lived up to the hype. But after I started pushing high Ascension, I gradually began to feel the kinds of problems you'd expect from a game in Early Access. The most obvious one, to me, is the lack of synergy between different archetypes within a single character—and this is especially noticeable on The Regent and The Necrobinder. The Regent's Forge, Stars, and Colorless builds each have their own highlights, but once your deck reaches a reasonably complete state, cards from almost any other archetype basically become dead draws. Still, this issue isn't that severe—it doesn't really ruin the experience. I genuinely thought the developers would gradually work on improving these problems. That is, until the series of updates over the past two months completely changed my mind. They didn't set out to "make the game more balanced." They went full throttle in the direction of "make it harder for players to win." At first, the Doormaker rework—I thought that was a decent attempt. But they pushed the update while the mechanical design was still immature, and the subsequent Aeonglass addition was a devastating blow to the gameplay experience. Fortunately, as someone climbing Ascension 10, I don't even need to worry about the final boss, because the post-update Act 2 Elites are already enough to leave me with zero tools to respond. Every time I enter an Elite fight, I'm just gambling that I won't run into the one that hard-counters my deck on a mechanical level. Infested Prism, in particular—I genuinely don't understand it. It applies massive defensive pressure through high damage and special mechanics, and it has a huge HP pool and piles on Block, making it nearly impossible to burst down. So what exactly is the intended solution for this enemy? Am I just supposed to have godlike luck? And the recent co-op card update only made me realize that the devs are treating card numbers like a complete joke. This game—one that so many people had been looking forward to—is slowly killing itself before it's even officially born. Just two months of changes have been enough to turn every fun part of it into one miserable session of self-torture after another.  杀戮尖塔2是我玩的第一款卡牌游戏。我是在朋友的推荐下在三个月之前入坑的，我必须承认在刚刚接触这款游戏后，五个各有特色的角色、大量有趣的卡牌，还有构筑牌组的过程以及对各种机制的利用和应对都给了我很大的惊喜。早在游玩之前我就听闻杀戮尖塔优秀的数值平衡与机制设计，而当初它也没有辜负我的期待。 然而在开始攻略高进阶之后，我也逐渐感受到了塔2作为一款EA阶段的游戏所具有的问题。我认为最明显的一个问题是一个角色不同流派（机制）之间的联动问题，这在储君和召唤师身上体现的尤其明显。储君的铸剑、辉星、无色体系都有各自的亮点，然而当你的牌组初步发展到较为完整的阶段后，几乎所有其他流派的牌都好像变成了一种废牌。但是这个问题其实不算特别严重，并不影响游玩体验。 我原以为开发者会逐步尝试优化这些问题，直到这两个月来的一系列更新彻底改变了我的看法。 他们并没有着手于“让游戏更平衡”，而是完全朝着“让玩家更难赢”的方向努力。最初门扉缔造者被修改，我认为这是一次不错的尝试，但他们在机制设计不成熟的情况下直接进行了更新，而后续的永世沙漏更新更是对游玩体验毁灭性的打击。 幸运的是攻略a10的我根本不需要考虑最终boss，因为更新后的第二幕精英足以让我没有任何手段应对，每次进入精英战我都必须赌这次遇到的不是在机制上**完全**克制我的那个精英。特别是感染棱柱，我非常不理解。通过很高的伤害和特殊机制增加你的防御压力，同时还拥有大量血量和格挡导致难以被快速杀死，那么这个怪的解法思路究竟是什么？完全依靠我有一个逆天的运气吗？ 而最近的多人牌更新更是让我意识到制作组完全把卡面的数值当成儿戏。 这个无数人期待的游戏还没正式诞生就正在逐渐自杀，仅仅两个月的调整足以让其有趣的部分全部变成一场又一场糟糕的自我折磨。

TLDR: Slay the Spire 2 is exactly what a Slay the Spire 1 fan would want in a sequel: it keeps the spirit of the original while making it both more challenging and more rewarding.   Slay the Spire (StS) was foundational to the now massive Deckbuilding-Roguelike genre and few games have come close to competing (looking at you Balatro). So when they released Slay the Spire 2 (StS2) I was skeptical. StS still held my heart for the feel of Deckbuilding Roguelikes and so many have failed to iterate in a way that wouldn't fade with novelty. And then I played my first run. I had heard from friends who were Hollow Knight fans how amazing Silksong was to play even with all the hype and expectations. With StS2, I get it personally now. As someone who generally played in the low to to mid 10s ascensions in StS, StS2 rocked my world. Act 1 was much more of a threat even at base difficulty.  The enemies were more complex with more numbers and multi-hits. These were foes you couldn't just stall out and win without a scratch.  But to combat this, our favorite characters (sorry Watcher) came back stronger than ever. Ironclads had better block cards and more ruthless attacks.  Silent can throw more knives, the poison doubling is a power happens every turn, and still can tank powerful boss attacks to the face. Defect gets more lighting channeling, actual darkness support, mixed orb builds are entirely viable, power builds are even more powerful and claw is still law. These characters feel like they have faced the original spire over and over again and came back with its shattered heart. The new characters are nothing to snub at either. Regent has a secondary mana resource that actually feels fun to use and can make the biggest sword. Necrobinder has a single summon but actually interacts well with it and has other fun and unique mechanics with doom, etherial, and souls. And to top it all off, the colorless cards are actually good across the spectrum. Sure, it'll take a number of runs to unlock everything, but it is well worth it. Yes, your average run is more likely to fail and is harder, but the victory is all the more sweet. I would not recommend this to someone who didn't love the first game, but if you did, you are in for a treat. As for the early access part, it is somewhat misleading. It often signifies a lack of content or polish; that you would be able to tell that something is missing. StS2 isn't like that. The early access is mostly for some balancing quirks and only occasional hard corrections. The game in its current state feels like a finished cake but they haven't completely decided which candles to put on it.

If you enjoy heroin but not so much track marks in your arm (hello fellow tryptophobics) then the sequel to Heroin 2.0 might very well be your thing.  Looking at Slay the Spire 1, it's easy to feel a bit catfished that the incredibly-balanced, just-challenging-enough, and time-vampiring original was just a bit fugly, but you're in luck.  Megacrit takes the formula of the original and does the proverbial *removes glasses, revealing that, really it was beautiful all along* treatment, giving STS2's art direction and non-gameplay systems a slick new coat of paint, with brighter colours, more cartoonish proportions, and new and interesting enemies and lore. (the Phrog Parasite can get ♥♥♥♥♥♥ though).  You also don't need to climb the titular Spire alone, with 2 new characters (the GIGACHAD Regent; and Osty the reanimated hand, ft. his sidekick The Necrobinder) and the welcome addition (addiction?) of multiplayer introducing a new mechanical depth, all linked to deeper lore revealed through the new Epochs system.  I've had a great time with friends unlocking powerful relics, useful equipment and interesting lore, playtime floors climbed soaring as we collectively slide further down the slopes Mega Crit have so kindly polished for us.  It's not without it's friction points though.  For me, the new art direction lose some of the grungy, quirky charm that made the original Slay the Spire, while fantastical, feel so grounded.  Multiplayer as it stands also needs serious improvement. Like any rogue like worth its 1 of 3-salt-options, Slay the Spire 2 is challenging, but fully beatable with the right preparation and strategy.  The main problem with multiplayer is that beyond drawing out your plan (or caricatures of your tardy mate) on your shared map, there's no visibility of your teammates capabilities, so playing to each others strengths is challenging. Admittedly, this is easily solved through a Discord call, but it's cool to imagine how this could be streamlined by the game itself, knowing when a block potion or fire bomb could come in clutch.  Another issue is that difficulty hits a massive, spongy wall when you're playing 2-player, and you don't have enough abilities or damage between you to adequately respond, sending you back to Neow, and leaving you sopping wet at square one. 3- and 4-player parties have the opposite problem, synergising SO well you cut through like a hot knife through... well... sponge.  These are nitpicks, not uncommon for addicts (the technical term is formication), and much like heroin it's still a blast alone or in multiplayer.  Every new designer drug needs to go through at least some testing before it hits the streets, and I am a very willing guinea pig. Although only a few months out in early access, by the time Heroin 3.0 fully releases, I'll have months worth of play time logged.  ~Rich Reviews

Most of the changes to the game these past few months have felt like the devs are actively trying to increase the amount of frustration there is in any given run, and the best way to deal with most mechanics is ignore them and end the encounter in less than 4 turns. Every enemy on every floor feels like a differently flavoured damage race, instead of an active interplay between the enemy and your deck.  Worse yet, a lot of the fights that feel like they would reward a more consistent deck end up either getting changed in the beta branch (e.g. Skulking Colony) or have some sort of scaling mechanic in a fight where you're asked to deal with 20+ damage per turn regularly (e.g. Phantasmal Killer). Slay 2 is quite a fast paced game on average (at least compared to its predecessor), but it doesn't feel like an organic change of pace. Rather, it's because if the player doesn't have a fast enough deck, they just get crushed.  Character decks feel very interesting, and synergies feel satisfying, but the fun I derive from actually playing a fight out gets sapped by numerous mechanics that feel overly punishing, especially to certain characters and archetypes (e.g. Vantom, Hunter Killer, Entomancer, new Infested Prism, 2 Chompers, Aeonglass, etc.). Further, because enemies are overly punishing to slower decks, the player is heavily incentivised to have a very slim deck for consistency, which means less opportunity to take more cards for fun and branch out to try new cards.  This is on top of the devs nerfing the ability of the player to draw cards basically every time they make a change. Infinites were a problem that feel like they got addressed pretty quickly, and rightly so, but now it just feels like it's intended design to just regularly dead draw if the size of the player's deck is any more than 20 cards. More enemies have debilitating punishes to playing certain cards, many enemies regularly status your deck, and all of them punish you for not actively spending resources on them.  Solutions to encounters feel much more one-dimensional than in Slay 1. Hunter Killer's a great example--if you don't have a Hulk Smash card or consistent debuff cycling, it's incredibly difficult to make progress on it. Oftentime even having a power card that increases your Strength and Dex doesn't feel enough.   This is all to say that many encounters in Slay 2 range from difficult to simply unfun to interact with. Combined with the overall increased power in Event nodes, most of my runs have boiled down to avoiding fighting after Act 1 as much as possible, and fighting only 2~3 elites per run. Hallways are significantly more punishing than they are in Slay 1, card rewards after Act 1 feel much less valuable, and gold ironically feels less valuable because you need so much more of it to have a good shop.  Relics on average feels much, much less satisfying to obtain and play with than Slay 1. Many strong relics in Slay 1 that have come back have bumped up a rarity (Nunchaku, Pen Nib, Art of War, Kunai/Shuriken, Meat on the Bone, Mummified Hand, etc.). The majority of new relics just don't feel like they've bridged the power gap either (Book of Five Rings, Festive Popper, Lucky Fysh, Beating Remnant, Tuning Fork, Sparkling Rouge, Reptile Trinket, etc.). Along with the fact that card rewards in general feel less satisfying as the player skips the vast majority of them on successful runs, it's often good practice to just avoid Elites altogether, as they're inconsistent power spikes at best for the amount of resources spent to fight them. What felt like the most engaging part of runs in Slay 1 became a point of avoidance, and since the launch of Early Access, the quality of the relic pool has only felt worse (Permafrost an Uncommon relic now?).  I understand that this is an Early Access game and that all of this can change. And within the first month, it definitely looked that way, as a lot of the game was changing quite quickly. However, now that updates have slowed down, and the direction of the game seems to be more set in stone, I can't recommend sticking with this game until further notice. Slay 2 had a wonderful honeymoon period (and honestly still does whenever I boot up multiplayer with friends), but the singleplayer experience feels to be falling more and more from the golden standard that Slay 1 set.     This was really just a Slay the Spire 1 recommendation in disguise. The more I play Slay 2, the more I crave Slay 1 instead. After 1500+ hours in it (Steam + mobile), I still love spamming runs in that game and trying to improve my 40% winrate on Silent A20H, but I feel no such motivation to grind to improve in Slay 2, especially when I feel like the game is degrading in quality.

An exceptional follow-up to one of the all time greats of roguelikes. Slay the Spire 2 is an extremely simple gameplay loop with excellent room for exploration and replayability. 150 hours in and I'm in no rush to stop playing. For all its simplicity, every decision is immensely impactful, all but the most unlucky runs have a possible solution to get you to victory, and each character has multiple distinct strategies that can all feel very powerful. I think I'm starting to reach my limit on replays unless more content gets added or significant changes are made, but I consider it a very good sign for an early access game that my biggest complaint is wanting more.

Luckily this is still in early access. In short this game is great with lots of content and really satisfying builds and monsters. There are tons of mystery rooms and events along with unique creatures (similar to the first) and fun new player characters (Necro binder and Regent) along with some funny interactions. I would recommend this game to anyone who likes deck building rogue like games.  The bad... I already got my moneys worth and I'm very excited to see the complete 1.0 version but as it stands there are some issues I noticed. This game does lack some agency for the players to really do a build. similar to last game a lot of it comes down to luck  but when you get REALLY lucky you get a super fun run through but this game feels like you just play what the RNG gives you and you get much less control over your play through. for example in SLS1 if you wanted to do a tank build you may not get "the best relic" but you would get a card upgrade you didn't expect which allows you to do the same with a new spin. In this game most card upgrades are lack luster (+2 damage or defend) which makes smithing feel like a waste of time aside from some power cards. Simultaneously you can get multiplayer cards but the regent, defect, and necrobinder have such different playstyles that I avoid them if I'm playing a certain character or in general (gaining focus as the iron clad or forging as the silent doesn't pay much dividends, but maybe im just bad at the game).   Also Whoever is in charge of the daily runs should really spice it up. some are fun but the last few have basically been "here are 35 random cards and you take damage whenever you block" lol. I love this game for the deck building, relic, and blessing combos you can find which gives each playthrough a fun twist. But when i get a completely random deck with no cohesion than its less of a fun playthrough and more tedious culling of cards and trying to make the 3 cards you can use last until you remove enough cards and HOPEFULLY pull something out of a card reward. Again if the card upgrades were improved this could fix some things instead of giving a little more attack or deend (reduce the cost or add retain instead)  Lastly I think the game needs some balancing when it comes to some blessings and cards. there are a few rooms and blessings that completely ruin a run. One being "if you add a card to your deck, add two extra" well when this happens you either never add another card unless its the exact fit for your deck or you get screwed over because you enter a "?" room and are forced to take a card or curse. This is just one example but there were a few that have a similar destructive effect.  All in all i still love the game and I'm excited for you all to continue to improve it. I am sure balancing all the  new stuff is not easy but pat yourselves on the back for another great game!

I played a ton of slay 1 and was wondering how they would follow up the quintessential deck builder roguelike. Basically, in this sequel you get a lot more variety and options for a run, for enemies who are also a lot more diverse and unique as you follow the same gameplay pattern of the first. Being able to find synergies out of card rewards on the spot becomes much more important, as you think how to cover for the number of alternatives for upcoming fights.  This game is significatively harder than the original, though. The fact there's considerably more mechanics means after every card reward you must be able to plan ahead and check where your build is heading, along with which cards you should or should not pick up after you manage to scrap together a bunch of coherent, synergistic cards and relics. I rarely skipped card rewards in the original, now you are often skipping as soon as act 2. On the other hand, more options means there is also considerably more ways to completely break the game when everything in your deck just clicks, and you simply manage to find all the synergies you need. At the same time, infinite combos are much harder to pull off than slay 1, where most characters could do it with few cards.  At the end of the day, this is an extremely creative and high quality sequel to the genre-defining original, where you are following almost the exact same gameply loop the original established, with ample more options and mechanics that fit right in, and it's up to you to figure them all out, which is why you should try this game. Review fluctuation is usually in response to minor balance patches to specific cards, which doesn't change this excellent game for the most part. I hope most reviews were just a little more grateful about how good this game really is at the end of the day...

[h3] As far as I can tell, this game is getting bombarded with unfair negative reviews from people suffering from a terrible affliction known as "Skill Issue." I'd like to leave a genuine review in spite of these poor unfortunate souls so readers can actually get a good idea of what they're buying. [/h3]  For context, I never played Slay the Spire 1, though I watched plenty of people play it. It always seemed like a cool concept to me, but I mostly play co-op games, so it wasn't something I expected to get invested in. When I heard Slay the Spire 2 had multiplayer, I was immediately interested. A friend gifted it to me, and we jumped right in.  After about 40 hours, I can confidently say this is a great game for what it is in [u]Early Access.[/u]  Having an RNG-based deckbuilder is something of a double-edged sword. Card games are already inherently random—you build your deck yourself, but once it's shuffled, you can't control what you draw (without cheating, of course). Adding another layer of RNG by having to build your deck from random rewards means every run becomes a game of "LET IT RIDE" with special relics or events that alter your deck flow.  [b]That's both good and bad.[/b]  On one hand, it encourages me to experiment with all sorts of different builds. On the other, I may only get to play my favorite build once every several runs because the game simply refuses to give me the cards I'm looking for.  [u]For example:[/u] > I play a lot of the Necrobinder. > I really enjoy the Doom archetype. > One run might hand me every Doom card I could possibly want, letting me build an almost perfect deck. > The next run might offer nothing but Soul or Otsy cards, with virtually no Doom support at all, forcing me into a build I don't really enjoy.  Once you've experienced all of a character's archetypes, you start recognizing pretty early whether a run is headed toward something you'll love or something you'd rather abandon because it simply isn't fun for you. I'm honestly not sure whether that adds to the replayability or takes away from it.  I also come from years of playing Yu-Gi-Oh! (back in the older days), where I never really minded running larger decks. I understand that the most optimal way to play most deckbuilders is to thin your deck until you consistently draw your strongest combos or assemble an infinite.  Personally, though, I don't really care for the "my deck is now eight cards and I instantly win every fight" style of gameplay.  Yes, discovering an overpowered combo is fun...  [i]...the first time.[/i]  But getting angry at the developers because they nerfed infinite loops seems a bit silly when those strategies completely undermine what Slay the Spire is trying to be. The point is adapting to what you're given, improvising with the cards you find, and making the best of each run—not assembling the exact same nuclear deck every single time.  If that's what you enjoy, more power to you. Just respect the developers if they don't want those strategies to be trivially easy to force every run. As far as I'm concerned, stumbling into an infinite should be a rare, exciting dopamine hit—not the expectation.  So far, I really haven't had any major complaints... except that I absolutely hate the Knowledge Demon, but I'm not about to leave a [strike]childish[/strike] negative review because one enemy bullied me.  My only real criticism is that some multiplayer enemies seem to have far too much health. Aeonglass, in particular, feels absurdly tanky considering what its passive does. My friend and I consistently struggle to even get it below half health, and on a good run we might push it to around 25% before Withering eventually wears us down. That's also the case with a lot of Elites, whereas in a solo run I always opt to grab the Stone Sword for killing 5 Elites.. I absolutely avoid it at all costs in multiplayer since those enemies REALLY slap hard due to the scaling.  I also think it'd be nice if there were some way to gently influence a character's build path. For example, if I'm playing Necrobinder and really want to pursue Doom, maybe I could mark it as a preferred archetype before the run. It shouldn't guarantee Doom cards, but perhaps it could slightly increase the odds of seeing them. Outside of expanding the existing characters or adding entirely new ones, that's probably my biggest wishlist item.  I'd also love to see some additional game modes. A Turbo Mode, for example, where a run is roughly half as long. Maybe you start with extra Energy, stronger cards, and more relics, but the enemies scale up dramatically to match. A normal hour-long run becoming a frantic 30-minute sprint could be a lot of fun.  And, of course...  [b] Please give us cosmetics. [/b]  I desperately want to put a tiny hat on Otsy.  ...Or Byrdpip, my beloved (also make him bigger when I upgrade the card or multiply him when I dupe it pretty please with a History Course ontop).  Overall, I absolutely recommend this game. If you enjoy roguelite deckbuilders and PvE co-op experiences, there's a lot to love in this'n. I sincerely hope the developers continue expanding it with more cards, characters, relics, events, and game modes.  Keep it up, y'all. You're doing a great job. :)  [h1]TL;DR 8/10 Absolutely a great title for some deckbuilding PvE fun with your friends, hope the devs keep up the great work[/h1]

If you are a casual fan of slay the spire or other roguelike deckbuilders, get this game. It's a great upgrade from the original that preserves the original's charm while building upon it with interesting changes, like ancients replacing boss chests, epochs revealing lore and new unlocks, and fun new events. If you enjoyed the first game, you'll probably enjoy this game too.  That being said, if you're a more extreme fan who enjoyed the unique difficulty of the first game, this game IS NOT FOR YOU. It's still in its early stages, so it's forgivable, but the balancing is atrocious at times. It's definitely a step down from the original. Some bosses are absolutely incomparable to one another. You're telling me the dumbass mordekaiser crab is supposed to be on the same level as the insatiable? In what universe? The crab stuns itself and hits high damage once every like 4 turns. The insatiable has upwards of 300 health, hits 30 damage every turn AND gives itself strength, while forcing you to waste energy on useless cards or you die instantly. It's ridiculous. Normal enemy combats aren't balanced either. If you play on ascension, you better hope and pray you get the underdocks instead of the overgrowth so you can avoid the dreaded flyconid + snapping jaxfruit encounter. It doesn't make sense that a supportive enemy should be able to apply multiple turn lasting debuffs that make it impossible to block anything, then attack for 20 damage with ANOTHER ENEMY in the encounter that also attacks each turn. Low hp in the hive? Hope you don't run into the hunter killer and his 20 dmg a turn with one of the most debilitating debuffs in the game or the 4 cockroach encounter that hits for 18 each turn and takes minimum of 3 hits to kill each one so you can't oneshot them. There's no way to play around these because they randomly exist in normal enemy combats instead of elite combats. The ascension modifiers feel mostly fine. I never beat all of them in the first game, but in this game they feel fine up until the last one. Having to fight two act 3 bosses in a row with no heal or shop or anything is ridiculous with how strong the act 3 bosses are in this game. The test subject lizard thing is crazy. I always found the awakened one to be the strongest act 3 boss in the first game so I don't really understand why it had to be buffed and transformed in this game. Having to fight it on top of another boss can be soul crushing.  In short, the game is wonderful for fans of deckbuilders or just the original slay the spire. Game is fun with awesome new additions and a neatly improved art style. Can be frustrating for more dedicated fans who enjoy playing the ascensions, it might be better to wait until the game is better balanced as it gets further into its lifetime.  also RIP heavy blade and doormaker lol
