Slay the Spire 2 improves on the first game while significantly upping the difficulty. Expect for it to take a while to beat the game, but that doesn't mean it's boring along the way. Like many other roguelikes, you get the satisfaction of progressing further and further on each run as you slowly unlock more pieces you can encounter next time.   Being able to play co-op is probably the biggest selling point of this sequel compared to the first one, and the new characters are a nice complement to that. It feels like the Regent and Necrobinder were designed to support certain mechanics in the original three character's repertoires (i.e. Necrobinder's doom pairs very well with Silent's poison).   This game is also significantly harder. Depending on how you like to play, that either makes this game more or less appealing than the first one. For me, I like having the option to play the first one for a more casual experience vs. the second one for more of a challenge.  My main complaint is that sometimes the Act 3 bosses feel out-of-pace with the difficulty of the rest of the run. You can be steamrolling the whole time, and then the Act 3 boss can just stop your run like a brick wall. That can be a little bit demoralizing when it happens on your 1 hour+ co-op run multiple times. But that is sort of just the nature of these roguelike, dungeon-clear games.

I debated for a while whether I should write this review for the game as it is, or as I believe it will be once it leaves early access. And I decided that I would write a review for the game as it is today, even if it changes in three months, because trying to predict the future never pans out.  I enjoy the game and I think it's good, but there are still a lot of rough edges. Enemy identity is fuzzier than in the previous game because almost all enemies follow the same set of mechanics. Spike damage to test your defenses, a turn for a debuff or card dilution, and strength growth in cycles. There are exceptions and cool ideas especially in act 2, like an enemy that will permanently steal cards, but in general fights feel more same-y. While it does mean the difficulty is less spiky (resulting in more consistent wins), it also makes most battles pretty forgettable because most of them play out the same. Also, once you realize that each character is built around a specific mechanic almost unique to that character, even decks that supposedly would have very different archetypes end up using 70% of the same cards and the same overall strategies. I got bored of the game well before I hit the 100-hour mark but I couldn't articulate why until recently.   Now that all sounds quite bad, but I do still recommend it because the basic deckbuilding fun of the first game is still here, the multiplayer is actually very nicely handled, and given the success of the first game we can assume the devs know what they're doing and the rough edges will probably be patched out.

Amending my review to a thumbs up because, while I mostly still agree with my review below, I think I had a misunderstanding of how beatable Act 3 bosses actually are. Leaving my initial thoughts for the dev's consideration, but I don't see it as negative enough to give this otherwise fantastic game a thumbs down.  Original Review:  This game has incredible potential, enough to be an all-time favorite for me. However, its current state is significantly marred by Act 3's boss fights, which you will see echoed across other negative reviews and for good reason. The bosses are overly restrictive and feel fundamentally unbalanced.  The difficulty of the bosses feel... mostly fine. The problem exists in their design. The mechanics currently force players to abandon fun or optimized deck-building from Acts 1 and 2 simply to survive one specific boss fight. This creates a whiplash effect. I build up anticipation, only for the effort to feel useless if the final act dictates such narrow solutions.  The difficulty curve is inconsistent. I can easily clear Act 3's intermediate floors, but the final boss feels disproportionately designed, making even a victory feel unearned and tedious.  While the core gameplay loop up through Act 2 is phenomenal, this single bottleneck severely degrades the experience for me. I'm changing my previous positive review to negative in hopes the devs will notice the shared sentiment from the player base and find a resolution without compromising difficulty. It’s a shame because the game has so much good content and is positioned to be a phenomenal follow-up to the first game. Here's to hoping!

I am shocked.   I don't think I'd ever be writing a review about this game in this way but my few (135 hours at the time of writing this post) I would genuinely like a change to happen.   Something doesn't feel right about going through run after run after run from going from completing entire runs to feeling like I'm getting beaten over the head time and time again with run after run that feels like the game hates me. Sure I understand skill issue can be a thing but why on Act 1 encounter 4 for a STANDARD ENEMY I am taking 20 damage a turn with a debuff only allowing my cards to block for 3?   Why does it feel like the cards I used to play with on silent with the poison builds suddenly don't feel as fun any more given how I have to try and build?  Why is it that even though I try to plan for the current room I'm in, I end up getting my entire deck destroyed because the new final boss has an unremovable, non-ethereal, Status card that you can't remove by standard card removal from most builds and there's no planning to end up to be able to succeed with major issues.  All the infinite loops that would make the game enjoyable have been nerfed into the ground that you could use to combat this were taken away while difficulty curve was increased MASSIVELY thus making the game just a struggle to the point where I don't feel like I'm enjoying my time spent in the game anymore.   "Get good"  Sure, I've played quite a bit of Slay the Spire 1 and 2 and I'd like to argue that even slay the spire 1 wasn't this bad when playing with builds. You could make things happen in standard that were fun and exiting to play but I feel this version of the game in its current state just doesn't feel good for me. and noticing the vast majority of non English language reviews speaking their minds to the same belief that I am presenting here... There's probably a major issue that isn't fully being discussed.   "I'm having fun I don't see what your issue is."  That's great! I love slay the spire! However, I feel like I am losing alot of fun element of the game by being unable to feel like at any point I am getting to a point where I am 'strong' in the game. In slay the spire 1? I could feel strong and it was enjoyable. In the EARLY release of Slay 2? I could feel strong absolutely! However in the current state? I feel like I'm getting beaten down harder and harder on earlier and earlier parts of the game to the point where I'm just not entering a run like "Okay I can get this going, I got this!" I think in the mentality now of "I hope it's not x thing because that would Kill my run before it even starts" - I find myself just looking at an Act board and seeing the boss and restarting a run more frequently. - I find myself getting a wrong first card for my first run and just deciding the entire run is botched because I'll never make it though the random Act 1 Encounter 4 18 damage per turn standard enemy that gives a 2x defense down debuff.  Which by the way, this encounter with that room, that's more damage than the Statue swinging for 17 a turn on turn 4 onward. this was turn 2.   I used to just play this game and enjoy my time trying out a build and seeing how far I go. "Maybe I got this." as a thought for most encounters and enjoying pushing myself to try and play better.  Now I'm just exhausted and unable to enjoy playing my favorite characters like Silent because the builds I enjoyed are gone and no longer as fun as they used to be and I shouldn't feel that way on any character. Good game experience and enjoyment shouldn't feel like you're getting punched in the face and laughed at because you wanted to casually enjoy a game and progress.   I would like the game to have it's fun casual mode for just having some fun with friends making silly builds that can be fun or stupid and still work. Now it's just the most intensive "I need the most meta perfect build or I'm dead" seeming game that I am enjoying it less and stressing more over even making a slight misstep. If you mess up it's over just give up and start again. Quit. Just quit. That is how the game feels. Not "lets make it work even though the world sucks and we are given the worst times to get through it and just have hope" no just "Give up. try again."   That's not the slay the spire that I remember and enjoyed and loved. This just feels like the developer is angry with their community.   Either way I still love slay the spire as a concept. Hopefully with it being Early access things will change but in its current state I cannot recommend it for new players looking to get into the slay the spire style game. Hopefully sooner than later thins will change.

Less stacks of artifact and less health gain on enemies would make a world of difference. 4 player - Very fun and can be very broken.  3 player - Solid. Slightly easier than single player. Allows a newer/weaker player get carried a little bit.    Characters and design  IronClad - Full offense is the strat. Sometimes defense works out but its rare.  Silent- Very solid all rounder but does get countered pretty hard by the new Aeonglass boss. This character could really use a bludgeon-esque card to build around.   Defect - You want to play his gimmick (orbs) but generally a beat down deck will do better as orb cards can get droughts Necrobinder - THE defensive character. The allotment of cards the necro has is fantastic and legitimately has multiple angles archetypes.  Argent - Solid character. Builds really heavily support kingly or star builds. Making a heavy forge deck really feels like a bait.   Overall for EA this is fantastic. The are still a dozen or two cards that could use some tweaks and the hard pool fights could use some balancing tweaks. Rewards from normal fights may need some improvements as events are VERY strong.

I unfortunately can't recommend the game in it's current EA form. But hey, it's EA, and they have plenty of time to work out the balance. Stability wise, the game is great in both single and multiplayer forms. Upgraded art styles from the first game is very nice, and more seem-less animations help it look even better. It's a lot more pretty. Unfortunately, as a RL, the replayability mileage may vary.   The deck building can be varied and awful. The game wants you to be working with what you get, but not all base decks work well with each strategy, and there are not enough removal options even seeking out ? and shops to get a deck optimized.   I am a good deck builder, and have played many Deck building games. I'm not the best player, but I can build a coherent deck by knowing what I need more of, reducing what i don't, and streamlining the process. I don't take a card every time I can, especially if it hurts my strategy.  The current deck variety is a bit stagnant. After over a dozen runs I'm fairly certain I know what strategies work with which characters at this point. I'm hoping they also add more possible End Bosses to the first and second zones, to help make this even better.  Elite bosses are not worth the effort. Most of the time they simply drain your resources or end your run. I literally just plan my routes to avoid them as much as possible. Not good to have a thing in your game I never want to participate in.   Final bosses (stage 3) are also a balance nightmare. I have 17 runs, all losses, and while I have come close, if you get a certain boss, it's better to just to restart than waste your time as the runs can go for hours, especially in multiplayer. It is not a quick, or smooth process to play together as priorty of play doesn't exist. Either it's the entire group of player's turns or it's the enemy. If it's the players, you better be able to discuss your plan, and not take a long time or you will never get through the whole thing. The balance of the game is very problematic, and I suggest you take that into account. I'm beginning to lose interest as I can't seem to beat any of the 3 stage bosses.  Overall it's fun, its not the worst, and in time it could be even better with a few more interesting balance passes.

I'm having so much fun with this game  Multiplayer is excellent, maybe towards the easier side with 3+ players with the insane vuln or doom scaling and multiplayer debuffs, but that's what makes it fun as hell. Multiplayer allows for easy synergies and shreading apart the harder bosses too, while single player gets surprisingly tricky on A9-10. I see a lot of criticism towards the higher ascencions on single player but I personally appreciate it. I dont expect to win every round and it forces me to try strategies and card synergies I dont usually go for. It's a deckbuilder rougelike so it is expected that rng has increasing importance in higher difficulties. What sets this game apart from the first one is how many different viable strategies each character has, Even within those there are opportunities to branch out. Maybe you get an early rare card to build around or a relic that completely changes how your deck functions, You are forced to adapt and make a deck that can counter a variety of enemy types. If you are the kind of player that becomes frustrated when their perfect build gets countered repeatedly, the game can become frustrating at higher ascencions, but I personally appreciate it. I think the devs are going in a good direction by experimenting with mechanics that counter certain types of decks. As fun as infinites are, i enjoy other strategies being viable. Balancing takes trial and error, let's please be nice to the devs <3  People have such different expectations and tastes that it's very difficult to cater to everyone,  I definitely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys having an easy way to kill off an hour or two of time while listening to a podcast or music. Excellent time killer, just like sts 1 and nothing is forcing you to play higher ascensions if you dont like losing, it is completely valid to enjoy the game at its base difficulties.

Let me premise this by saying that: - I don't like deck builders, so I do not usually play them; - I'm very picky about roguelikes; - I wasn't even going to buy let alone play the game.  That being said, this review is mostly to show support to the devs and balance out the absolute madness that's been going on with the negative reviews.  I like this game. Despite being absolutely terrible at strategies and building my own decks (there is a reason I don't play these kinds of games, oops), StS2 has been a very good experience and a change of pace. The art is gorgeous, the mechanics are clear and simple and you can always make use of a character's unique kit without adding obnoxious amounts of complexity. Ascension levels are balanced to be difficult and give a challenge without actually trying to punish you for wanting higher difficulties. I reached A10, in coop sure, but I did and that's something I've never tried to do but for a few, selected games. That alone is an achievement in my book.  The ability to draw on the map has to be one of the best features for the cooperative games. It's simple, yet it works very well because now if I'm afk I get to come back to the most unhinged doodles on the page and a good laugh.  Not only that, there is A LOT of content to be played, let alone reveal with each Epoch. So really, I only see pros about this.  The game is in early access, but it still feels very polished and less buggy than any 80-bucks AAA game on launch, so this alone should warrant a kinder approach to feedback.  TLDR; the game is worth the full price and the time spent playing it.

My recommendation depends on whether you intend to play at the base difficulty of Ascension 0 or believe the game should typically be played at a higher ascension. If you expect the normal difficulty to be A0, then I would likely recommend Slay the Spire 2.   I believe the highest ascension to be the expected difficulty and in that case the developers have created a frustratingly unbalanced game. A game where even the choices made, such as the nodes chosen can be totally beyond your control. They also continue one of the worst elements of the first game, random events including both a regular enemy encounter or a shop. The game is full of RNG already, it is totally detrimental to force players into base encounters they chose to avoid. When a player avoids a shop because they have little gold only to be forced into a shop is just another lazy punishment.  Another holdover they rely upon for Ascensions is crippling the player to make the game more difficult. This is just an additional lazy choice that doesn't require the developers to introduce any new elements to the game. They just reduce the options at your disposal instead of adding something new to the game.  To start, I do not consider the "Early Access" tag for a game that has been in development for over 5 years. I know they changed the engine for the game part way through, but this isn't an excuse to release a version that there is no way these developers played through on A10 and imagined it was in any way balanced. I truly wonder if they had members of all the teams play through the game and offer any criticism for the difficulties. This is extremely relevant for A9 when every enemy just does more damage and simply chips you down until you end in an unwinnable situation due to the awful RNG.  The reliance on enemies constantly buffing themselves and neutering you is disappointingly lazy. Although it is difficult to desire more interesting mechanics due to the developers inability to create a unique and balanced enemy ability. Bosses such as Vantom introduce a frustrating mechanic from slippery, which is an incredible defense while allowing them to decimate you on certain turns. This is most obvious with a boss such as the Doormaker that they simply removed from the game due to their inability to balance an interesting idea.  Their inability to balance the game is even more odd since there are almost no new aspects to the game. They tweaked 3 of the old characters, but aside from the Defect they do not appear to have any new elements to their character. The Regent is the worst of the new additions mainly due to an entire resource they must produce in order to play certain cards. This is exacerbated when other characters have an event or other opportunity  to add a Regent card to their deck and must consider the fact that they probably can't even produce the Star resource to play one of their cards.  The most disappointing part of the game is the lack of many fundamentally new aspects. Aside from 2 of the 5 characters being new and the rare opportunity to enhance a card (i.e. something Monster Train already introduced in its first game) there is nothing particularly surprising in this sequel. The change from boss relics to the Ancient system is one more awful introduction of RNG. There are 2 Ancients I almost never wish to see, Tezcatara and Vakuu. These two are at best mediocre for 90% of runs and often simply useless. To make Act 2 even worse, Pael is also a coin flip if you are offered anything that truly aids your run. The new mechanic for boss rewards should never end in a deflating experience where you know you will just be limping into your next encounters.

I don't review games still in early access, as if you're buying a game with the understand it isn't finished you've done so to support the creator or because you're impatient. But seeing the flood of negative reviews left by tourists and people unable to comprehend that balance changes will happen has pushed me to at least try to curb the negativity.  This is a good game. If you are picking this game up as your first roguelike deckbuilder then I recommend it- it's forgiving at the early ascensions (difficulties), there's variety with character identity and within each character's card and build selection, and it provides a fun challenge once you've climbed higher. Several friends I have picked it up as their first introduction to the genre and they love it.    If you're returning from STS then I still consider it a better game at its roots (and I have 100'd STS on mobile). That's partially because it's still being balanced- there are cards and relics in the first game so laughably bad you just ignore them, including entire build philosophies that don't function. Each character has more builds they can go through, and the cards overlap easier so you're not tunnel visioned on specific picks. I put a lot of emphasis on variety in roguelikes, and in STS you would often be looking for the same broken combos every run. This game has more variety by far. I'd also say it's a LITTLE easier on average, but that might be because the end boss isn't done (and STS is easy if you're not fighting the heart).  Don't be discouraged by the flux of negative reviews. The game is being balanced, there will be periods it's harder or easier as the dev team works to correct playstyles or enemies that are too strong or weak. The game is in early access, they have a beta branch enabled for playtesting, and things will change.   Good game so far, 8/10, will keep playing.

This review is based on playing mostly on A10 difficulty but it's general enough - I hope the developers can read this and at least give it a think. I was going to leave a negative review amid recent updates, specifically the balancing on Aeonglass and the second level elite, but I think a negative review it's not fair to the game overall and the honest opinion is that I would still recommend this game to people if they enough a roguelite deckbuilder game. But devs, please read my below thoughts on balancing and game contents.  The game is in early access and I think most players general expectation is that there will be more contents coming, maybe not week after week but at least there should be a stable stream of content (new cards, mechanics, enemies, maps, even characters?). It's worth noting that adding new content will inevitably change the game dynamic, which could mean a previously weak card can now become a strong pick against certain enemy, or a new card enables more synergy with a pre-existing weak card, making it stronger overall. Given these potential interactions, any balancing efforts prior to new content seems pointless and becomes especially irratating when it seems like it's purely buffing enemies and nerfing players - note that I don't think this is true objectively, but I don't think Doormaker would give you a bad review if it got nerfed (or deleted), but real player would (point being, balancing is important but keeping your players happy is also important, there is a "balance" in that as well).  What I would recommend the devs to do is to really ramp up new contents in their regular updates, and maybe see some of the good ideas generated in the community on card design, mechanics/synergies, even mods that enhances the game visuals (I know there's a Regent special effect mod that's amazing). If players can see new cards unlocked from time to time, and new mechanics / synergies, I'm sure they'll spend more time exporing those options instead of focusing on that 1-2 less damage dealt from their favorite cards.  There's still so many possibilities of this game, please make it to be what it could be. You also have one of the most engaged community so maybe try listen to them as well - maybe not on balancing, but on new contents, ideas, and the all the positive it can bring to your game.

I rarely post reviews, and I think this is where steam lacks a bit. I've definitely got my money's worth at this point but it has been a bit of an exercise in frustration. Do I post a positive review, or a negative? I've played the crap out of it, but it has been frustrating. I want to give it positive as I got my monies worth, but I also want the game to improve.  I have no idea the current drama is with the game, I'm just here to share a general review of the game in general.  I did a ton of hours in the first one, and of course immediately bought this in early access - and it of course it is early access.  My main beef with this one is it feels a bit different as it scales up, you pretty much have to hit the "magic" build to get through it for each class. There seems to be a rare few really good builds, which happen few and far between but are easy mode. Other than that the fail rate is high. It's been a while but in the first one, you could kind of I want to say have a mix of things and was more creative, and could win in any number of ways. In number 2 it seems like you just have to hit the "super builds" to have a chance as the elites are just so brutal damage wise, or just general mobs.  Maybe I suck or "git good", but there seemed to be in number 1 way more ways to be successful and many more interesting builds to win. In number 2 it seems like you are shoehorned into some really specific builds to get the win.  I can't put my finger on it, but the relic choices in general seem to be a bit lack luster in interesting out of the box builds.  I hope the best for them, and still had fun playing it, but most of the time was just grinding it out because my OCD was taking over. I don't care about achievements or anything, it's just about finishing it. I just want to see more 'variety' in builds/relic options. After about level 5? or so on each of the characters as I would rotate them around, I got pretty bored.  Overall it just seems that there isn't many creative options, it's either loading as much damage you can or avoiding it, which fails most of the time. I've never been a fan of the discard or ethereal card mechanism. In the first one it seemed that the relics had more of an impact and you can tailor that to a build, now they come to late, or aren't meaningful enough to make a difference unless you get a really specific one.  Other than that, the game runs great, I think the graphics are great and I've never had a crash. 8/10 I'm starting off by saying that I've played a decent chunk of roguelikes across my time of gaming but haven't played slay the spire 1 so this is more looking over the game as someone who hasn't interacted with this series before now.   Where I'm currently standing, this game is good, all things considered but there are a lot of gripes I've had over my time playing it and I'm writing this to address the problems I've had so far in both singleplayer and multiplayer. I'm currently yet to beat the act 3 boss as I've only gotten through 13 runs that all resulted in a loss but I'm still trying to beat it currently.  - The game tends to have terrible scaling at times for a game so focused on RNG. - The player should lose strength and dexterity debuffs each turn if the enemy gets to as is just makes for unfair combat where the player is constantly punished with debuffs they cannot counteract often and enemies just get to bulk up their damage a bunch if you don't manage to kill them in a few turns. *Possibly adding a card that increases in cost depending on the debuffs you have from 0 cost at no debuffs up to 3 if you have 3+ debuffs, then just remove stacks of it. - Enemies in multiplayer get to hit every player for no logical reason, seeing as players can only hit one enemy per person and the whole point of multiplayer in lots of games it to make it easier so it just doesn't make sense that enemies get over double the health per player plus any buffs they start with. - The damage most enemies get to do is incredibly high 90% of the time and there is very little you can do to stop it unless you are running a specific build. Getting the build you want is tedious because of how much RNG the game relies on for everything. - Enemy health pools are weirdly high so that you can pretty much never win on turn one and therefore must take damage at least once unless you get lucky on your card pulls. - The whole point of roguelikes is to keep trying until you get a really good build but this game just won't let you make a good build as card enchantments can only be applied once per card and cannot overwrite other cards. Even if you make a good build you still rely on the RNG factors that you get the exact cards you need for it when in combat. - Pretty much all the elites are not worth the health loss when the relics they can give are incredibly likely to just be bad and yet they all can do 5-20 damage each turn in just act 1. - Although not applicable to everyone, pretty much every run I've done has resulted in the same enemy pool with the same encounters each run with 1-2 differences every 4 or so runs which I can only assume is terrible luck on the RNG part of the enemy layouts for the map and there is no way that I've found that lets me circumvent this. - The item pool of both relics and potions throughout the game are basically a 60-35-5 split of either being just bad, alright or actually useful which results in most runs feeling really slow and unsatisfying.  I feel like there is potential for the game in future updates but currently the balancing for the game as a whole is driving me away from playing both solo and multiplayer anymore as it feels like I'm just sinking time into it with basically no reward as the unlocks come in incredibly slowly and doesn't feel like it helps me when I end up getting the same loot anyway.

It should go without saying that StS2's art and music are fantastic, so this review is just focused on the gameplay and its balancing.  StS2 has a similar but different design than StS1 and thus requires different play strategies. That may alienate some StS1 players, especially those who were used to building in certain ways in anticipation of certain enemies (prioritizing attacks for Gremlin Nob, needing consistent AoE for Act 2 elites, etc.). I do think that StS2 could use a few more enemies that soft-counter certain deck archetypes, but not [i]hard-counter[/i]. To those who complain about Doormaker: he was rightfully removed off the Beta branch, and I think Aeonglass replaces his role very well as an "anti-infinite" Act 3 boss.  To those who say StS2 is currently too easy: aside from the fact rebalances will continue, do keep in mind that the addition of the alternate Act 2 and Act 3 will add to the difficulty (because you will need to keep your deck more flexible for more kinds of encounters) -- along with the addition of Act 4.  To those who say StS2 is currently too hard: I gotta be completely honest, that's a skill issue. Learn more about the enemies you can encounter and the decks you can make to face them. You're not meant to win every run, but you can certainly win more if you don't always blame the RNG for your mistakes. Current StS1 is DEFINITELY harder (and IMO more luck-dependent, as more of StS1's relics can be duds). Don't give up after just two or three runs.  These are all of my personal design complaints with the current beta: 1. Juzu Bracelet just needs a straight-up redesign. It's low-impact (sometimes [i]negative[/i] impact) and you don't particularly strategize around it even when you get it. 2. Ironclad needs more ways to apply Weak (only 1 card, where every other class has more), either more ways to stack Strength (RIP Spot Weakness, RIP Limit Break) or more payoffs for stacking Strength (RIP Heavy Blade), and maybe one or two more cards that capitalize off of stacking (not just applying, but stacking) lots of Vulnerable. That isn't to say he's currently unplayable; I just think he needs a few more possible synergies. 3. Pael's Eye and Toasty Mittens are a little too specific and niche. IMO both relics could benefit from allowing you to actually choose (to some extent) which cards are exhausted, which would make them more tolerable options more often. 4. IMO Hunter Killer and The Obscura are both just a [i]little[/i] too powerful compared to the other hard pool Act 2 encounters. (But it's better for Mega Crit to listen to the data to determine if that's true.)  I can't think of other complaints. I think the balances between the other relics, between different deck archetypes, between resting or upgrading, between taking events or not, etc. all seem just fine so far. I think it's worth especially pointing out that StS2, more-so than StS1, allows larger decks to perform well when built carefully, and removing Strikes and Defends is not as critically necessary to win (if, again, you have the right cards/relics to accent them).

Updated review to the recent public patch:  'Metabuild or lose' starts to sum it up more and more.  I do not understand this obsession with adding more and more enemies that hard-counter 'skills'. Not specific OP decks, but Skills. As in, the class of cards that you should at least have 50% if not more of.  Last patch to me was fine. Even with the doormaker. But this patch hard-counters core-parts of the game by RNG chance. Last patch, you could have bad card-drops, and still make it work. This patch on ascention 10, it feels like you have to either get super lucky by not getting unlucky with the enemies, or you forcibly need some specific cards to prepare to not be hardcountered for something as basic as playing block. That would be fine, if it wouldn't be pure RNG of which cards you even get to choose from. But sometimes, those cards that you need? You will not even encounter once for 20-30 runs if you are unlucky.  And that is my issue with this patch. Last patch, if you thought about what you should add to your deck and what made it work? You could even turn a bad row of cards into something that could somewhat work and at least had a chance to somehow make it. But this patch feels like, it swapped that 'adapting and finding clever ways to make it work' into pure RNG of hoping that this time? You get something good enough to brute-force your way through bad encounters if they happen.  Some RNG should be there, but the mixture of these odd enemy/boss mechanics coupled with the nature of this game, just makes this game kind of frustrating. And it gets you into a habbit of not playing out a run, but just giving up on it once you realize, that you haven't been dealt a good lineup.  (I will change this review as soon as this game becomes fun to play again. TLDR: Gameplay - 10/10 Co-op - 10/10 Early access enemy balance - 4/10  Brand new to the series, but I got the first one recently and someone recommended I get the 2nd to play with my friends so I did and oh my word are we having a blast. I typically am not a big deck builder gamer so the series never grabbed me, but it definitely has me now.  However....The balance in early access is pretty....how do I say absolute insanity without just getting mogged by a bunch of "git gud" eye rolls...Look, I'm not gonna pretend I'm great at the game, but I've definitely played it enough to understand it and I have beaten it (twice) but good lord, some combats are absolutely insane (I'm looking at you, Knight's Posse) The different mechanics are neat and often a fun obstacle to work around, but the sheer NUMBERS the game throws at you in some of these fights is insane. It's a constant "play around this niche (but interesting) mechanic while the enemies have MASSIVE HP pools and hurl huge numbers at you while often negating all of your damage" My problem is the game feels balanced for singleplayer and the solution for multiplayer balancing is just doubling everything's HP, but that doesn't work in practice especially when even in singleplayer, the enemies tend to be meatbags. Like how do I shield for 20+ dmg every turn and still pump out enough damage to kill the thing beating on me before it scales to an even more unattainably ridiculous power level? I guess the complaint just comes down to certain fights feel impossible without good RNG and that doesn't feel good to play into at all. I love the game at its core, but this needs fixed desperately.  Overall, I'd say if the balance issues get fixed this is without a doubt something I'd recommend to anyone. With the balance issues though....ehh, bring a thinking cap, some determination, and a can-do attitude (maybe a few buddies and a couple of beers too) and you'll get to the top eventually.   As it stands right now -- 8/10

I really didn't think it could get worse than removing the door maker for the hideous eonglass boss after a certain community review bombed the game as the first beta update was released because they didn't like him. But here we are. The developers decided it's a good idea to replace PRNG for RNG. So now whenever you play all of your card rewards are completely random and what happens as a result is the same issue all rougue likes have. The more you unlock cards and relics, you are less likely to play the way you want. you are at the mercy of rnjesus and maybe once in a while you get the things you want to craft the deck you had in mind or wanted to play. Before the second major update you had some level of influence over the card rewards you get, I could get the deck I wanted with every class pretty consistently. And that's what made this game fun. That's what separated slay the spire from all the other deck building games out there (other than being a great game and we'll balanced). But now even that isn't the case anymore. I understand the desire to make a game difficult and I'm all for it. But this is way too much. The recent changes to certain enemies were way over the top and unjustifiable in my opinion. The flying Doritos change made him a run ender. If your deck relies on spells, you can hit that give up button the moment you see him. Every turn for every spell you play he gets 3 attack, and of course he multi attacks every 3rd turn. The door maker was replaced by the eonglass boss. So if you meet him and your deck is not exhaust warrior, status defect or minion reagent, you can go ahead and hit alt F4 on your keyboard because most likely you're not going to survive 35 dmg first turn with immunity for 4 turn and of course every 6 cards you play you get a status card that deals dmg to you at the end of your turn. And of course he makes them stronger as the fight goes on, and of course he scales infinitely. This boss just feels like something they slapped last minute just to appeal the review bombs. Too many enemies just counter certain deck types to the extent that you have no point even trying to play with them. The game doesn't feel fun anymore, unbalanced and completely random. Until the game goes back to what it was on release, until test subject is not balanced or reworked, until the door maker comes back, until they balance game, until they bring back PRNG, I don't recommend.

It's such a frustrating game. The core gameplay loop is awesome and highly addictive but it is a 25 dollar DLC that just copy pasted 60% of the original game. And that's a perfect encapsulation of the baffling design choices. Why just remake part of the first game and add two new characters and a handful of new content? Why not include everything from the original if that's how you're going to design it? Why make some of the regular encounters harder than elite encounters? Why have no consideration at all to balancing encounters? Why have a large percent chance to have encounters in ? rooms? Why don't ? mark room triggers activate when there are encounters in them? Why are draws seeded rather than randomized? Why is there so little synergy in most runs if they are seeded and not randomized? Why is it so common to not draw any useful cards during major rounds? Why does the Vantom have 9 Slippery!? It does 45 damage in 3 turns and you have to attack it 9 times before you even start damaging it? Most runs will allow maybe 4 cards per turn on average and you need to block 45 points of damage and attack 9 times before you even start ticking away at the 170HP it has? So with 12 cards you need to literally waste 9 of them and then with 3 remaining cards you need to block 45 damage? 60% of all characters starting HP? When in most cases you can get maybe 15 block from a card on average? And with the aforementioned often not drawing any block cards when you are attacked for 27 damage? As an Act 1 boss? And that's really not even one of the more poorly designed enemies. With the right character and run it's completely trivial. It just brings into question basic game design questions. What challenge am I supposed to be overcoming in this encounter? With Vantom at least there is an answer to that question: Have a ton of free damage cards that you can burn him down quickly and just enough block to survive. There's really only one answer which is why it never feels challenging; it's either trivial if you meet the challenge or impossible if you don't. But at least it has an answer. Many of the encounters don't. The enemies in them hit hard, and have high health, and can negate damage, and limit your block, and start out strong, and ramp, and do sustained damage, and do burst damage, and limit your ability to draw and play cards. So am I supposed to focus damage? block? status? balance? single target? spread out damage? speed? longevity? No. You are either supposed to have a God tier run or just take so much damage that your run is effectively over. You might as well just have a number flash on the screen that tells you how much damage you took in the room. I get that there is always going to be randomness but I would like a bit of strategy in there as well. It could just be so amazing and instead it feels like a mobile game.

I've played up to ascension 10 in multiplayer, so this isn't a complaint about difficulty. The game up to that point is genuinely good, and lower ascensions are worth your time. You can draft a strong card early and spend the rest of the run finding nothing that synergizes with it, or find the absolutely most broken deck but get screwed over by a single bad draw. No amount of fixing can repair the run. You either get the build, or you don't. That's not a challenge curve, it's a lottery. Multiplayer feels noticeably harder to balance than single player, but getting through act 1 with two players can already take multiple attempts. The more you push the less your choices matter compared to what the RNG decides to hand you. I'm not recommending it yet, not because it's hard, but because at higher ascensions the game stops rewarding skill. Wait for it to leave early access.

I struggled immediately with this game, but it was managable in it's release, i've felt as if i was playing ACT 2 while on ACT 1 multiple times and i don't belive that to be good, as the first few encounters are the only ones that feel appropriate, and even then whenever i see i have landed in the water themed ACT 1 i knew already that the first enemies will still cost me some HP no matter what i will do, i miss the jawworms.   Finally i could not loose the feeling that i have to avoid every and any combat i can get out of, not because i was stingy with health, but because sometimes what is a normal encounter feels like an elite fight, where I am to fight one huge enemy that can easily scale out of proportion and destroy me, while i was prepared for something simpler when i picked a route into a simple encounter before a "real" elite.  I won't lie and say the game isn't fun because it is, as long as you have other people you can harp on the RNG with, but otherwise i have never felt a sense of completion from winning, it has only ever led to dissapointment soon after as i know my next run is probably not gonna be nearly as enjoyable as this one was, purely because of the RNG if not for just how utterly tired i was too after the boss fight.  Speaking of which, I have always preferred to not be too hard on bossfights as they can be enjoyable, and most are, the only two bossfights i have ever struggled on were at first just the Fysh, since the deck bloat quickly got out of hand unless i had an exhaust build, which is rare for me because i don't exactly enjoy it. Second, was the Doormaker. Originally i've enjoyed the boss fight, the multiple phases as the portal opened and closed again were easy to deal with but fun to see, now the Doormaker became awful, if i have attempted to go with shivs i suddenly have no energy, if i have chosen to go with powers i am stalling while it can scale into oblivion, and if i went into block, I'd be met with average of 30 damage each round, which i simply cannot produce when every card of mine costs two energy or dissapears the second i use it. The best way of dealing with these types of situations in my experience was deck cycling, at least in StS 1, now you can't even do that, as you will soon find out you will not have energy to use anything you've gotten through it, and all the cards you used might be gone into the aether.  My ending thought is just dissapointment, as i am recommended to just drop the game and stop playing, because clearly the point of the game now is to be harder, which for most apparently means better. Maybe i am just bad at the game, maybe i should just go back to plating Minecraft, I'm not sold.

We've been in pseudo release for months now, and the Act 1 issue still isn't fixed and hasn't even been touched. I strongly believe this is the type of game you can really commit to, put thousands of hours in, and really feel like you're developing some skills. That being said, my frustration with the sheer lack of balance knowledge shown is starting to mount. It's Slay the Spire, but more. Honestly, it's an almost surprisingly unambitious sequel in the nicest way I could mean such a thing - it interferes with basically nothing that worked in the original, down to the returning characters all having a new toy or two but feeling relatively similar, the vast majority of old relics and cards remaining if not in the default pool then in special events, and run structure that's basically 1-1 with the original.  But how does the saying go? While you could commend the fan-made Downfall expansion of the original for reinventing the wheel, Slay the Spire 2 just looks to expand in straightforward yet appreciable ways.   Visual polish is the most immediately obvious thing. I honestly have little issue with the overall aesthetic of StS1, and despite admissions in the neowsletter that a lot of the game's look was more a result of "good enough" instead of being something they were truly satisfied with, I think the spire has always evoked a sort of uncanny eldritch terror that combines very geometric and strange shape language with organic details. Combine this with the whimsy in a lot of it's sillier and more traditional creature design like the gremlins, and the game look delightful. STS2 keeps this all intact but with much more focus on the details. The unique attack animations on characters they've been slowly adding, the visual effects like cards afflicted by status effects having unique overlays, and stuff like the physical representation of factors like Otsy or the Regent's Sovereign Blade all just give this game a level of polish in it's early access state that isn't always obvious yet is night and day when you compare it to it's predecessor.  The other thing that stands out is that their number one goal really seems to be to increase the diversity of runs, which is the thing I really appreciate about this game. While the addition of two whole new characters and the admission that they've got at least one, *likely* two (there's a pattern that implies at least 7) more on the way already does a lot for variance, it's not actually the main reason I think there's a lot more variance to enjoy. No, StS2 has a lot more unique ways to influence your deck and presently features two entirely distinct areas that can take the role of Act 1, with 2 and 3's alternates to come later. With Card Enchantments via Events, Relics, or sometimes other Cards, you have a lot of ways to influence what the cards in your deck actually do. It can be as innocuous as adding 2 damage to every hit of your multi-hit attack to adding a modifier that allows your strongest cards to replay themselves multiple times in a row. On top of all of this, the boss relics have been entirely reworked. Instead of just getting a selection of three "boss relics", each floor will generate a random deity from amongst Slay the Spire 2's seven-strong pantheon, and each of them have their own selection of three items that are often much more interesting than the average "Gain 1 energy per turn but <x>" items from 1. Not to say that those are all gone, though. One of the ancients might just have your old favorite...  The last elephant in the room is multiplayer. While I was interested in it, I was always a bit worried that it'd purely just be a novelty mode. That in comparison to a more action-based, free-flowing roguelike, the extremely tight gameplay of Slay the Spire that revolves around creating the most well-crafted, properly put together deck to deal with every threat you expect to deal with would just result in multiplayer feeling like single player with extra steps. It kinda does, but credit where it's due: they've made it very fun. Multiplayer features a number of entirely unique cards both in the neutral and per-character pool, which allows for a lot of funny stuff like granting your teammates access to normally unique mechanics like giving everyone one of the Defect's plasma orbs, or more simple and straightforward benefits like the Ironclad sharing block or taking damage in place of his teammates. Vulnerability and weak stacking is, unsurprisingly, a bit ridiculous when multiple people can do it, but enemies are scaled up *just* enough that they still can feel like a threat even with it. There's also a lot of thought put into how the various mechanics interact with multiplayer. You can throw many of your potions at your allies instead of just yourself, and while some events allow you to choose for yourself, some require the group to make a specific decision that'll affect everyone. It's not the absolute cream of the crop multiplayer, but honestly it still does better than I expected and to manage that with a game that's so meticulously tuned around the single player experience is worth commending.  At the moment, it's incomplete, but still has more content than Slay the Spire 1 and gets biweekly updates that all tend to feel meaningful. I haven't run into any major bugs or technical issues, so nothing to say other than it's great and worth your money.

**Slay the Spire 2 Review — Poor Balance Is Holding It Back**  I really wanted to enjoy *Slay the Spire 2*, but the balance keeps getting worse instead of better. The biggest problem is that many updates do not feel like careful tuning. Instead of making small adjustments to problematic mechanics, the changes often swing way too far in the opposite direction.  As a result, entire archetypes can go from strong to basically unplayable overnight. Rather than encouraging experimentation, the game often feels like it punishes you for not finding one specific key card that makes a build work. If you do not get that card, the whole archetype falls apart.  This makes the game feel less strategic and more dependent on whether the run offers you the exact tools you need. A deck-building roguelike should reward adaptation, but right now *Slay the Spire 2* too often feels like it bans certain playstyles through overcorrection.  The foundation is still interesting, but the balance philosophy is frustrating. The developers should focus on smaller, more precise changes instead of huge swings that erase archetypes from viability.

Slay the Spire 2 is, for me so far, a very mixed sequel to the first game. This is largely due to the fact it's in early access, so a lot of the balance and mechanics are subject to wide, sweeping changes at any moment. Unfortunately I cannot do that with Slay the Spire 2 - the game has been plagued with truly awful balancing decisions thus far, and is in a very unfun state currently. However! I still think the core mechanics and vision is there, just not yet. Strong recommend to anyone looking to play this game to at least wait a couple months for more (and hopefully better) balance patches, or even wait until the full release. If you're still hankering for a deck-building roguelike and really want to play this game, I would recommend getting a friend or two to play Slay the Spire 2 with. Multiplayer has been a significantly more enjoyable experience than singleplayer, outside a couple expected rough patches with player scaling. Plus, there's a lot of cards and cool combos you're missing out on if you're going solo.  TL;DR Early access balancing issues, very bad Core game, very good Conclusion: wait for better balance and play game in several months, or on full release

Everything Slay the Spire 1 was and more. The game is ridiculously difficult at some points [which might just be because of early access] but that's just how it is sometimes, you know? No two runs are the same, even if you run the same character and manage to get the same options to start the run off with.   The notable changes/additions  You meet an NPC at the start of each chapter who offers fun and often times run altering [in a good way] gifts to choose from. This is one of the things I love the most going from the first game into this one, adding that to the start of each chapter feels like a gift for all the hard work you put into beating the snot out of [or getting beaten to a pulp by] the act boss and without it, the game wouldn't feel as rewarding.  The game currently offers five unique characters with each of them having fun and interesting playstyles. We have a few returning characters and a couple new ones too. Returning we have The Silent, The Ironclad and The Defect.   For those who have played the first game, you already know what kind of playstyles they have, though I will mention that in this game they expanded on each of them, offering new character unique relics to unlock, as well as having more special card unlocks behind just playing the characters. [more on the unlocking stuff in a bit]  For the new characters, I'm gonna go a little more in depth because I F***ing LOVE THEM. We have The Regent and The Necrobinder, both of which have the ability to have minions. While the Regent's minion is more offense focused the Necrobinder is a little harder to describe because it can handily do both offense and defense.  The Regent is a warrior from the stars. They have a special resource unique to them called stars, alongside stamina, the Regent's more powerful cards and abilities often require a handful of [easily obtainable] stars instead of a butt load of stamina though this is not always the case. The Regent's primary ability is to summon a giant sword called the Sovereign Blade, it decends from the heavens as a minion of sorts, with various cards you can build up something called "forge" which increases the damage your sword does, often leading to absolutely insane damage. Overall I do like the the Regent, they have a lot of potential to do combos to do major damage, but I feel like block is a difficult thing to manage with them, on top of that the Regent is very resource heavy, without a couple cards to build up the star resource, you will struggle a lot. Its all about finding the right balance for what you wanna do with the character and making sure you don't have too many cards that consume the star resource.  The Necrobinder is my favorite of the new characters added to the game is second only to The Defect in terms of favorites to play. The Necrobinder is a character that truly blossoms under a slower playstyle, offering insane potential to be a tank because of her minion Osty who more or less acts as a giant physical shield.   Osty starts out with very limited HP, and is automatically summoned at the start of each combat [and every turn it dies]. Using cards you can build stacks of "summon" which bolsters your current minion's hp, effectively allowing you to stack up an ever increasing number of health points which will only go down if something attempts to do unblocked damage to you. At which point Osty [god rest his soul] takes all of the damage that their HP allows acting as a sort of block for your character, meaning you take whatever damage Osty couldn't block. Best part? If Osty survives you can heal him by gaining more stacks of "summon" up to the max hp he was at prior to being attacked. On top of that Osty can also do damage, and usually that damage is packaged with an additional effect like debuffing the enemy, buffing you or the cards in your hand/deck.   The Necrobinder also has a unique mechanic called "Doom". Doom automatically executes enemies if they have doom stacks equal or greater than their HP. Doom is completely unaffected by block. Its such a fun and rewarding mechanic to build for, though make sure you have enough block because unlike poison, doom applies at the end of the enemies turn, not at the start, meaning they still get to do whatever the hell they want before they get stomped into the ground.  The last thing I will mention before ending this review is something I'm only going to briefly describe because of how cool and interesting it is.   When it comes to unlocking new stuff there is a new menu to look at, called the "Timeline" this is your metaprogression whatever the hell, you know? It is divided up into sections called "epochs" which are unlocked by accumulating score, doing specifc things with characters such as beating x number of elites/bosses or just finishing the acts, and each epoch you unlock tells a story usually with some awesome artwork [a lot of it is WIP but it is Early access for a reason] and they often come with new item unlocks.  Thinking about it as I'm finishing this up to post, I failed to mention an untold number of things and I apologize for that, if you wanna know about anything before purchasing the game lmk in the comments or something.  This game is everything I wanted out of it and so much more. I cannot wait to see the game in full release. If literally anything I mentioned here remotely peaked your interest, play this game or the first one, they are both so damn good. I would 100% say its worth the full price as someone who has played both slay the spire 1 and 2, even with it being in early access.

From strictly a design, performance, and concept standpoint; StS2 stands head and shoulders above its predecessor.  From a balance and mechanics perspective; there is still a ton of room for improvement.  + Awesome art style: Characters look awesome, environments and backgrounds are immersive and thematic, and there's a strong consistency across all of the (completed) artwork  + Interesting card designs: Lots of cool returning cards, many of which have been rebalanced, and *most* of the new cards are engaging and worth at least considering for a build.  +Multiplayer: Huge addition to the game that adds significant replay-ability  - Overly punishing enemies in the first two acts at higher ascendancies.  Higher ascendancies become very RNG dependent early without forcing very specific builds.  - Regressive Elite/Boss design that *forces* specific builds thus reducing player agency.  Infection is probably the biggest culprit here; Act 1 elite that stacks multiple status cards that do damage and do not exhaust on play every other turn, then it becomes 4 smaller enemies that each repeat the initial boss' pattern.  It becomes a DPS race or requires ample exhaust utility at a point in the run where your choices preceding the fight are exceedingly limited.  - Co-op:  Up to Ascendancy 8, co-op is awesome, but for some reason the scaling is not proportional for co-op vs 3-4 man teams.  This makes Ascendancy 9+ in co-op a literal scratch ticket and its frustratingly un-fun  The game's in early access, and MegaCrit are transparent and active about fixes/balancing; so I'm sure the majority of my complaints will be addressed before 1.0; but its a $25 dollar game, and if you're gonna buy it, you should know about its pain points.  If you're willing to ride out the questionable balance, the game is absolutely worth it.

I have enjoyed this game more than I did the original, and I have felt the same sense of discovery I felt upon playing the first game.  [i]Ironclad:[/i] While clearly the old ironclad, this character has a cornucopia of new cards adding to the classic feel of The Ironclad.  [i]Silent:[/i] This character has expanded on it's old gameplay with great improvements and reunification of old ideas, the most noticeable for me being the new [i]Sly[/i] keyword, though I have not played this character a lot.  [i]Regent:[/i] This character is an interesting addition to the game, with the absolute [b]powerhouse[/b] that is the Sovereign Blade, along with stars (which make me feel like a wizard) and other, smaller, features such as debris.  [i]Necrobinder:[/i] This character includes Osty, a little hand that [i]can[/i] be used as a meat shield (you monster), but can also be an ally that, with the right cards, can carry you through a combat. That said, I still do have one minor gripe that I don't think will change much (but I'd love to be proven wrong, and it's entirely possible that I will be). The multiplayer mode relies really heavily on just boosting enemy HP, which I feel like really messes with playstyles that focused around early bursts. Some cards become kind of useless, and scaling damage over time becomes more important. But it's important to note that it's a side mode, and it's still a blast to be able to play with friends.  At the end of the day, it's Slay the Spire but bigger and with some fun new changes, and all the charm and fun of the original. It's shaping up to be an excellent sequel.

Whether or not you get past the boss, even the first, is pure luck in this game. Every single card and every relic you have counts. But these are provided to you randomly out of a large pool. If you don't get the right combination of cards and relics and elites and bosses which match your deck, there is no chance to advance. If you get a  card which is useless for your deck, you die. If you get a relic which only becomes useful later, you die.  The game is more fun in the beginning because you start out with a smaller pool of cards relics and events. But then new cards relics and events are unlocked with every playthrough. Having this larger and larger pool of of randlomly selected things means it becomes harder and harder to play any of the valid builds or strategies. I also feel like the devs made the game generally much harder with recent updates. I used to finish the game regularly, but now I can't even get past the first boss.  I also wish I could sell cards for at least a little money in the shop, choosing the wrong card reward is penalized way too much. The only way to get rid of a card is paying for it to get destroyed. But this is very expensive and can be done only once per shop. Getting new cards on the other hand is free after every fight. So your deck fills up and it's very very hard to keep a tight deck. If you happen to run into a random elite or boss your deck was not optimized for, you have no way to defend.

As someone who enjoys roguelikes, playing with friends, and experimenting with randomised builds, I honestly think Slay the Spire 2 is worth the money. A big part of the fun for me comes from trying different builds and seeing whether they actually work. Sometimes the build becomes really strong, sometimes it completely falls apart, but that randomness is what makes the game enjoyable.  I have seen quite a few negative reviews, and while some of them are fair, I also find it a bit funny because the game is clearly still being balanced. Games like this are not easy to tweak, especially when there are so many cards, builds, characters, and interactions that can become either too weak or too overpowered. I am looking forward to seeing how the game improves with future updates.  One reason I enjoy games like The Binding of Isaac is because they allow crazy, overpowered builds that do not always take themselves too seriously. I think Slay the Spire 2 can benefit from that same kind of energy. As long as the developers keep adding more content and continue scaling the difficulty properly, I think it is completely fine for the game to “go ham” with wild builds and fun combinations.  I am also excited for future expansions, mod support or tweakability, and hopefully even more co-op potential. Right now, an average clear with my friends can take around one to two hours, so I think a faster game mode would also be a nice addition for players who want a shorter session.  The game has a lot of potential though it may not be perfectly balanced yet, but for players who enjoy roguelikes, random builds, experimenting with different strategies, and watching the game grow over time, I think Slay the Spire 2 is already a worthwhile experience.

The first phase of the Multi-subject experiment is fundamentally a design flaw. Stacked Strength effects should be calculated individually for each player. Not to mention lifting the player limit for co-op: in the original 4-player co-op mode, a single defensive buff from one teammate is practically useless. A defense that holds for the first round will always fail the second.   This leaves players with only a few workarounds: bursting down the boss in one turn, using intangible effects, or having one or two players solo the boss while the rest self-destruct. The first phase of Multi-subject experiment has wildly inconsistent difficulty spikes. Even on extremely favorable runs, you can get wiped out on turn one.   Total losses across the entire third floor in a 4-player run are nowhere near the damage dealt by just one hit from the experiment in its first phase. The more players you have, the harder it gets. Hopefully this multiplayer experiment will be reworked in future updates. Calculating stacked Strength per player would make far more sense for game balance.

I’ll be completely honest here. I never played Slay the Spire 1 or many other roguelikes like this, so I do not have any nostalgia for the genre.  That being said, this game is great. It is very fun and extremely replayable, which is honestly pretty rare nowadays. Even after 200 hours, I still find myself coming back to the game and enjoying the Ascension system.  The main flaw I have with the game is that some of the Ascension balancing feels a little strange.  For example, A0 can actually feel harder than A1. In fact, getting through A0 can be surprisingly difficult when you are still learning the game. A big part of progressing is taking risks by fighting elites so you can gain stronger relics and buffs. The problem is that in A0, you often do not get enough opportunities or resources to become powerful enough consistently. Because of that, the early learning curve can feel rough.  However, if you manage to push through A0, I genuinely believe you will enjoy the game much more later on. Do not let your first few runs discourage you. The game takes time to learn, especially when it comes to understanding card combos, builds, and finding the character that fits your playstyle best.

[h1]Should you buy the game so you could just review-bomb it? [/h1]  I honestly can't seem to find the problem the review-bombers have. As someone has said in their review: If you liked StS1, you're gonna love 2 as well. Yes, second installment is not drastically different, why would we want that? It would get review-bombed (oops). Instead StS2 does what any successor should - improves all the previous aspects, adds what was missing.   We get a full-fledged official multiplayer and let me tell you - card game, well-working MP, is a rare thing. There will be new classes, fleshed-out mechanics, new mechanics, new interactions, new event types, new card types, full alternate acts, QoLs, improved graphics. What more to ask?  I recently noticed that Steam reviews are becoming more virile, and I have posted at least two reviews which would fit that criteria just because I got angry at the game, how pitiful is that? Very. So I took to a new review approach - rebuke the negative reviews or acknowledge negative reviews with my own review.  [h2]Game is more of the same[/h2]  Is it? It's the same formula that gave rise to a whole genre, yes. Is it more of the same? It's an evolution, rather than revolution. We are forgetting a crucial thing - the first installment has sparked a revolution, it was a fresh bombastic idea for a card game. Creative minds get only a handful of such ideas throughout their lives. If Mega Crit comes with a brand new idea, it won't be StS, it will be something new. So if you want StS2, it will build on that core idea previously presented.  I, as an ADHD hamster, understand what it is to crave dopamine. You might crave the dopamine of something new, but familiar, but we have to understand - that's our fantasy, the unattainable dragon. Monster Train 2 is an evolution of MT1, same goes myriads of other titles, even the famed oldies - Thief, Warcraft, Bioshock.   All of that was an evolution, and that's a fine line between stale and new. People disappointed that StS is more of the same are actually saying "I miss that dopamine spike StS1 gave me, because it was so new. I expected StS2 to give me the same ultra high while maintaining what I like about the game." That's a literal definition of a fantasy considering underlaying mechanics of the process.  [h2]Game is suddenly too hard[/h2]  Let me tell you a secret: It took me 3 years of on and off gameplay to finish StS1, because I suck at the game so much, I love to force my fantasy builds in a game that is RNG based in what deck it will allow you to play with each run (or rather - seed-based). Now, I have finished all the first tier runs for all the current characters for StS2 in a few days and added a few ascension tiers of Silent to it.   The game felt much easier to play, and not just because I was better at it, there were simply combos and events that I could nigh-abuse for gains without pains. In StS1 I was dreading elite encounters, here I invited them for easy relic rack-up.  After the recent rebalance, I feel like the game forces me to plan more again, to feel that adrenaline evading elites bolting for that rest site, but right - I have to gather more relics, too, but my health is low!  Now some players claim that a mob is going to hit you for 30 while you have 5 value block. On lower levels? Absolutely not. Starting Act 2 both elites and the boss, however, can swing for 30-40 sometimes. If you can't deal with that at that point either your deck is weak, or it's a skill issue.   If Ascension 10 feels very, very hard now, that's ok, that's why it is Ascension 10, not 1. I think it is healthier to voice balancing discontent in a public beta for an EA game instead of resolving to review-bomb. Some people might agree.  [h2]Bad cards are still bad while the good were nerfed[/h2]  Going through recent balance changes, I see buffs for cards not just nerfs, I went into the game to try out Silent and yes, her card combos are still pretty much there, the seed offerings however feel more optimized which is a plus ofc.  Now, it is entirely possible that some busted mechanics and interactions were removed or otherwise mitigated. Conveyor belt event for example seems like it's much harder (or impossible) to get a big streak going without any trade-off, which is actually pretty cool; it's one of those things that, if they landed, just made things easier without us having to try or consider the trade-offs.  I suspect that some people might be reasonably angry that their combos don't work in a certain way anymore, because it effectively rendered a power fantasy of being good in a deceptively hard game useless. Is that a bad thing? Might be, might not be, again that's something I would consider relegating to beta suggestions and complaints instead of going nuclear.  [h2]Game is changed![/h2]  Now, see there's a reasonable phenomenon any EA game might run into - the weight of expectations. I would argue that many Early Access players of any game are actually emotionally unaware that the gameplay is still subject to change and the game is still being actively developed.   They know on a conscious level, but emotionally they treat this as a "I am buying a game I can play right now instead of waiting for an official release", and then they become disappointed later down the road. Either they run run into bugs, or reach an unfinished late game, or have to adjust to changes in an environment they were starting to perceive as "this is how it is".   They then go and write a review such as "the game is bugged", instead of submitting a bug issue (which is usually very encouraged at that point), a review on "how the game misses some mechanics and content" or "how builds they liked get nerfed and busted", because, based on the incoming data, devs are balancing the game in the background, something they would not be able to do comfortably, because they would not have the access to a playtest group large enough.   [h2]What is actually worth noting about StS2 [/h2]  The negatives? Of course it's hard to seriously critique an unreleased game. The core gameplay loop is as excellent as ever, better even I'd say. Personally I want to animations and game speed to be able to go much higher, I am a hamster, I want my sht to flow as fast as possible, just as Monster Train allows. I would like to see more new mechanics for recurring characters, one such cool example is SLY combos for Silent.   I would like to be able to execute degenerate combos if I hit the gold mine for the occasional dopamine high without compromising the boss' ability to one-shot me at the same time, I think that adds to the overall adrenaline rush the game provides (surprisingly so for a card game). I want some more variety in sounds and music. But all this I am talking about - that's subject to change still, so I can't really critique absence or "not-enoughness" of it.   [h2]Too long, didn't zzZZ... [/h2]  What I mean to say is: Skip all the review bombs, weigh your decision. If you like the card game genre, you won't make a mistake supporting this game, though. And don't forget the ability to draw on the map! You can't do a low game score with that, come on!

I think there are a few serious flaws in this game that get overlooked because the game is carried by a few (admittedly very good) parts. Please be aware that this game has strong reviews because its audience is on average much more serious/sweaty than the average player. As someone who wanted to play casually, the game felt more unfun the more I played. Overall would only recommend it if you plan to play mostly or exclusively with friends and if you are a relatively serious player. Here are the issues I've seen after many clears of this game and the previous one:  - STS 1 and 2 are highly RNG-dependent games. The rewards you are offered generally have a much bigger effect on your chances of success than your actual skill, unless you are very, very good or at the top levels of play. It feels fun to get good synergies, and it feels very unfair when you get poor cards, routes, etc. I lost count of how many times a run was doomed because I was never offered strong cards, or the runs where I was offered part of a synergy but no way to execute it. - Enemies feel too strong. The game forces you to play defensively until your build comes together because sources of healing are limited, but enemies also scale quite aggressively during fights. Random regular enemies will have mechanics that punish all but specific types of builds/cards (for example, enemies with 5+ stacks of debuff negation) or have very strong stats/debuffs to you (hunter killer). Sometimes these enemies feel as strong or stronger than the elites. Similarly, some of the elites feel more punishing than the boss for that area. Many enemies literally scale exponentially, making slower-paced decks very hard to play. - You may end up getting some of the easier fights or significantly harder ones. Some of the bosses are a joke compared to the alternate boss for their area. Fights with 3-4 enemies are nearly guaranteed to significantly drain your health. - Some of the reward choices you get at the start of each area are significantly better than others. You can get offered a card that upgrades your entire deck for a fight or an item that only upgrades a few of your cards if you take on an elite. - The game's only real form of progression is expanding the loot pool as you complete certain feats, which usually unlocks more synergies/strong cards and relics. As you might imagine, this means your first few runs are probably gonna be quite rough. Even when you do unlock stuff, you have to be lucky enough to draw what you need from that expanded loot pool. - Some of the characters feel significantly more forgiving than others (necrobinder with lots of defensive options, ironclad with free healing after every fight). Some characters also have very limited coop synergy (regent, defect). - 2-player scaling is quite unbalanced and often feels much more difficult than solo play. Feels like an easy miss here, why would devs want to make you not want to play with a friend?  Because of these issues, you end up being forced to play in very specific ways if you want to win, and you still have to get lucky enough to get cards that will facilitate your success, especially because most enemies, elites, and bosses effectively put you on a turn limit due to the aggressive scaling. If they rebalanced the game significantly and let you control RNG more often, I would give the game an easy 10/10 especially for the coop experience. As it is currently, it feels like a 9/10 some runs and a 2/10 on others. Can't recommend when the game basically feels like gambling most of the time rather than actual skill expression.
