Slay the Spire 2 is a great deck builder, rogue-like, strategy game. The basic gameplay is easy to learn but complex enough to allow players to have fun seeing how overpowered their builds can become.  Featuring 5 unique characters, each with multiple potential build (strategies). For an early access game. there is a HUGE amount of different enemies, mystery events, cards, and relic (power-ups). Each run feels unique and it will take dozens of runs to experience it all.  A few tips for new or returning players: - Prefer using larger decks; there are many enemies that punish players using small decks (people review-bombed the game because of the Doormaker boss does this). I typically have around 30 cards when I reach the final boss - take risks early to get better rewards, elite may hurt but those relics are worth the pain - treat health as a resource. Health is often the cost to aquire better cards and relics, so manage how much you can afford to loss per potential gain. Remember that all (or most) is healed at the end of each act. - Go with the flow. When life give you “Shiv” cards, make a “Shiv” build. Sometimes you may try to make a specific build but you can’t get the right cards or relics. Don’t be afraid to pivot to a new build, you may even discover a powerful hybrid build or card combo.

I figured with all the recent negative reviews I'd give my own, it seems there is some review bombing going on solely based on beliefs rather than the actual content of the game. Let's ignore that and focus on the game itself for this one.  Some additional context for this review regarding potential bias: I have been a huge fan of the original game ever since it's release. I beat A20 on all characters across this account and the phone app version, both of which I purchased with my own money, which was well worth it for me.  Having said the above... this game is even better, is the short story.  The upgrades are numerous, with the main two being many quality of life features added to the game as well as multi-player.  Ascension only goes up to 10 for now, but A10 is just as hard and engaging as A20 is in the old game.  There are MANY cards to pick from, there are enchantments for cards, there's crazier relics, etc. The list goes on.  The ancients are such a nice touch, too! Each ancient offers wilder choices than the last, and each option is properly themed to the respective ancient you find.  And the best part? Despite the game throwing so much at you, it's not nearly as overwhelming as it sounds on paper. The game does an amazing job of detailing what does what along the way, with few items that require looking up in advance (i.e. what does this event do, how to interact with this event in the case of divination). All the deck archetypes are amazing to play and feel more engaging than the first game.  The game balance itself is being worked on diligently, but you can tell how much effort was put into all of this from the start and it already feels extremely polished. I could wish for more or for certain interactions to be added / certain balance changes to be made, but I've already been given so much with this game that I fear that would be greedy of me.  Even the dreaded Doormaker holds a place in my heart, and though I know they will be removing it I do hope they add an option in settings to enable him in case we want to go back and play against him again :)  And of course the multiplayer is super fun too, and completely changes the game balance and adds new synergies in some fun and unexpected ways.  TL;DR - so long as you hold no odd moral judgements and allow the devs their creative freedom (which has been fantastic btw), then this is the deckbuilder/draft roguelike for you :)

Great game. There are of course some balancing issues as expected of an early access game, but by and far there are very few cards that are just objectively unpickable. Everything has it's niche. I would say the biggest boon for this game over the first is multiplayer, which is exceptionally fun and improves the longevity of this game enormously.  The game is quite difficult at higher ascensions, requiring extensive knowledge of all content in the game in order to predict build possibilities and best choices to consistently win. If you enjoy challenging games, STS2 is especially rewarding when you master it. Not least because of how many people seem compelled to drop a negative review solely [u]because[/u] of the difficulty.  If you are concerned about the odd review distribution, I took a little time to skim the negative ones and most of them are one of the following:  There is an ebb and flow right now of various patches and changes and the vast majority are reactionary to these updates. As far as I can tell, MegaCrit is highly aware of player sentiment and is actively trying to balance the game in a way that caters to both newer players and those who go on 20 win streaks on A10. For example, a lot of the recent frustration has revolved around changes to the Doormaker boss. Many newer players argue restricts gameplay styles and is unreasonably punishing, while many experienced players argue the changes have made him the easiest boss due to the exhaust phase allowing for fast deck thinning. Even though winrate statistics show that this boss is not significantly harder than other final bosses, MegaCrit has still heeded public sentiment and is already planning on replacing Doormaker with a different boss called Aeonglass, which can be accessed in the public beta branch.  There are complaints about multiplayer scaling being too difficult, which I genuinely believe is just a case of skill issue. I cannot recall losing a single run in the past 20 multiplayer games I have played with friends who are far less involved in STS2 than I, and this is because the game scales player damage MUCH faster than enemy health/buffs. Status effects like weak/vulnerable, skills like flanking, cards like gang up, these are all things that become exponentially more effective the more players you have in a session, and honestly, the multiplayer scaling needs to be a little harder if anything, in my opinion.  There are a handful of people that are stuck in 2014 and somehow still care about Anita Sarkeesian's name being in the credits. These GamerGate crusaders didn't even notice her involvement until recently, months after the game went live, so I think it's safe to say that whatever your politics may be, she clearly didn't have any noticeable effect on the game. Regardless, review bombing a game because of an ancillary name in the credits is not only petulant and irrelevant, it's laughably hypocritical how they're basically engaging in the same exact culture war mobbing that they accuse Sarkeesian of inciting.  All in all, I wouldn't be too concerned about the review bombing. If you liked the first game, you like playing with friends, and you like an especially challenging game, I would highly recommend STS2. It's a great improvement over the first game.

Slay the Spire is the Dominion of roguelike deckbuilders. It's core functionality and how it works as a game is so clean and fun that it is very hard to make a game that builds on that without losing some of what makes the game great.  Almost every derivative falls into one of the two buckets "Basically just a slay the spire clone" or "loses some of what makes StS so great".  The changes aren't large for StS2 but they manage to cleanly make Slay the Spire a better and noticeably different game. For now I won't discuss balance and specifics, but rather will discuss systems.  As far as I understand there are approximately ~3 new systems in slay the spire at a macro level:  1) Ancient Relics -  Now after each Act you get the choice of three randomized "ancient relics" like you got the Neow bonus at the beginning of the first game. Really this isn't that different from boss chests with boss relics except that they are more themed and more diverse. It might seem a small change but having your most powerful boons in the game become more diverse is a huge deal. Also taking it from a "looting the body of the boss mob" sort of thing to a boon of an ally improves the flavor imo.  2) Enchantments - In Slay the Spire 2 cards not only can be upgraded, which uniformly and consistently makes them better at what they always do in the same way every run, they can also be enchanted, giving them separate affects (that sometimes will be doing more of the same thing, sometimes entirely different). This brings combinatorial diversification not only to the deck through the list of cards but also to the card+the enchantment attached, allowing for circumstances where a basic card could easily become the best card in your deck for much of the run. This is a great mechanical change, and allows even more diversity and replayability with minimal added true complexity.  3) Multiplayer - This is the thing that has made the game what it is for me, so many hours of playing with my friends. Multiplayer adds another layer of combinatorial complexity to the game because not only is your deck different, but you have to work with a different ally deck every time. I find it really enjoyable to argue over who would use which relic best and to decide between decks that have some of the incredibly strong supportive multiplayer cards and play around those and building my own individually strong synergistic deck to compliment my allies'. The balance is not perfect in multiplayer at the moment but the game is still early access so I mostly lay my review on the mechanics not the fine tuning.  Overall this game passes the threshold for being different enough from Slay the Spire to be a true sequel and not "an expansion pack pretending to be a sequel to change full price" but kind of barely. If you did not like Slay the Spire it is not likely you'll find this game any different. If you did like Slay the Spire you may love this, if you have not tried Slay the Spire, I strongly recommend buying Slay the Spire 2 and giving the genre definer a try.

Takes the original Slay the Spire formula and adds enough to it to make this sequel as compelling as the original.  Adds two new amazing characters (the Regent and my new favorite, the Necrobinder) and updates the Ironclad, the Silent, and the Defect enough for them to feel fresh.  The main new addition though is the multiplayer, which adds a whole new level of replayability to the game.  It's cooperative, with you and up to three friends fighting scaled-up versions of the enemies you'd encounter in a single-player game.  Multiplayer allows you to explore synergies between characters, and there are multiplayer-only cards that make this way more than just people playing solo games of STS2 in parallel.  I've found the multiplayer tends to be a bit more forgiving than the single-player; if you have a run of bad luck on a given fight and die, that doesn't end the game for you, as you'll come back with 1 HP after the fight if even a single member of your party survives.  This game is in early access, so balance tweaks are ongoing and more features/artwork are still to come, but it's still a very highly polished gameplay experience.  There is the occasional stability issue, and multiplayer connectivity has been a bit shaky on my old Steam Deck (which can require the restarting of fights in multiplayer).  It is a lot harder to play with a keyboard (near-)exclusively like it was in STS1; hopefully that functionality will be restored later in Early Access.

Great game. Been playing it since EA launched in March. This game is approaching infinitely replayable. Sound effects are satisfying. The game is tough, but fair, which means 'rewarding' in my book. Built in difficulty slider that I can only increase as I defeat lower difficulties. Some of the fights feel unfair until I remember that I've had some builds that went to the absolute MOON. It's completely possible to trivialize a lot of runs, even at the highest difficulty, if I build appropriately. Game knowledge is key to winning at high difficulty, which takes time, but that's the point of playing the lower difficulties first, is to teach me the ropes so I can be prepared to win at high Ascension.  This game deserves so much love. It's an excellent successor to the first game, which I also adore, and have spent thousands of hours in. And the game is still in early access so things will continue to be added, and improved.  Also: MULTIPLAYER. A great way to change things up when I'm feeling discouraged or burnt out with the climb. A great shared experience that throws in a completely different kind of challenge to keep things fair and rewarding. Usually don't see a solo-carry in teamplay. It really is a team effort to win those fights, and my first win in duos at A10 felt amazing.  Honestly: not a fan of the music. Maybe that's just the thousands of hours of hearing the same (harmonic?) minor key that starts to grate on me, but this game's music seems to be in a similar vein to the first. It's a personal hang up, and not a fault of the composer, I just don't really like it. Although I will say that dynamic changes in the music during boss fights (when we enter a phase 2 of the fight, or we only have 1 final turn before defeat against the Insatiable), are really really nice... and I'm pretty sure I'm not making it up and it actually happens dynamically and not statically (ie: it isn't a consequence of the prerecorded music just becoming more dynamic on its own, but the game actually starts a SEPARATE track that changes the feel of the fight, which can be very exciting). Even in the thing I don't like very much, I'm describing what I like about it.   Ironclad is great for beginners, but still has high skill expression. Regent is the most 'beginner unfriendly' because there's so many moving parts in his kit, but he can become absolutely unstoppable. My favorite is the Silent. The value of this game is not reflected in its price tag. It's a worthy purchase, and an exercise in 'getting good'.

Slay the Spire 2 honestly feels like exactly what a sequel should be. I’ve put around 109 hours into it already and about 49 hours into the first game, and after playing both a lot, Slay the Spire 2 just feels smoother, cleaner, and way more polished overall. It keeps the same addictive gameplay loop from the first game while improving almost everything around it.  The game runs extremely well. Load times are super fast and I dont think I’ve ever waited more than a few seconds to get into a run. Gameplay is really smooth too — I average around 144 FPS and haven’t had any lag, frame drops, screen tearing, or freezing issues at all. The game is also surprisingly easy to run since its a pretty small PC game, and I was even able to have other games open in the background without any problems. I did get a couple crashes from bugs here and there, but nothing major, and the built in bug report system made them easy to report.  Visually, the game looks really good. It keeps the same style from the first game but everything feels more polished and detailed. Animations are smooth, the UI is easy to read, and I never ran into any visual glitches or texture issues. The soundtrack is honestly amazing and fits the game perfectly, especially during boss fights.  The only real downside is theres basically no tutorial at all. The game kinda just throws you into it and expects you to learn as you go, which could be rough for newer players at first. Still, thats also part of what makes the game fun because learning from failed runs is a huge part of the experience.  The difficulty is really well balanced too. Normal runs feel fair, but Ascension levels get insanely hard later on, especially around Ascension 6 and above. Some runs can feel impossible if your RNG is bad, but most losses still feel like they’re your fault and not the games.  Overall, Slay the Spire 2 feels like a proper sequel done right and somehow manages to be even more addictive than the first game.  Final Score: 9/10

EDIT: I really wish there was a middle between recommend and not recommend. After several long conversations with people who all have differing opinions on STS 2, the general consensus is that there's still time for the game to progress, and what they have changed already sets a good precedent for the future updates. I will be changing my review to positive to reflect this.  Slay the Spire 2, how I wish I could figure you out. The art direction is wonderful, especially on the full art style cards. The music is incredible, and is dynamic in some boss fights which is such a nice touch. New characters. New cards. New relics. Throwbacks to STS 1 that felt more broken in this game than in the first. I absolutely fell in love with this game.   After almost 400 hours playing, I have discovered my limitations for that love.   Slay the Spire had an incredible feel to it. Hallway fights were interesting and varied, events felt fun and engaging. If you had a good deck, you felt unstoppable, even if you died to a random hallway fight because you smithed instead of resting. At first, I felt the same with Slay the Spire 2. Cool combos, cool enemies, even cooler events with outcomes I couldn't have even guessed. Updates have made the game fresh and interesting, with problematic bosses reworked or removed (doormaker *cough*) and card changes that shake things up in the best way (buffs AND nerfs are healthy when done correctly).   However...  There is a big issue. I understand this is Early Access. I understand the game is NOT a live service game. But there has been 0 substantial content updates. We got two new cards in the past 2 months. Sure, some cards have been changed a ton as well, but in all honesty, this doesn't count as new content to me, because I'm still fighting the same enemies in the same acts. Bosses have been reworked, sure, but that's opened up a whole new issue. Neow relics have been changed.  It's a small team, yes. There is discourse surrounding the developers that, in my opinion, should not even be considered when playing the game. People are review bombing the game in a temper tantrum that their favorite strategy was removed or weakened. In my mind, the developers are under a lot of pressure, so it's understandable if it's not all set out just yet. They have a vision for this game, I'm sure...  ...I just can't see it currently. Enemies range from pushover to elite-in-a-trench-coat. Elites range from fun and interactive to genuinely oppressive. The most recent change to Aeonglass, an Act 3 boss, has made playing against it near impossible without a super specific deck tailored to fight against it that needs to draw perfectly. Other bosses play fair at first, with very limited exceptions. Aeonglass doesn't. EDIT: After a good amount of playtime, I've actually found that Aeonglass is by and far the best boss fight in the game at the moment. It requires you to think about your deck differently than most other bosses, and it's actually quite fun, if a bit annoying against certain characters.  Not to mention events are either genuinely interesting to mull over, or OOPS you ruined your deck because SUPRISE we're adding cards to it you didn't ask for.   I spent a lot of time thinking this over, and I genuinely love this game. I just don't think I'd recommend at the current status. Wait until either a substantial update... or until 1.0. Until something changes, I'll keep this as a not recommended.

You'd think Slay The Spire couldn't be improved, but they managed to do so, while staying very similar to the original.   The new additions are great: The change to the floor reward relics is super interesting, now it's no longer always the same tired "+1 energy with a downside", but a buuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuuunch of different and interesting strategic options that can elevate your decks beyond what a simple energy per turn could do. Some of my favorites are "Make all your defends goopy, adding exhaust to them but increasing their block value by 1 each time you play them" or "The first card you play each combat is played an extra time", and there's loaaaaads of more different options. The combinations you can make with them are very fun and nice to discover.  Speaking of combinations, the ability to enchant your cards (through events mostly) is excellent and lets you craft unholy overpowered card combinations, like putting "Replay 3" on some very powerful Power card can completely demolish any semblance of balance. I was playing as Silent one run and got the "Accelerant" power, which makes poison trigger additional time every turn, and let me tell you, having 3 stacks of that buff is incredibly busted, since a simple 10 poison will do 10+9+8+7 = 34 damage that way. Really cool.  Another interesting thing is that every class, even the ones from the first game, got an extra archetype with their keywords and tons of new cards, and some of them are really wacky and fun. Silent getting the "Sly" keyword which autoplays cards when you discard them makes for really interesting discard deck combos, and there's plenty of other new keywords.  If I were to say something negative, it's that one of the new classes, Regent, feels very weak when you try to play him with his starting mechanic of Forge. Maybe I haven't unlocked the right cards yet, but I've not been able to make a run that works with his Forge at all. Only when focusing on his Star cards was I able to finally get some wins.  All that said, if you liked the first game, you will definitely like this one, as it's more of the same + better of the same.

I started playing the EA version partly because I loved STS1, and partly because I genuinely hoped that my playtesting data would help STS2 become a better game. Has the game gotten better as of today? At least overall, I don't think so.          I greatly appreciate and enjoy the art team's diligent updates — they've made the game's puzzle feel more complete. However, I deeply dislike the balance team's updates. Although I haven't played the EA version for a very long time, I've been following the updates every week. Whatever happened to the new characters, new cards, and new bosses you promised back then? Reworking monsters counts in some sense, I suppose — but that's not what I wanted. What I wanted was a fourth or even fifth act.  Comparing the launch version to the current one, have the card balance changes added any fun to the game? No — if anything, they've introduced a lot of design choices that actively worsen the player experience. If you placed these design choices in a fourth or fifth act instead, I believe player complaints would be far fewer.         At launch, we spent enormous time and effort clearing all three acts at Ascension 10 — that was our achievement. Nobody complained about the monsters back then, not because they were too weak, but because players saw them as a challenge worth attempting over and over again. I'm not against balance changes entirely, but after so many weeks of updates continuously piling pressure onto the first three acts — nerfing and buffing characters back and forth — isn't that just repeatedly tearing down everything players had previously accomplished?         Finally, this is a single-player game, not a PvP online game like Hearthstone. Players should have the freedom and the right to play whatever build they enjoy. In STS1, I could clear the game with either a large deck or a small deck — when I got tired of one, I'd go back and play the other. In STS2, playing a small deck makes you feel the dev team's hostility coming from every direction, hemming you in and making your experience miserable. This is honestly the first time I've ever felt this way in a single-player or roguelike game.

It took me a couple of runs to get the idea and now I am really impressed by the creative concept. A combination of TCG, turn-based combat with different classes and rogue mechanics. I was bothered by the fact that there is no realiable way to optimize a run due to all the randomness, but I started appreciating the random system mechanics because they would expose you to ever new challenges and puzzles. Not sure how I feel about the grind of unlocking new cards, relics and potions after runs in order to even come across them in later attempts. It certainly is meant as an incentive to keep playing. People love unlockables and completionist content. But these unlocks ever dilutes the pool of powers you can come across in a way so that you won't see your preferred ones as much in the future. It also keeps the game fresh and the complexity picks up progressively. At the same time I am not sure what it does to synergies and balance.  edit: I realize, I dislike the massive RNG in this game. Yes, knowing the card pool and how to draft for synergies, planning ahead depending on map and end boss, countering enemy patterns all play a large role. But there is just way too much learning involved in all of those aspects and the learning curve is flat and linear (or even logarithmic). The game does not feel rewarding, even when you become completely overpowered in endgame (because it is by a huge portion of chance). The skill aspect does not offset/compensate the RNG enough. Having played this game for 40+ hours I should be at a proficiency level where my game picks up in consistency. As a math guy I expect improving my odds with every added card that is better than my average card. In addition I pay attention to synergies with my current deck and make sure to thin out the weakest links. I still get annihilated brutally way too often. At a certain point I seriously question if the reward is worth the time invested into the learning process. Personally, I don't think that's healthy game design, when it feels like your decisions are inconsequential. Especially, when you really put thought to these decisions.

Since the release of Slay the Spire 2, female characters have been constantly nerfed while male characters have been continuously buffed. I consider this a form of bullying against women. As an ordinary Slay the Spire player who cares about women's equality, I initially didn't think much of it when they announced the removal of The Watcher prior to the release of Slay the Spire 2. As a game franchise full of equality and inclusivity, the first game's handling of gender and gameplay was quite excellent. The Watcher and The Silent, the two representative female characters, were powerful and beautiful, easily holding their own against—and perhaps even surpassing—male counterparts like The Ironclad. But all of this changed in Slay the Spire 2. First, Anthony deleted the strongest female character, The Watcher, and as a replacement, added The Necrobinder, a female character meant to symbolize inclusivity. Obsessed with diversity and inclusion in Slay the Spire 2, Anthony designed this generation's female characters to be less aligned with mainstream aesthetic values. The Silent went from a beautiful young Black girl to no longer being beautiful; The Necrobinder is presented as a skeleton, which some players even find somewhat terrifying. I originally thought this was a progressive step toward women's equality, never realizing it merely reflected his deepest hatred for women. Soon after, the Slay the Spire 2 beta was released. Slay the Spire 2 is everything i hoped from a sequel. More roguelike deck building glory with new faces and new ways to play. However, there are a few frustrations I have with the current game in its current state. I understand it's in early access and the game may be completely different by the time of full release, but I'd still like to point out the flaws I'm seeing.  1. Lack of 4th energy. A lot of the ancient bonuses are fun to play with and around but when you go through the entirety of the game on 3 energy(which happens quite often) it starts to feel like Slay the Poverty. And then to make it worse, energy from cards got nerfed due to easy infinites, which i agree was a problem as well. So something either in the card pool or the bonuses needs to change because it feels really suffocating to try and do it with base resource of 3 energy the entire time when the enemies start to ask for more solutions.  2. Act 1 and Normal enemy encounters balance. Act 1 right off the bat asks a lot from the player, and is felt even more oppressive in high ascension. Why am I taking more damage in Snapping Fruit and Flyconid encounter than I am from all 3 elites combined? By turn 3, most of the hard hallway fights are swinging at you, consistently, for 30+  damage when Byrdonis and Statue are doing 20-25ish at the same point in turn. I as the player should not be avoiding every normal encounter possible after the easy pool because I need to budget 15-30 health per elite in case of bad draw or whatever and I may as well get better rewards from losing my health. Is that not lopsided design? I should be taking hallways to look for cards to feel confident to take mini bosses, not hoping my first 3 card rewards offer me a damage, block, and AoE solution and just sending it.  3. Co Op Balance is out of whack. So the biggest difference between the co op runs is entirely based on player count which changes the health pools and that's where it stops. So what happens as a result is most if not all the multiplayer cards become unclickable in 2 player and insanely busted in 4 player.  Regent has easily the worst multiplayer options by far. He has Dying star at rare and Largesse which is essentially -1 draw for POTENTIALLY something helpful. And the card is not free or at the very least discounted. The cherry on top is it doesn't even trigger Arsenal or Pillars of Creation so why the hell would i take that card ever??? Meanwhile Silent sits pretty with flanking: 1 mana win the fight, piercing wail at common 1 mana block anywhere from 24-infinite for the team(Rally is 2 mana RARE block 48 btw). Necro gets 1 mana give everyone 0 mana 8 card draw and enfeebling touch, 1 mana block 40-infinite for the team. Are you starting to see the issue here? Every co op run becomes one dimensional because you click on these cards every time you see them because they are simply too good and nothing else comes even close. HUGE problem.  All in all, I still greatly enjoy the game but I do hope some of these things get addressed at some point, because I love this game and can't get enough of the pain. 10/10 would rant again

The long and short is that I highly recommend Slay the Spire 2. As a disclaimer, I never played the first Slay the Spire and have minimal experience with this particular type of game. That being said, I was pleasantly surprised by how engaging the gameplay loop is overall.         The game has a cohesive and readable art style that lends to a strong visual identity, relatively easy to understand mechanics, and quite solid pacing on a per-encounter basis. While I'd say that enemy variety is currently somewhat low, this is made up for by most every enemy encounter having at least one unique mechanic to strategize around. Mixing in the relatively distinct gameplay styles of the five characters and the drastic ways that relics can alter the game all mean that each run is different without feeling too chaotic.     This gameplay loop is smoothly rounded out by the epoch system, which slowly unlocks new cards, potions, relics and one new area at present (though at least two more are due to be added). This is all defined by clear milestones, such as beating a certain area as a certain character. This drip feed of new content that can appear in your run, along with epochs being the primary source of information about the games lore and story, makes for a game that's easy to come back to and satisfying to play even when a run is lost.     Now to be clear, this game isn't perfect. As would be expected from a game in early access, there is still room for the game to expand. And some cards and encounters could definitely use some more balancing. But what's here is highly engaging, highly varied, and as snackable or hardcore of an experience as you want it to be. I eagerly look forward to where this game goes and what the devs over at Mega Crit add next.

This update clearly shows the overall direction the team is taking. I’m a player who specializes in the Ironclad, and I’d like to share my personal take.  Changing [Bloodletting] from common (white) to uncommon (blue) is a very wrong decision. Whether it’s blue or white, the pick priority of this card won’t drop much – but the Ironclad already has far too few white cards that deserve high priority. This also makes the choices in certain “?” event nodes more uniform from the Ironclad’s perspective – take the Cheese event, for example. The designers shouldn’t upgrade a card’s rarity just because it has a high pick rate or strong power. This change severely affects how A10 Ironclad players survive the early game. In my opinion, it’s a completely failed rarity adjustment – just like another card I’ll mention below.  Changing [DOMINATE] to gold (rare) is even more idiotic. It’s not about the card giving some “high payoff” – the real problem is that this change makes its pick weight drop to near zero in A10 runs. Under high pressure, the normal pick timing for this card would be mid‑game, when your deck has enough support to make it worthwhile. Overall, it’s a versatile all‑rounder that fits perfectly into the Ironclad’s core playstyle. The Ironclad would often pick supporting cards because of this one – but making such a broadly useful card rare effectively kills that small sub‑mechanism, turning it into a mere occasional gimmick. As a gold card, its power level simply doesn’t qualify. I would almost never give up other plug‑and‑play gold cards early in a run for this one. For A10 players, this undoubtedly cuts off a familiar and reliable path. You can’t force this card into gold rarity just because it has strong synergy, even though its individual strength doesn’t meet the gold standard. This greatly undermines players’ deck‑building strategies. When I’m going for A10 win streaks, I need solid, proven strategies and a stable card pool environment. The DOMINATE change completely breaks one of those supporting pillars. This has nothing to do with pick rate or raw power – it’s about asking: what other options do I have left? Anyone can get a lucky power run, but the mindset for A10 streaks is totally different. Does your card pool really support the current environment you’re offering?  One more thing – please fix the elite “Coral Group” mechanics as soon as possible. When your deck isn’t fully prepared, this boss design is utterly devastating. Countless A10 attempts are effectively GG the moment they see it. Please listen more to player feedback. We all want the game to get better, not to fall into a data‑driven black hole. After all, this isn’t a PvP card game. I played this game for a few hours after I bought it and I didn't enjoy my time. After coming back to it a few months later I rediscovered a hidden gem in my library and I can confidently say that Slay the Spire 2 has earned it's place as the best game I've ever personally played.  The game play in Slay the Spire 2 is unlike anything that I've ever played. You can feel like the most powerful creature in the game while still knowing that you are only one mistake away from dying. The game is difficult in an unfair way that can initially be very frustrating as it feels that you have no control over your environment. One of the best parts of this game is it's simulated environments. Due to the fact that everything is simulated independently from you, it really makes you feel like you're just an observer in a real ecosystem. The creature AI in this game is really detailed and helps the feeling of an actual ecosystem with both predator and prey.  You play this game as a creature known as a Ironclad or Silent or Defect or Regent. The best feeling in this game is the feel of getting stronger, not just from in-game upgrades or weapons, but from your skill increasing and learning new mechanics and techniques with the tools available to you. The floors in this game are procedurally generated, which leads to the gameplay sometimes feeling unnatural or clunky, but then as you learn new techniques the game becomes far more fluid and natural, which leads to some of the best feeling gameplays in a game that I've ever played.  There's so much more to this game that I haven't covered here, but I'll leave that up to you to decide if you would like to try the game and become more familiar with it. This game is truly one-of-a-kind and itself is an experience. It certainly isn't for everyone but it is so unique and enjoyable that if you can make it past the first few hours of game play and get the game to "click" with you, then you may just find one of the best gaming experiences that you've ever had. Game's good, but I don't enjoy single-player as much as the first game. Part of that is just because it's early access--there are a lot of experimental additions and reworks biweekly--but part of it is that it's much less predictable on a macro level.  In StS 1, the card, relic and elite pools are small enough that you can build multiple contingency plans as you make your way through the spire. It's sort of like chess, where you'll have a different play ready for each of the three or so moves your opponent is most likely to make. This gives the game a lot of its depth and makes planning ahead very rewarding.  There's already way more content in StS 2 than the first game. Each Act can be one of two random areas, each with entirely unique enemies and elites, and the 11 'Boss relics' at the end of each act have been replaced with  a pool of SEVENTY-TWO 'Ancient' relics. This makes trying to plan an act ahead pretty much impossible. The 'random event' rooms are also much more powerful, so much so that it's often better to gamble on them than to take a regular enemy or elite. One event room can (and often does) change the tide of a run.  It's a VERY different style of gameplay. I think players that enjoy the crazy synergies and unpredictability of roguelikes will enjoy this installment far more, and the players who really enjoyed the deckbuilding in the first game might find this one frustrating.   It's worth buying in its current state (especially for multiplayer!), but I think it still has a ways to go before it's as good as the first game. The devs are making excellent progress and balance changes already, so I think it'll only get better with time.

If Slay the Spire basically created the modern roguelike deckbuilder obsession, then Slay the Spire 2 feels like the genre coming home after years of imitators trying — and mostly failing — to capture the same magic.  What makes Slay the Spire 2 so exciting isn’t that it’s trying to completely reinvent the formula. It’s that the original game was already so absurdly good that all it really needed was expansion, refinement, and smarter design. And somehow, the sequel immediately feels sharper, deeper, and more polished without losing the brutal elegance that made the first game legendary.  Every fight still feels like a puzzle where one bad decision can spiral into disaster, but now there’s even more synergy, build variety, and strategic flexibility packed into every run. The new cards, enemies, mechanics, and visual upgrades all feel purposeful instead of bloated. That’s the biggest difference between Slay the Spire and the endless wave of copycats it inspired: every mechanic exists for a reason.  The pacing is still unmatched. You start a run thinking you’ll play for twenty minutes and suddenly it’s 3 AM because your deck “almost works” and you need to see if one more relic breaks the entire game open. Few games understand dopamine loops this well without feeling manipulative. Every reward matters. Every route choice matters. Every upgrade feels meaningful.  And maybe the most impressive part is how confident the game feels. Slay the Spire 2 doesn’t chase trends or try to become some giant live-service monstrosity stuffed with filler systems. It knows exactly what players loved about the original and simply doubles down on it with better art direction, cleaner presentation, more tactical depth, and that same unbelievably addictive “just one more run” energy.  A lot of roguelike deckbuilders are fun for a week before the illusion wears off. Slay the Spire 2 already feels like one of those games people are still going to be obsessing over ten years from now.  Some sequels try to justify themselves by changing everything. Slay the Spire 2 just proves the original formula was timeless to begin with.

Slay the Spire 2 builds on what made the original fun, and adds some fresh twists. Highly recommend.  The biggest change - and improvement - is the addition of multiplayer. I'll admit, I was skeptical of how co-op would work in a game like Slay the Spire, but after a few rounds with a friend, it felt incredibly rewarding and interesting. It takes a straightforward approach in that all enemies hit all of you, and their health is increased in direct proportion to the amount of players - after all, if there's two of you, that's twice as much damage as you can pump out (in theory).  But being able to coordinate with allies opens up a lot more tactics and strategy, and the addition of the multiplayer cards can add some interesting depth to things - but perhaps the biggest benefit is having an ally helps blunt the edge of bad luck. If you're not getting what you need, hopefully they are, and if you end up falling, so long as they manage to clinch the victory, you're back in the game (admittedly at a very risky 1hp unless you can heal soon). It allways for some clutch comeback situations that would end a run otherwise.  The new characters - the Regent and the Necrobinder - have fresh new mechanical bases as well, which makes them feel distinct and interesting when contrasted against the returning forms of the Ironclad, Silent and Defect (although I do find myself wondering if the Watcher will also return). An increased variety in bosses and enemies, some frustrating and others merely neat, is to be expected as well, but I find myself most drawn to the new lore.  There were always implications of things in the original, but nothing really felt all that explicit beyond vague impressions - but now there is clear logs and descriptions, and I'm quite invested in learning more.  The only comment I will make on the recent spate of negative reviews is simply that whilst I do find myself wondering what, exactly, Anita Sarkeesian brings to the table as a consultant and I disagree with her opinions, I think Slay the Spire 2 speaks for itself.  It's a good game and you should buy it.

A Great Hand Ruined Poorly — Complaints About Slay the Spire 2   As a roguelike card masterpiece that accompanied countless players’ youth, Slay the Spire earned its place among the greats with perfect balance, smooth deck building and a well-designed difficulty curve. When the long-awaited sequel Slay the Spire 2 came out, players expected a continuation of its glory. Instead, it started strong only to fall flat, full of flaws and a huge letdown for longtime fans.   The original game became a classic thanks to a comfortable gameplay rhythm, reasonable stat balance and free deck construction. Yet the sequel has completely abandoned this essence. It blindly pursues innovation while ignoring player experience. Its difficulty curve is totally broken. Regular and elite monsters in the early floors are filled with frustrating mechanics. Curses, maximum HP reduction and stacking damage appear as early as the first floor. New players can hardly enjoy the game, and even veteran players die constantly. High-pressure mechanics that should only appear in the late game are moved to early levels. Players spend all their time struggling to survive, leaving no chance to plan their decks. Climbing the tower has become endless tedious suffering.   Broken balance is another fatal flaw. Developers keep changing core gameplay back and forth, cutting popular infinite combo builds and ruining all mature strategies. They only adjust cold numbers without considering actual gameplay fun. They nerf enjoyable builds repeatedly and force players to follow their fixed way of playing. Bosses like the Gatekeeper have been revised over and over with more annoying mechanics, dragging down the gaming experience. Popular builds are severely weakened while weak classes remain underpowered. Deck-building options have become limited, greatly reducing replay value.   The highly anticipated online multiplayer mode is also a big disappointment. The official co-op mode only makes players suffer together. Monsters get massively increased HP while their attack power stays the same, leaving very little room for mistakes. Random teams lack coordination, and turn waiting makes each match drag on for hours. Frequent disconnections with no save recovery, unfair relic distribution and countless bugs make multiplayer more trouble than fun. The pure joy of single-player mode is ruined by tedious and tiring online gameplay.   Innovation feels lazy and shallow, and its price is not worth its quality. It copies most of the original framework with no groundbreaking upgrades, feeling more like an overpriced large DLC. Removing cards costs too much. Most events bring only negative penalties, forcing players into messy deck builds with clumsy draws and poor pacing. The soundtrack is plain, combat feedback is weak, and translation errors are everywhere. Such rough details are unworthy of being a sequel to a legendary game.   Slay the Spire 1 was polished for years to deliver fine balance and pure fun. By contrast, the second installment wastes fan trust with messy updates, terrible balance and lazy content. It quickly slid from high praise to negative reviews. Hopefully the official team can fix the difficulty, redo balance and patch bugs, return to the original spirit of the series, and keep this legendary franchise from becoming a lasting regret in players’ hearts.

[h1] Slay the Spire 2 [/h1]  There’s a fine line between a hard roguelike and a game that feels like it has already decided you’re dead, and Slay the Spire 2 keeps stepping over it.  [hr][/hr]  [h2] What Frustrates Me [/h2]  My biggest issue is how often the game relies on the same tired trick the original already abused: [b]the boss does not just threaten you — it calculates your exact funeral expenses[/b]. You can play carefully, block what you can, manage your cards, reload the fight, try again, make different choices, and somehow the result keeps landing in the same ridiculous place: [b]the boss deals exactly the amount of damage needed to kill you[/b].  And that is what makes it feel so cheap. It does not matter how many times you reload the save and face the boss again; the game seems determined to recreate the same “wow, you were so close” moment by removing [b]exactly the health you have left[/b]. I assume the goal is to create a false sense of tension, like [i]“you almost had it!”[/i], but after seeing it happen repeatedly, it stops feeling dramatic and starts feeling embarrassingly artificial.  [hr][/hr]  [h2] The Bigger Problem [/h2]  This is not scalable difficulty. This is [b]basic arithmetic disguised as game design[/b]. A difficult card game should punish bad choices, greedy builds, poor resource management, or risky pathing. But when the punishment feels this surgically timed, it does not feel earned — it feels like the game simply waited until it could say, [i]“Actually, you have exactly this much health, so here is exactly that much damage.”[/i]  The worst part is that this is not even new. The developers have been doing this since the original Slay the Spire, and seeing the same design habit return here is frustrating. Difficulty should feel like something you overcome through better strategy, not like a scripted execution wearing a roguelike costume.  [hr][/hr]  [h2] Final Verdict [/h2]  [i]Not Recommended in its current state[/i] if you are looking for difficulty that feels fair, adaptive, and genuinely strategic. Slay the Spire 2 still has the bones of a great deckbuilder, but this recurring “you die because the numbers say so” design makes too many runs feel less like a battle of skill and more like waiting for the game to decide your turn is over permanently.

Slay the Spire 2 completely surprised me with how polished and content-heavy it already feels in Early Access. I never played the first game, so I came into this fresh after it was gifted to me, and within a few runs I understood why people sink hundreds of hours into these games. The core loop is incredibly addictive: climb the Spire, build your deck, collect relics, adapt to random encounters, fight a brutal boss, then immediately queue up another run because you know you can do better. With five characters already available, each with their own mechanics and playstyles, there’s a ridiculous amount of variety in how runs can play out. Some builds become unstoppable power fantasies, while others fall apart halfway through and force you to improvise.  What impressed me most is how much content is already here. There are countless cards, relics, synergies, and unlocks that constantly change your strategy from run to run. One attempt can feel completely unfair with terrible luck, while the next gives you the perfect combo that steamrolls everything in your path. That randomness is part of what makes it so hard to stop playing—you’re always chasing the next build or trying to make a failed strategy finally work. The multiplayer was also a surprise highlight for me. Playing solo feels focused and strategic, while four-player runs become chaotic in the best way, especially with cards and effects designed specifically around supporting teammates or buffing the group. It makes multiplayer feel like more than just “single-player with friends.”  I also think a lot of the negativity around the game right now is overblown. A good chunk of the review bombing feels tied more to people being upset about exploits or balance changes than the actual quality of the game itself. Underneath that noise is a genuinely fantastic roguelike deckbuilder that already feels feature-rich despite still being in development. The game constantly gives you reasons to come back—new unlocks, tougher climbs, better builds, harder bosses—and even failed runs feel worthwhile because you’re learning something every time. If this is the state of the game in Early Access, the full release has the potential to be something special.  —The Ember Archives https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45601239/

The game is far from polished and, honestly, not even in a state that feels ready for early access.  -The wording on countless cards does not match how they actually function in-game. -Card text in general is often poorly articulated or outright misleading. -Multiplayer card interactions frequently fail to operate as intended. -Cards and relics with identical wording often behave differently, which makes no sense in a game built around precise mechanical interactions. -Runs are not always winnable as currently designed, which is pretty absurd in the context of a single-player roguelike. -Enemy attack patterns feel wildly disproportionate. The same three common enemies might all attack for 6 on turn one, then randomly shift to either 0 or 16 damage without any buffing. There’s often no meaningful way to prioritize targets without simply restarting. -Some standard hallway fights are noticeably harder than elite encounters. -Draft consistency is all over the place — being offered the exact same card 10 consecutive times should not happen.  These issues are serious foundational concerns, especially for a game that depends on precise card text and interaction clarity. For the price, it’s reasonable to expect the game to at least function consistently at a mechanical level. I understand early access comes with rough edges, but the problems here go well beyond what should be considered acceptable for an early access release.   It's an overall frustrating experience for the player and and lacking the transparency in updates required for the current state of the game. Things are currently progressing at economy ocean long haul freight pace despite the sticker price currently on the game.

The best way for you to know if you'll like this game is to play the prequel, Slay the Spire. Slay the Spire 2 retains the core gameplay loop while overhauling everything else. I think what changed the most from Slay the Spire to Slay the Spire 2 are: [list]     [*] Everything is deadlier! Although the player's arsenal is better than in the prequel, the enemies hit harder and more enemies have unique ways of mitigating the player's damage output.     [*] Infinitely playing cards is harder to do. Getting your deck thin enough is troublesome because you need to quickly improve your survivability and strength to avoid dying, and cards like Heel Hook are missing.     [*] Consistent energy generation is scarcer than in the first game. The rewards for beating a boss rarely provide a way to get 4 energy per turn.     [*] Lore! Slay the Spire 2 has more dialogue and an Epoch system to do worldbuilding. However, most of the art is currently placeholder art (rough sketches) and every unlock is a handful of words. Moreover, gameplay, not story, is the focus of Early Access, which means I'm not expecting any lore updates until the game gets fully released. [/list]  The game is still in Early Access, so expect balance changes that might make the game harder. If you don't want to spend the time experimenting after every patch, you should wait until the game fully releases before buying.

I meant to write a review anyways, because the game deserves one, but now it comes from wanting to counteract the miserable and toxic playerbase in China that is review bombing the game because of a balance patch.   For context, in a deckbuilding card game, there is the concept of "going infinite". Going infinite means that you reach a point during a combat where you are able to play one or multiple cards, and have them shuffle and re-draw themselves back to your hand when played in succession. This prevents the enemy from ever taking their turn, and in doing so, you end a fight during the turn that your deck goes infinite. Generally, this is an unhealthy mechanic for card games, or something that should require extreme precision and setup, and should not always be an achievable win condition for every deck to reach.  In China, the "meta" of the game for every single class was to find combinations of cards that were able to either thin a deck down rapidly in size, or create massive amounts of energy (mana to play cards) and draw cards to fill their deck so that they could reach an infinite deck state in every fight on every character. This was making the hardest difficulties of the game unintentionally too easy to clear (as there is no interaction with enemies, so game difficulty doesn't mean nearly as much).   The developers decided to balance the "problem" cards that were being commonly used to go infinite on multiple classes, and in doing so, China believed it was so unfair that they collectively decided to review bomb the game as a community. The hope is that Steam/Valve will correct this behavior as a review bombing period and remove those reviews from the ratings, because these crybabies don't dislike the game, they just want it to be easy for them to beat without having to actually build a deck that can manage to clear a run without cheesing it.  With all of that aside, I will review the game. If the review-bombing eventually ends up behind us, I will remove the top half of this review so that people can read my actual thoughts without the dialogue beforehand. If you are on the fence about STS2, pick up a copy. It's an incredible game with thoughtful art and dialogue, fun to play with friends, and infinitely enjoyable. If you are looking at reviews, sort them by language, and you will see that the only 2 languages with negative reviews are both Chinese. Don't let those idiots take away an amazing game from you.  Slay the Spire 2 is not just "STS with new enemies". The game is actually quite different than the first in several ways. First of all, the pacing of the game is very different. It plays much faster, enemies scale faster and do more damage in a faster period of time, and you will very quickly learn that you will not be able to just "block" your way through 90% of runs. Energy relics were the staple boss reward in STS, but STS2 does not have as many energy relic options that are comfortable to take. Many runs, you will end the run with the same 3 energy cap that you started with, so 2 and 3 cost cards will generally have a lower value in your deck on average than they might have in the first game. Instead of regular energy relics, many of the relics from the bosses can wildly affect the way you play a run, or play your deck, and can frequently be win conditions if circumstances are right for them and you utilize them correctly. Overall, they feel much more creative and colorful to use. The classes that you played in the first game haven't changed too much, but the Ironclad especially has a very different playstyle than the first game. The 2 new classes are both very unique and have clear identities and mechanics that are very fun and rewarding to play around, and every class feels more balanced after the few patches that we have had so far. I will update this review again as the game updates, content is added and balanced, and the game comes closer to a full release.

TLDR: Slay the spire 1 with more content and polish but has the frustrating balance of a Gacha game.  I'm writing this review because for once I think it's necessary as I don't find my opinion represented in both the positive and negative reviews.  The game definitely does not deserve all these angry negative reviews. It reuses the gameplay formula of Slay the Spire 1 that works amazingly well. It is well polished and full of content. The game also runs fine with only a few minor bugs to report. If you like Slay the Spire 1 or roguelikes where you fight with cards you’re probably going to like Slay the Spire 2. Overall I had hours of fun playing it which is why I don’t think it deserves this amount of negative reviews.  However, I don’t agree with all the positives reviews that say this game is perfect either. I would go as far as to say the negative reviews aren’t 100% baseless. This game has one big flaw: balance. I could write a long essay about the balance issues this game has but I’ll try to give you the picture in a concise way: this game is balanced like a Gacha game and it ruins the fun. Basically, the probabilities (card draw, card drop, enemy attack…) are playing against you. Building a working deck is hard. As a result, at higher difficulty levels most of your runs will fail even if you play decently. You don’t want to know how many resets it actually took to get that “I became OP in Slay the Spire 2 A10” Youtube video.  I really hope they use the early access phase to improve the game balance but I feel like the devs are way too good at their own game. It would explain why the balance is the way it is. It doesn’t help that increasing the difficulty is the main way the game tries to add replayability.  I ended up uninstalling the game because I realized this game was more addictive than fun. You always think the next run will be the one. It never is.

At the time I'm writing this, I've got 180h and am at A7/7/7/6/10. Despite that, I don't feel like I can recommend it in its current state. It's extremely overtuned, to the point where it feels like a chore to play more often than not. Too many elites and even regular enemies have hard-counter mechanics - e.g., the Skulking Colony (in Act I!) - and in general the damage is ramped up across the board from StS1 so there's an increased feeling of arbitrariness in how far you get - if you can't chart a course that avoids most enemies, you're going to have a bad time because even optimal play with a well-chosen deck will usually grind you down. This makes the higher Ascension factors  The devs are putting too much work into making it hard and not enough into making it challenging, let alone fun. The way it plays rn is grinding, and it's plainly not newcomer-friendly. It would probably help to go back to 20 Ascension levels and tone down individual encounters (especially the bespoke mechanics) until higher Ascensions, because out of the box a lot of normal encounters feel like they could've been elites in StS1. I can't imagine how frustrating this game must be for a new player, because it's pretty annoying for me right now even though I obviously have seen enough potential to play it a lot.  (The king of bespoke hard-counter mechanics is obviously the new iteration of the Doormaker. It's just straight-up not fun to fight, because of how much randomness it adds by shifting mechanics every turn. Its mechanics aren't interesting or challenging, they're just difficult. There's no amount of planning or clever play that will see you through; either you have a broken enough deck to win despite them, you get a luck draw with a less over-the-top deck, or you lose.)  For now, I'm going back to StS1. Downfall just updated, so there's a new character to explore. Hopefully the balance in StS2 will get tweaked towards something more enjoyable sooner rather than later. If and when it does, I'll revisit my review, but for now... overtuned, cannot recommend.

A Brutally Honest Verdict on the Spire's Difficulty Difficulty: The "Everything Matters" Gauntlet - Many claim the game never cheats you, but that's only if you misunderstand what cheating means. The genius of Slay the Spire is it makes you cheat yourself. It’s a game where the card you didn’t take in Act 1 comes back to sabotage your run in Act 3, turning every victory into a sigh of relief rather than a cheer. For new players, it's a black box; the game is notoriously terrible at teaching you its own rules. You don't learn why you lost—you just know you suck. It isn't until hundreds of hours that you realize your bloated, 40-card "fun" deck was a death sentence from the start.  The Gatekeeper Bosses: A Rigorous Audit of Failure - Each gatekeeper is a hyper-specific tool designed to expose a single flaw in your run, often instakilling you for having it.  Act 1 The Chumps: Low health pools teach you basic game mechanics: damage races against Slime Boss’s slam, and tool management against Hexaghost’s status burns. It’s a tutorial for your early game failures.  Act 2 The Punishers: The Bronze Automaton and the Collector are pure DPS checks. If you haven’t found scaling damage by the midpoint, they will annihilate your block and tear you apart.  Act 3 The Meta-Critics: The Awakened One punishes power decks, forcing you to ignore the core of your strategy or die. Meanwhile, Time Eater directly counters card-spam infinites, enforcing a hard turn limit. The community is currently tearing itself apart over Slay the Spire 2’s "Doormaker"—a boss that directly punishes deck bloat by removing your cards entirely.  The ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Doesn’t End (A20 Hell)  RNG vs. Skill: The eternal debate is whether a loss is bad luck or bad play. The answer is usually both. RNG provides the gun, but you’re the one who loads it and shoots your own foot.  Ascension 20 Spikes: The top difficulty isn't "hard"; it's sadistic. Enemy attack patterns become so brutal that a single turn of bad card draw means taking 30-40 unavoidable damage, ending a 90-minute run on a coin flip.  The Player's Grind: The game forces you to adopt meta-strategies like pathing for campfires just to heal "like a maggot wriggling to the top"—a depth of suffering you only accept after you’ve Stockholm-Syndromed yourself into believing the "git gud" philosophy.  Conclusion Slay the Spire is a vicious cycle of self-destruction and triumph. The bosses aren't just enemies; they are toxic, gaslighting relationship partners that exist to remind you of every bad choice you made. It will break your spirit for thousands of hours, and you will be grateful for every second. The Spire doesn't just kill you. It makes you explain why you deserved to die.

♥♥♥♥ First Multiplayer 3/10  A huge selling point for me on this game was that I'd be able to play co-op with my friends in a series that I think is absolutely amazing especially since we play loads of other card games together. The issue is that this currently feels like a why not addition than an actual feature of the game. Cards and encounters rarely seem balanced, with most encounters just being a a multiplier of how many people are there across the board of hp and block. The other thing of afterthought is that there are multiplayer cards, and often they are either the most broken cards to ever exist or do nothing, sometimes much worse than nothing. A few examples, gang up an attack that does damage for all attacks played by all players scales with every person in the game going from okay with two to absurd with four, same thing with golden axe a card available in base game but breaks with multiplayer in which it often scales into a 100 damage drop very quickly. For the truly awful though we have Tank, an ironclad power that makes him take "double damage," but reduce the damage all teammates take by half. The thing is it actually does multiply the enemies damage to you by the amount of people in the game. Barely serviceable in two player against some normal encounters, but in four player turns every 15 into a 60, while only making your allies take 7 less damage each. Then on the other end of the spectrum is what seems to be the absurd, the necrobinder can usually strength lock out enemies as their only game plan and let allies do all the work while actually making them take zero damage and taking none herself. I don't want the necrobinder nerfed because the same build in single player is far more tenuous. Lots of other multiplayer cards just give absurd rates such as two mana on someone else for free, and universal card draw. There are also some connection issues in which matches randomly lose one person, which is rare but frustrating since most multiplayer games take twice or two and half times as long as a normal one. The final issue to me with multiplayer is that you have to have a majority of people win their own personal minigames of singleplayer slay the spire. The teammate that is dying round 1 or 2 each combat, has low synergy, and is now falling behind isn't having fun. That means whoever won their own minigames of deck building and relic lottery need to be so strong that they now carry the deadweight of every enemy having an absurd bonus amount of bonus hp and armor.   The Good Singleplayer - 8.5/10  This is the meat of the game, cream of the crop.   Its slay the spire, but more of it, with beautiful environments, better animations, new cards, returning the great and adding even more. I really can't say, I had a lot for multiplayer because its exceedingly easy to say how things frustrate you, its hard to explain how good the new content is, how impactful enchants feel, how hard but rewarding the decisions the new floor patrons give you each floor are. You get a lot of power to drive your deck with options granted at each floor rather than just the start of the game now. The only one issue of expanding card base, is the difficulty of winning the rng of getting the things that you need for deck synergy. If you just needed that one thing its now even more difficult to find JUST that one thing. Some cards aren't entirely balanced but there is an bit of wiggle room that this is an early access version we are all actively play testing and giving feedback on.   The one bad part currently is that a lot of elites, and even normal combats especially in act 2, are incredibly steep difficulty curves that really want you to have a fully fleshed out decks that are running fantastically. Something you get close to at the end of act 2 on a lot of runs, meaning that certain combats, the triple beetles with the big purple one, entomancer, and hunter killer, when encountered right before the power spikes out rather than after usually spells instant death. It is on you as a player to do what you can to counter these fates, which you can do to the best of your ability. But it feels very abrupt how big the power spike is here compared to the same power spike in the next area.   If you liked the first one, even a little bit, this version has enough sauce to motivate you to play this one more than the first ever motivated you to play it, or at least it has for my friends who played a few hours of on sale slay the spire 1 now already have 40 hours on the this fresh version. Don't be discouraged by the negative reviews, the game is great and worth trying out.  As a sequel to Spire 1, it's mechanically the same, but with much more interesting boss rewards (ancient boons) and an alternative Act 1. I expect alternative Acts 2 and 3 to greatly increase not just variety but also strategic depth because you will have to prepare for twice as many challenges while drafting in Act 1. There are two new characters, and all of the characters ported from Spire 1 have new synergy spaces. Status Defect is peak. If you are new to Spire, it's important to realize that Spire is a game that leans hardcore; the base difficulty, A0, is meant to be challenging for people new to Spire, while the highest difficulty, A10, is meant to be challenging even for people who have spent hundreds of hours playing. Do not feel like you have to play on higher difficulty just because it exists. You may face challenges that feel insurmountable, but one of most fun aspects of playing Spire is dying to some elite or boss, recognizing that you might want to be wary of that enemy, drafting cards strong against that enemy in future runs, and improving at the game in the process.

I was genuinely excited for Slay the Spire 2 because the first game is one of the best roguelike deckbuilders ever made. The gameplay foundation is still strong, but finding out that Anita Sarkeesian was brought in as a consultant honestly raised some concerns for me.  Whether people agree with her or not, she has been a very divisive figure in gaming for years, and for many players her involvement is seen as a red flag because it often signals unnecessary ideological influence being brought into games instead of focusing purely on gameplay and player experience.  What frustrates me most is that developers keep involving controversial consultants without being transparent about what their role actually was. Maybe her involvement was minor, maybe not — but when players see names associated with activism and culture-war discussions attached to a beloved franchise, it naturally creates distrust.  I play games to escape politics and modern social messaging, not to wonder whether creative decisions were filtered through consultants pushing a particular worldview. Even if the gameplay is still solid, this kind of decision hurts my confidence in the future direction of the franchise.  I’m not leaving this review out of hate. I just think developers should understand that many longtime gamers are tired of ideological influence creeping into entertainment, especially in franchises that never needed it in the first place.

I have played cards games for over two decades and accumalted thousands of hours total in rogulites like Slay the Spire I, Monster Train, Monster Train II, Across the Obelisk, Vault of the Void, Indies Lies and I have reached top ranks at multiplayer card games such as Hearthstone and Shadowverse. My takeaway from all those games is simple:   There's a fine line between well designed difficulty and overreliance on RNG that leaves you hanging dry unless you're offered the right options at the right time. Slay the Spire II suffers from low value upgrades, (slightly) overtuned enemy damage, and partially overtuned oppressive boss mechanics. It does get better once you have more versatile cards unlocked and it is doable if you find the right relics at the right time; but overall - looking at all the card game rogulites I played in the past - Slay the Spire II falls among those where I felt that my decision making had the least impact on the outcome of the run; or in other words - balance is still lacking severely, resulting in a huge performance difference based on RNG.  As much as I want to like Slay the Spire II because of nostalgia for Slay the Spire I, currently it definitely ranks amongst the worse rogulike card games. Should Early-Access improve, I will update this review, but for now I am simply disappointed.

Pros:  - Fun gameplay loop - Interesting card mechanics - Co-op play - Visuals and Audio are good - Decent enemy variety  It's enjoyable, especially if you are playing with friends. Even some mechanics like Sly from Silent or Summon from Necrobinder are interesting, which can lead to fun decks to build. For the team that has spawned a genre, I am glad that they released a sequel that is enjoyable, even amongst my friends that don't usually play card games. We've played until we finished Ascension 10 a few times since that is the current end game limit and are waiting for more updates to come.  Cons: - Balancing seems more focused making cards in line with other cards, viable but not fun, more nerfs over buffing - No gameplay resume on co-op - Hiring someone that has a record of bad faith behaviour/attitude towards games  If you are aware of Arrowhead's approach to Helldivers 2 balancing in it's first few months, then you basically know that this is the same pattern. Rather than trying to improve cards more, they only increase maybe a few but nerf a lot. I understand that there are stupid decks (like ones that let you infinitely stack on a single turn) but they are more looking to make things less fun and more of a struggle. All decks can work normally but once you introduce ascension, they make you focus on certain builds that can be fun but just ensure they aren't getting screwed over. You should prioritise what makes decks fun to play but also other decks that could be viable and fun if the cost/benefits were there.   Multiplayer is also rough because if someone has a bad connection, the game needs to reset into the lobby and play again from the start of the battle.  Then, the team hiring Anita Sarkeesian was really a bad PR move and also, when time will tell, the direction of the game will be worse off. For those who don't know, she is one of the original people that caused 'Gamergate' back in 2014. Since then she's actively attacked gamers for liking their own industry for what makes things fun and pushes agendas to fit their 'unrealistic' idealogies. Games are meant to be an escape, a medium where you can just enjoy yourself and take a break from reality. With the unfortunate shift of Western developers looking to make you want to believe and play a certain way, other companies have given a lot more agency to players to decide how they engage in their games providing the tools related to the game.   Conclusion: I am giving a benefit of the doubt that because it's Early Access, there is a lot of fine tuning to be done. As of now, I can't really recommend the game in it's current state. Right now it's a 'depends on if you want to try it out' but since there is no neutral review, because of more negatives outweighing the benefits, I cannot recommend it. It's fun the first few gameplays but the direction that it's going towards is not something I can confidently ask others to partake in.

I've gotten nearly 38 hours out of it while it's in EA, and while I'm just about done withe the game emotionally I suspect I'll get in another 5-7, if only to try and get the last of the timeline unlocks I have access to right now.  The game is incredibly polished (I'm not saying "balanced", I'm saying "polished" here, to be clear) and I really appreciate it for that. Being able to check the minimap/my deck/discard/draw/exhaust piles at pretty much any time, even while choosing options for ability is A) super helpful and B) ticks me off when I can't do it in other games, and when you're one hit away from killing an enemy the game letting you "queue up" an attack as it draws your hand for the turn is super nice as well.  The thing that has thrown me off is that at time of writing I find the game HARD. In StS1 I could reasonably expect to make it to Act 2 or 3s final boss pretty regularly, even if I made a mistake or two along the way. I pretty regularly have trouble making it past the boss of the first Act, and in some cases past the ELITEs of the first act in StS2. Thank you in advance, I am aware I should git gudd.  My personal theory/feeling is that this is due to how encounters work in StS2.  In StS1 I felt like most enemy encounters were relatively static: they presented a relatively fixed threat level. If you could block for "x" you could mitigate most of the threat, and eventually take them down without taking too much damage. This wasn't always the case, notably the cultists using Ritual, some(most?) elites and obviously the bosses,  but most encounters didn't feel like they scaled inside of the encounter itself.  In StS2 enemies that don't have a way to give themselves permanent boosts to strength are, I believe, at least less common than enemies that can't. I want to say "enemies that can't buff themselves are the [i]exception[/i]" but I don't want to risk being hyperbolic. This means most encounters are a race not to beat a relatively consistent threat, but against snowballs that will inevitably outscale anything you can reasonably handle outside of infinite or meme builds.  My lightbulb moment was fighting the Sewer Clam, which on Turn 7 was swinging at me with +12 strength. It was the fourth encounter on Act 1, a regular enemy room. After digging further into it the wiki suggests that the claim gives itself +4 strength every other turn, which matches my experience. What throws me for a loop is comparing this against Donu and Deca, Act 3 bosses from StS1. Donu [i]also[/i] buffs himself (and Deca), permanent increasing their strength every other turn. By [i]3[/i]. A random mook on the first act of the second game has a stronger permanent self-buff than a boss of Act 3 of the first game. I am aware of the fact that the extra damage is scarier on Donu/Deca because they each hit twice, it's still wild to me, and acts as a great microcosm of my experience with lot of the game's encounter design.  So yeah, game is polished already, in EA so I expect balance will get there, and I've gotten my money's worth, so it gets a thumbs up, but I'd probably have enjoyed it more as a full release and EA has kinda put me off of it. I might finish my timeline as it exists for "completion" but I probably won't revisit it on full release.
