(Mixed / Not Recommended)  Slay the Spire 2 delivers incredibly satisfying gameplay. The core deckbuilding loop feels tight, the new cards and relics add fresh depth, and runs have that addictive "one more try" quality that made the original a standout roguelike. Combat is engaging, the art and sound design are strong, and it scratches the same itch as the first game while expanding on it. If it were just about the mechanics, this would easily be a strong positive for me.  Unfortunately, I can't in good conscience recommend it. MegaCrit chose to list Anita Sarkeesian as a consultant in the credits. Sarkeesian has a long history of criticizing and actively working against core gamer culture and the games industry through campaigns that painted gamers broadly as toxic or problematic. Paying her for consulting work (whatever the exact scope) feels like supporting someone who spent years trying to reshape the medium in ways many longtime players strongly opposed.  Gameplay alone doesn't exist in a vacuum for me. Developer choices signal what kind of audience and future they want for their series. I enjoyed my time with the game, but I won't pretend the credits don't matter. If you're unbothered by that or separate the art from those decisions more easily, you’ll probably love the actual Spire runs. For me, it leaves a bad taste.

I already have more hours in this than the first game, so figure it out yourself (and I think first one is a masterpiece). I love it! A few points to mention, though.  Balance here is all over the place. Clone is OP, quite a few interactions between relics and cards are OP (some easier to get than others). It's expected since it's just an Early Access. I'm not complaining though - difficulty wise I can tell that A10 in this game is comparable to A20 in StS1, but not as grindy to get to, which is really nice. Balance between characters is non-existent. I can win 30 to 40 percent of Clad runs on A10, but for the love of God I cannot win a single run with Regent. Regent is my favorite character btw, so I have most runs on them. But they're difficult to win with, at least on the highest ascention. Animations and visuals overall are a glow up from the first game. When I first saw this, I was not sure if I like it or not visually. But now, when I watch old content from Spire 1, I doubt I had eyes at that point in time. Fonts, card arts, enemy animations and sprites are SUPERB. I love how it feels to play.  Audio in this game is good. Music is a solid successor to the first game, nothing to complain about. Love that some enemies already have their unique sounds.  And what about mechanics?  If you played the first game, you know that there are boss relics. A unique set of relics that offer much stronger, one off benefits, often including additional energy every turn, with a significant downside. This game has an alternative, and what an alternative it is! Ancients are NPCs that welcome you after each act to offer strong upgrades to your run, with much (MUCH) more difersity than classic boss relics from the first game. Even Neow got their upgrades sorted out, and a few more getting added with patches on a Beta branch. Overall this is the strongest upgrade for me. Enemies? I feel the change to recognizable patterns in enemy intents is a welcome change. Enemies overall feel more difficult, but the fact that you can predict what they can do on their next turn is cool. Augments on cards feel interesting, but I'm not a big fan of Queens Bound augment that allows you to play only 1 card out of 3 possible. When it comes to the Doormaker, that developers already removed on the Beta branch, I have a strong opinion that this decision was a bit rushed because of how some players just didn't figure this fight out. It felt like a third act boss more than any other. It didn't counter any build as many say, as you could potentially win with a smaller deck or draw heavy deck. And yes, I've beat his ass with souls build on Necromancer on A10, so skill issue, I guess. Also, nerf Decimillipede, it killed more of my runs than any other enemy in the game.  Characters?  3 out of 4 classic characters return in this game, with familiar mechanics, but with an addition of new ones too. Ironclad got some cool cards that expand his strength and exhaust synergies, Silent got a new keyword (that existed in the first game as a mechanic but didn't have a name), and Defect got completely new archetype with status cards (awesome, you should try it out!). For the new characters, I think Regent is the highlight, offering not only quite a few brand new card mechanics, but a completely new concept - a separate energy source that doesn't exhaust at the end of the turn. Necromancer is an honorable mention, I love interactions with Osty, soul builds and Doom mechanic, but it felt more one sided at the moment. Overall: I just love how the developers mix those mechanics, offering Sly cards that interact with Shivs, Status cards that interact with Orbs, and Forge cards that would love you to gain more stars. This is what it's all about - not fall into a single archetype, but build unique solutions for every fight that you have to face, prepared in advance, because the end goal always is to Slay the Spire! 9 out of 10 at the moment of this review. Slay the Spire 2 is a phenomenal game. It has everything I want in a roguelike: challenging gameplay, thoughtful card design, and downright addictive replay value.  Since it is still in Early Access, I definitely would not say it is perfect in every regard. But honestly, that is also where STS2 stands out above a lot of other games. The development team has been exceptionally communicative, responsive to feedback, and genuinely seems committed to making the best version of this game possible. It is beyond refreshing to see a game that feels like it is being made for the players, not just built to squeeze out as much money as possible.  I have clearly put a lot of time into this game, and I will continue to do so. The first Slay the Spire quite literally saved my life. I will not go into detail on that, but I am beyond grateful for this series and for the developers behind it. I fully believe in this game and its continued development.  That being said, my biggest complaint is not even really with the game. It is with the community.  ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the community can be downright infuriating. From review bombing to childish tantrums over changes that have not even fully played out yet, watching parts of the community try to bully their way into getting what they want is frustrating. As gamers, we constantly complain about triple-A games being overpriced, unfinished, soulless, and built around monetization instead of fun. STS2 is the opposite of that. We have a responsive development team, a game that is already well worth its price, and a satisfying foundation that is actively being improved.  And the response from some people is to throw childlike tantrums on the internet?  You can literally send feedback directly to the team through the game. You can be passionate, critical, and invested in wanting the game to improve without trying to damage its reputation in the process. Supporting a team like this should be a no-brainer. Acting otherwise just helps justify the exact kind of gaming industry people claim to hate. Enjoy Call of Duty 30 for the low price of $199.99, I guess.  My only real complaint is that parts of the gaming community have become exhausting to watch. I hope the team keeps creating, experimenting, and perfecting Slay the Spire 2. This game deserves patience, support, and honest feedback — not tantrums.  Highly recommended.

I genuinely don't know what to think of this game. I don't have a truly huge amount of time in Slay the Spire 1 and was never particularly good at it but it felt like STS1 had a kind of basic learning curve that would get you to reasonably hit the end of a run frequently enough at A0 without too much unnecessary friction.  STS2 right now is built like one of those modpacks you might come across in well loved games that are designed by and for people with thousands of hours poured into the vanilla experience where the learning curve and basic balance are not even tertiary concerns in the face of just making the game more challenging when everything else has been memorized and optimized. The problem is that STS2 is being sold as a full product and can reasonably be expected to be people's first experience with that kind of game, in which case it's incredibly frustrating.  Runs in STS2 either take off at orbital velocities and become unstoppable or they die sad, pathetic deaths against a considerably harsher roster of encounters. It's not uncommon for your average hallway fight to be harder than some of STS1's nastiest elites. Most of the "easier" cards to build around are now gone and replaced no real equivalence, which further destroys accessibility for newcomers. Ascension climbs much more rapidly, but the base A0 entry point is also harder by an order of magnitude.  There's obviously a lot of buzz about this game but I think it's quite telling that a crushing majority of the positive opinions about this game come from people who have absolutely polished the first game clean. Roguelites have this kind of problem sometimes where they have to contend with a sequel being both "the first game but harder" but also potentially the entry point for many people, which is why STS2 isn't just throwing everything out but obviously is trying at its core to revamp and overhaul aspects of the first game.  I kind of found my experience with STS2 unpleasant. I very quickly lost the drive to keep my patience through profoundly uninteresting runs. More than frustration, what I felt playing it after a while was ennui. I really hope this game eventually manages to be built around having an actual learning curve that does not involve either hundreds of hours of unmitigated pain and frustration or looking up optimal builds to aim for to optimize the fun out of the learning experience. If you're the kind of guy to already have four digit playtime in the first game you can safely ignore this review and get in, but I wouldn't recommend this thing for newcomers. It's a terrible first impression for anyone who might have heard good things about Slay the Spire.

This review is subject to change should gameplay quality improve.  Coming from being a lover of the previous game, and wanting to play STS with friends, the sequel has provided at least that much. Alongside new characters, reworks to the original ones, and new challenges in the climb, it does accomplish a sequel's goal of building off of its predecessor well.  Now for why this is a negative review.  To begin, why on God's good Earth would a company with a cult following and almost certain success with a sequel to a beloved game sign on a consultant who has made her fame over the past decade for attacking and harassing gamers, the gaming community as a whole, and anyone who dares not share her aggressive ideology? Were you held hostage, Megacrit? Was this some sort of tithe given as payment for some sort of blackmail? What was the expectation of benefit for the game and your business to have a radioactive person like her onboard? Thankfully, the gameplay doesn't seem too deeply affected by this inclusion, but these people cannot be seriously considered anything more than enemies of the gaming community as a whole, to pay one as a consultant has been the mark of death for a dozen games before.  Now for less current event issues: The game feels much more difficult than the previous game, but not for the same reasons. When I failed a run in STS1, I had misplayed or run out of options and didn't have the health to soak the consequences. In STS2, you can just die at any point because a non-elite enemy chip-damaged your max HP to 0, a non-elite enemy had an opening gambit of a 12+ dmg attack and a buff, or the actual ELITE enemies apply max-stacks of crippling debuffs onto you in a single turn and obliterate you for taking too long. By turn 4. The difficulty doesn't feel fair, like you can make a variety of builds work. It feels like the game is tuned for an insane meta that some characters keep pace with better than others, but that just isn't fulfilling. It doesn't feel fair in that when you fail, you don't feel like there was anything you could even do to salvage the situation or do differently, you just failed to scale as insanely fast as the game arbitrarily decided you should have. That alongside nearly every single enemy in the game being able to strength boost infinitely makes the idea of a defensive build impossible to take seriously anymore. Enemies will always hit you harder next turn than they did last turn, in one way or another. And if they didn't, it's because they gained ~4-7 strength stacks instead to blast through you next turn. That's not fun gameplay, that's a stat-check.  Multiplayer is particularly punishing in that regard. Enemy health is at least doubled PER PLAYER, which wouldn't be as bad if damage wasn't ALSO spiked to the moon in a similar way. Many of our multiplayer runs start by getting whacked by double digit damage through our block on the opening turns. With 14 floors left to go before we can get to Act 2. The upside to multiplayer is that if one player gets lucky (or necrobinders hard enough), they can carry the entire team by managing to match the scaling. Anyone who doesn't get lucky or make a god build ends up becoming dead weight and just pumping the stats on the enemies, causing more difficult encounters for the people who actually can participate in them. I've been on both sides of this extreme multiple times, and it's not a good sign of game design for there to not be a flow state of difficulty and challenge to recovery and growth for the next challenge. This isn't so much as a diffculty curve as much as it is an exponential chart where the equation skips a few X values every 5 units.  If you want to play STS multiplayer, I'd suggest Together In Spire, it's very well made and has multiple characters and converted bosses with their own unique decks, really a labor of love to the game. If you want to try out being a lazy star king and a cursed skeleton, consider picking up this game. If you liked the original and want to support the devs, consider picking up this game but more preferably share the original around with friends. If you want to experience more slay the spire content and this game is looking to provide just that, I recommend browsing the workshop for STS1 instead.  For the time being, a message needs to be sent that a player vs developer mentality is caustic for game design and that no community should bear for it's creatives to be advised by its enemies.  It's got my money, but make your own decision.

Beautiful game.   Loved the extended lore, the artwork, the immersive events. Loved the new characters!   Loved the concept of different Ancients giving their specific gifts (or offering questionable contracts) instead of random boss loot. StS 1 mostly gave you more energy as boss drops - here, there's diverse options that challenge you to really think about the strengths and weaknesses of your deck and how you want to develop it - but that turn out as strong, or stronger, than just being able to spend more each turn.  The muliplayer mode is an incredible boost, with dedicated cards that work for the entire group, or support other players. Honorable mention to the option of drawing on the map, which is perfect for coop/ negotiating on the path to take (or doodling when everyone else Takes Too Long, Again!). The only small drawback to this so far is the Ironclad's weakness of almost never getting enough block (carried over from StS 1). This resulted in us going through some intensely frustrating runs where Ironclad got the rare Tank power early without ever getting more than two or three block cards over the entire run - or constantly getting offered cards working with said inexistent block (Body Slam!). We still love multiplayer, hanging out with friends or partners, giving each other boosts, and finding out about the synergies of the different characters.  re Difficulty: I made it to Ascension 10 with two characters pretty fast, one of them Necrobinder (new). This honestly surprised me, given that my highest on StS 1 was still 15/20, after years of playing. I still would not consider StS 2 as lacking challenge. Especially for new players, just as with StS 1, there is a learning curve. It's definitely doable, though, and rewarding - and for enjoying a more casual playstyle, playing without Ascension is always possible.

I can see people being frustrated with just how precise some of those builds have to be to be successful.  In solo mode in particular there's no room for error. Running Silent on a classic poison build is pretty reliable, so if that what you want just run with it. I already count it as a winner, let alone after they get done tinkering with the balance a bit more.  Two thumbs up!

I find it a little unfortunate that the game is suffering from its own success, having drawn a large enough crowd to include people that don't seem to understand what the game is doing. It's fine to want to win at a game playing your way and not having to think too hard, and there are plenty of games that let you do that. But this game isn't (and can't be) for everyone. I feel bad for anyone who hoped to figure out a simple, reproducible strategy and then win every time while choosing the same cards, but that honestly sounds like a garbage game to me. I don't want to play a deckbuilding roguelike where I build the same deck each time.  I put 1500+ hours into StS1 and I've already put several hundred into this one because they have the depth to not only allow but demand that each run be played differently. This is challenging but rewarding, each run feels like a new puzzle. I want to be challenged and have to think on my toes and adapt when the card I want doesn't show up in a card reward or my draws really suck for a whole fight so I need to plan a new route through the act. And thankfully it seems like that's what the devs are trying to make. It's unfortunate that some people didn't get that and got drawn into a popular game that wasn't their cup of tea. But if learning a challenging game where success relies on your wit every time sounds fun to you, then I can't recommend this game enough.

TL:DR -> It's good for people new to the genre or who like mild to difficult puzzles. Those who were already happy with StS1 have new features to look into (new characters, multiplayer, new cards, etc.), but may find that the changes are too subtle.  What is this game? It's a roguelike deckbuilder, which means you have a deck of cards that you improve over the course of a playthrough, and that every playthrough is theoretically unique since it is procedurally generated using a "seed".  Why is it good? There is a bit of a challenge and learning curve to this game, though it's significantly reduced if you have played games like Hearthstone or Magic: the Gathering. The appeal tends to lie in the challenge, and the satisfying feeling that arises when a highly synergetic deck comes together. The animations and art also show marked improvements from the original game.  Anecdote: I tried the board game version of this with a couple family members. The one who regularly solves puzzles (sudoku, mahjong, etc.) now plays StS2 daily. The other ... wouldn't play video games anyway.

I personally disagree with what the "reasonable asks" of the gameplay demand. It feels less like you're creating a dedicated build and more like you're trying to "solve" the next problem you have to face, which also means your survival is dependent on getting the "correct" cards after a fight.  There are times where you're against a Hunter Killer and the game didn't feel like giving you any high-value cards prior. There are times where you need snap defenses and it gave you zero Block. And there are most certainly times where the Act 2 or 3 Ancient gives you three flavors of "ruins your build" with no option to skip their offers, killing the momentum of an otherwise generational run. The luck element creates variance that is important to gameplay, but is in conflict with the excessive strategization necessary to clear floors reliably.  THAT BEING SAID, the game is very fun. Relatively bug-free for an early access, stellar moment-to-moment gameplay, really solid artstyle, and generally a great time with friends. Be careful if you're running it with first-time friends though, because the difficulty ramps up severely if a new player is struggling to contribute meaningfully to fights and they might not have a good time as a result. It's a game you'll enjoy if you're more on the same wavelength with what the devs expect you to do.

I have played a lot of this game. I think It's a great example of what I (and hopefully others) enjoy about deck building roguelike games. You start with a basic set up that will definitely lose before you even get to the boss without carefully considering how you improve the deck. There might be a bit of an issue for players who are not used to creating their own builds, as roguelike games require you to base your decisions on what is available during your run. You can't always get the same synergies between cards themselves, the cards + relics, or enchantments onto specific cards to build game plans.  The characters are artistically and mechanically distinct. The progression is straightforward: simply expanding on the mechanics as you play the game more without twisting the core gameplay enough to feel like a roguelite. The difficulty spike is a great OPTION (reminder: you don't have to play max). I'm sure there will be a lot of changes to gameplay from a dev team that has been passionate about working with the community to create a challenge that feels rewarding (no stakes, no triumph).  I don't have online friends to play multiplayer, but I'm sure that will be a massive plus for people looking to buy the game. Adding my review to the pile regarding Anita Sarkeesian as well as just about the game in general since I have some issues with the game balance and design philosophy that is being implemented.  I'll start with the gameplay issues and design problems. To be warned, these are just my opinions; I'm not a game designer and I don't have an input regarding how to fix these issues beyond pointing out why they are a problem to me specifically.         Enemy damage limits - I can see the thought process here, limit the amount of damage that can be done to stop the game from being a rush to infinite attacks to win the game like how slay the spire 1 eventually ended up. The problem here is that this slows down game play in a way that feel awful. To provide an example: Skulking Colony lets you deal a maximum of 20 damage in a turn. In order to deal that amount of damage at the point you are finding this enemy in the game you are spending your entire energy to do so, leaving you open to attack. This wouldn't be the worst if that was the end of it. The problem comes in now; this enemy is a damage race. If you take too many turns fighting him: either by not dealing the full 20 every turn, or using a defensive build, or - god forbid,  block while low on health. You have already lost as the next turn when you shuffle your deck you are adding a minimum of 5 dazed to your deck assuming that he only used a smash attack once, the other attacks also will add strength, and provide block when you are already damage limited in the first place.         Next is the punishments for attacking enemies - This one I don't think I can be even a little nice about. It's one thing for a couple of specific enemies to have things like thorns one turn, or taking less damage the more times they are hit. IT IS AN ENTIRELY DIFFERENT MECHANIC WHEN YOU ACTIVELY PUNISH A PLAYER FOR ATTACKING AN ENEMY NO MATTER WHAT TIME YOU DO SO OR WITHOUT WAYS TO FACILITATE MITIGATING THE NEGATIVE AFFECTS. Entomancer gets stronger as the fight goes on, retaliating more and dealing more damage as they cycle through their move set. So why the hell is it that I get punished for attempting to end the fight aggressively? Scroll of Biting removing Max HP for unblocked damage when you have multiple of them is also a ♥♥♥♥ fight since you need to block a minimum of 14 damage or lost max hp for the rest of the run. and again these guys get stronger as the fight goes on gaining 2 strength whenever they buff. There are multiple of these types of design choices where an enemy is designed around a mechanic and then if you attempt to negate that mechanic with an appropriate counter strategy then you are punished for not taking it on the chin. Best case scenario it is frustrating but a decent challenge. At worst you lose the game due to no fault of your own because you were punished for merely attempting to be logical when dealing with a challenge.          Moving on to the elephant in the room. Using consultants that have a history of attacking your target audience, is mired in political controversy, and has shown no remorse for their actions even after continuing to work in the industry that they have ridiculed is a poor choice; one that the developer is free to make but should be aware of the backlash that will come from it.          To put it simply; Mega Crit may have thrown away a massive amount of customer sentiment and good will with no explanation to the players as to why they made the choice to do so. They have made no public statement regarding the decision, and have failed to communicate a decision that should have been known would be controversial from the start.        I hope that they will have taken the right lesson from this backlash in that even if they create a good product, a loyal fan base, and have an abundance of good will from their community. It can be lost with the wrong choice; not a mistake, not an accident, but a choice. In this case a number of poor choices; the choice to use Anita as a consultant, the choice to hide her involvement in the credits of the game given her inherent controversy, the choice to not communicate with their fans.         Do better.

The gameplay loop feels to me, as a noob and amateur, very much like a soulslike. Over time, you familiarize yourself with the details of each possible enemy you encounter. You learn which risks to take and which to pass up on. Every resource, of which you have a limited supply, matters. Every decision must be made with care. Yes, it is a difficult game, but no, it is not impossible, nor is it unbalanced. I will say that you should not go into this expecting your first run to lead you to victory. Once you greet minibosses like old friends, that is when you truly enter the game. The time investment to learn the game and enemy patterns and the many quirks and specialized rules they possess is well worth it in my opinion. Above all else, this game requires patience and an openness to loss. In that, each hard-earned victory feels exciting, just like a Souls game. I do recommend it to those who bring patience and the willingness to solve difficult puzzles. If you want a faster pace, more randomness, and less grim an atmosphere, other indie roguelikes like Peglin might be more your cup of tea.

Trying to counteract some of the review bombing that's been going on. Others have explained it and I'll try to give a summary, first briefly stated: this game is in early access and it's interesting to play this way - you never know if a mechanic is going to hold up/if a card or element of the game you've learned to build decks around changes, it might make a previously viable approach to winning on the highest difficulty no longer meta.  To me, that's  just the interesting part of a game that has early access. We get to play it sooner than we would otherwise,  and it's the reason the game isn't on consoles yet.  If you've played the first StS, never fear. This is a worthy sequel. The new characters are interesting, the old favorites (minus the watcher) are back as well, with pretty similar (or, in many cases, the same) cards as there were in the first StS. There's a lot of new stuff, too; just about every enemy has been reworked or is new, the bosses and elites are all new. You get interesting blessings offered to you at the start of each floor rather than opening a treasure chest along with the rare card following a boss. And in my opinion what they've already got going on is top-notch.  Nothing beats the thrill of turning the deck you slapped together to beat the first act into a scaled-up mega powerful version of itself (and of course you often die trying, but when it hits it's very satisfying)  The review bombing is a result mostly of the difficulty in communicating with China - their internet is so heavily restricted , steam reviews are really the only way they can give feedback to the devs. English-speaking players can use an in-game feature to send feedback. This game is super-popular in China and a lot of people (around the world, including China) play the game on the highest difficulty levels and thus have to rely on certain mechanics which could be the only logical way to maintain a high win rate. The devs rebalance the game as they go through early access and sometimes they hamper one of the major meta pieces somehow. Dont give them too much of a hard time because it's the only way they can give feedback, but at the same time, this game isn't ONLY for them, so it winds up being unfair to the review score. Plus, seems kinda boring to just play the game over and over expecting to find the same synergies, there's no way to guarantee what cards you're going to see on your run, so there's a lot of short-term problem solving (how do I win this fight/how can I do more damage with whatever card I pick after it's over) with long term problem solving (how do I make sure I fight 2-3 or more elites on this floor with the path I choose/how do I effectively upgrade certain cards I've chosen to maximize their synergies)  If early access isn't your bag, you could wait, but life is short and this game is good, so I recommend it to anyone who loved or even just liked the first game, as well as any new folks that may discover this love letter to trading card games and rogue-derived games.

It's not just more of the same; it has a distinct feel to it, with more dangerous opponents than the first game but much more powerful player cards to compensate. Overall, this feels like a faster, harder-hitting game than its predecessor, but I'm glad it has its own identity. (After all, if you prefer the pace of the original game, that's still available too!)  My only real complaint, at this point, is the storytelling. The first game had some very lightweight worldbuilding that never really explained what the Spire is or what's really going on, leaving it up to the player to infer and imagine things. In the sequel, by contrast, the worldbuilding is given a painstaking amount of explanation through "Epochs" that you unlock over the course of the game - and the story we're told is, unfortunately, boring and silly. This is one of those cases where less is more.  All in all, if you liked Slay the Spire, then you're almost certainly going to enjoy Slay the Spire 2. Just bear in mind that it's still in Early Access, and might not be the same by the time you pick it up!

They really made one of the best roguelike deckbuilders of all time and said "Hey, why don't we just do it again and make it better?" and they somehow did.   Slay the Spire is already such a good game, a sequel was almost guaranteed to be good. Yet, even in early access, Slay the Spire 2 is such an improvement. All the characters have fun archetypes to build around, the new characters have distinct playstyles that are easy to learn once you start doing runs with them. The Ancients are a really good improvement from the boss relics in the first game, it feels like I've considered taking nearly every reward for each run I've played. And the art, it's so well-crafted. The animations for the characters, the card and Epoch art (even the dev art is really charming and cute, I hope it sticks around), enemy animations, even the card debuffs are so visually satisfying.  Plus you can even play the game with your friends! Co-op has its own separate Ascension system and even a few unique cards so you can take advantage of certain strategies and synergies that wouldn't be attainable in a solo run.   I've been playing this game since release, and genuinely it's shaping up to be one of the best roguelikes ever made. It's one of the few games in the genre where I feel like I could play a bunch of runs in a row without getting bored. If you're a fan of roguelike deckbuilders, or even just card games in general, I cannot recommend Slay the Spire 2 enough. It's a great time for a great price.

Edit: Coming back after a few updates and the realization that savescumming really helps my frustration level. Each combat can be replayed (no reshuffle of the deck or anything) by save and exit. I'm not ashamed.  :-)  I liked this game at first, the multiplayer aspect is fun. In multiplayer it seems pretty balanced, with maybe 50-75% win rate since the RNG gets balanced out and there are huge synergies across players.  In single player, it's a slog. I can maybe win 10% of the time (which results in some streaks of 20 losses). The RNG is awful, some runs are just impossible just from the card options they provided.  Then random enemies that do 1/2 my max health in a turn in the first act. Many of the boss debuffs are just brutal, e.g. 99 vulnerability, 99 weakness, AND you can't use half your hand? Permanently? Yeah, you can still win, sometimes (when you get multiple Hang cards with a bunch of draw from discard for example). But many builds, even if built and played perfectly, just won't work.  Then when you DO finally win you unlock... more card and relic options to dilute your options and make it harder to build a good deck.  But only for about the first 3 playthroughs, then there's no progression whatsoever, except in making runs harder. Discourse aside, here's a quick rundown of my personal pros and cons:  [h3]Pros:[/h3]  [list] [*] Sauce - This game has such strong artistic design and fun factor baked into it [*] Strategy - Having to plan around every card and effect presents so many ways to play the game and adapt [*] Multiplayer - Being able to play with friends or solo without the game becoming cumbersome or obtuse with more  or less players. [/list]

One would compare this to Slay the Spire 1, which is a classic and a game that has no glaring design flaws. I wish Slay the Spire 2 would be like that and it is, but it is not quite as well balanced and obviously since it is Early Access it is missing quite some things, but it is very much playable in this state and it is indeed again a good game. However the same problems persist, the game is anti-consumer and it does not allow you to actually 'play'. This is a pure knowledge check and even then luck is often required to actually get anywhere in the game, at this point it is just not a game people can properly enjoy unless they subscribe to this Stockholm Syndrome. I know many do, but if after about 40 hours I am burned out on it something is wrong as it never happened with STS1.  Pros: - The new characters are fun, although The Regent is a tad undercooked as for now. - The graphics have received a nice boost. - It doesn't stray far from the gameplay we know from Slay the Spire 1.  Cons: - The game is more difficult, leading to issues when trying to get creative. - Balance is a bit rough here and there. - Minor bugs and things like placeholder graphics (although the actual placeholders are hilarious) - As Act 1 is a disaster, the game will punish you for trying to actually have fun. - Too much ramp for monsters, especially at higher ascensions it's problematic. - Anti-consumer practices with how save games are handled. - Too many design choices where the player just is not informed well about what is about to happen exactly, it kind of coerces you to make mistakes that you would normally not make. This is ultimately a skill issue, but when compared to other games it is grating. You will be forced to calculate a lot.  Then as a sidenote: The game has Anita Sarkeesian credited. She seems to not understand that cherry picking some examples is not science, nor does she seem to realize that a push in the industry for more inclusivity predates her and her ilk and as such one would wonder what her role is exactly. [h1]The King of Deckbuilders Returns[/h1]  If the first Slay the Spire was lightning in a bottle, then Slay the Spire 2 somehow manages to bottle the entire storm. It keeps everything that made the original endlessly addictive while polishing the rough edges and adding just enough new ideas to make every run feel fresh again.  The combat is still incredibly satisfying, with every card choice and relic pickup feeling meaningful. What I love most is how the game constantly pushes you to adapt instead of relying on the same broken strategy every time. One run turns into an unstoppable poison machine, while the next becomes pure chaos built around weird synergies you never expected to work.  The new visuals and animations give the game a lot more personality without losing the charm of the original. The soundtrack also deserves praise, and even in Early Access the game already feels incredibly polished.  What really stands out is how easy it is to lose hours without noticing. You tell yourself “just one more run” and suddenly it’s 3 AM. Few roguelikes manage to stay this replayable while still feeling rewarding even after repeated failures.  Slay the Spire 2 doesn’t reinvent the formula completely, and honestly, it doesn’t need to. It understands exactly why people fell in love with the first game and builds on that foundation beautifully. If you enjoy deckbuilders even remotely, this is one of those games that will completely consume your free time in the best possible way.  It’s a genre-defining game, and it absolutely deserves all the praise it gets! Early Access review, currently at ascension 9 in progression.   In brief: Decent follow-up to the original and has a promising future.  Cons: Compared to the original, combat is more about damage and block values and has less interesting enemy mechanics that would encourage thought about enemy selection. Decks are generally more bland with many of the infinite or high-scaling combos from the first game removed. Elites, especially in the first Act, can only be overcome with lucky rng due to their over-tuned attack/block design. Scaling for multiplayer on elites is sometimes exponential in its effect and leads to singleplayer being the easiest version of the game by far.  Pros: The new characters are very well made and offer meaningfully different stats to optimize around. Random events are more predictable when they might occur but at the same time offer more varied rewards than the first game. Multiplayer is exceptional and really makes this game shine.   Overall, I might rate this sequel lower than the first game if not for the fun of multiplayer. With some scaling tweaks to multiplayer and swapping high damage and block values on some enemies for interesting mechanics, this could be the pinnacle of the genre.

If you want a game that is simple, can be played in about an hour, and yet still feels different every run, then give this one a try. But be careful, it can get addictive. I’ve put about 50 hours into Slay the Spire 2 over the last two weeks, and honestly? I’m struggling to find the "2" in this sequel. Don't get me wrong—the original is legendary—but after years of waiting, this feels more like a chunky DLC or a "Remastered Plus" edition than a true evolution of the genre.  The Good (Because it's still StS) The core loop is still addictive. If you like the first one, you'll like this because it’s effectively the same game. The new Necrobinder class is cool—managing a pet (Osty) adds a layer of positioning and resource management that feels fresh. The move to the Godot engine means the animations are smoother, and the 4-player co-op is a chaotic blast if you have friends who actually communicate.    The Bad: "Haven't I Been Here Before?" The biggest issue is the crippling sense of déjà vu.  Recycled Content: You’ve got the Ironclad, the Silent, and the Defect back. Their kits have been "reworked," but 80% of the time, I’m just playing the same archetypes I’ve been playing since 2017.  The Map is Stagnant: It’s the same node-based climb. Merchant, Elite, Question Mark, Campfire. Rinse and repeat. I was expecting something more dynamic—maybe branching biomes or actual side quests—but it’s the exact same structure.  Placeholder Art: I get it’s Early Access, but seeing "MS Paint" style icons on half the new cards and the progression tree really kills the immersion after a while.  The Ugly: Balance and Gimmicks The balance right now is all over the place. The Regent feels like he requires a PhD to pilot effectively compared to the raw power of the Ironclad. Also, the removal of the traditional Boss Relic system for "Ancients" encounters feels like a change for the sake of change. I miss the simple, run-defining choice of a Cursed Key or Sozu; the new system feels unnecessarily bloated.  Final Verdict If you’ve never played Slay the Spire, just buy the first one for $5 on sale. If you’re a veteran with 1,000 hours, you’ll probably buy this anyway, but prepare to feel like you’re just playing a modded version of the original. It’s "more of the same," which is fine for a patch, but for a full-blown sequel? It's a bit of a letdown.  Bottom Line: Wait for a few more major Early Access updates or a deep sale. It needs a lot more "new" to justify the price tag.

Slay the Spire 2 brought me back to Slay the Spire 1. Thanks, I guess, but this is obviously not a good sign...  [h3] What's unchanged [/h3] At first glance Sts2 seems like a HD remake of the first game. 3 of the 4 main chars of Sts1 are re-implemented, following the exact same mechanics. If you have played the first one, you will find yourself re-deploying your old builds - but with less powerful relics, which is a bummer. I am still in disbelieve that 95% of the cards from the old Sts1 cast are just there with maybe miniscule rebalancing. We've had that years ago. Whatever is worth mentioning beyond this that you could maybe get out of Sts2 is hardly justifying a new set of playthroughs.  [h3] What's new [/h3] As for the other 2 chars, I will reluctantly give them maybe one or two more attempts, but that's when I will ultimately ditch Sts2. I don't like them, I can't snowball with them properly and even if something works out, it doesn't feel like an achievement for whatever reason. The new mechanics feel like somebody had a hard time fitting them into the existing framework.  What's also new is that you get placeholder graphics as unlockables. Not a big thing actually, but at this point I wonder what has taken so many years of development. It's just nowhere to be seen aside from the much needed graphical overhaul.  Some cards certainly look better, but that would perhaps justify a patch, not a sequel.  [h3] What's actually worse[/h3] The first thing that struck me when coming back to Sts 1 was how amazing the music was back then and how not amazing it is now.  Sts 1 OST hits and it sticks. Sts 2 OST: run of the mill orchestral stuff, underdeveloped empty themes - harsh downgrade...  [h3] What you should do now [/h3] You should check your library and see, if there's juice left to squeeze out of Sts 1. If you see some 100+ hours played, you may wanna check if you've already cleared runs on Downfall. There I gladly add more hours, subtracting from Sts2 as it simply doesn't deserve any more.

[h1] Slay the Spire 2 — A Review from Someone Uninterested in Deckbuilders [/h1] [b] I am not interested in deckbuilding games. [/b] I have never been drawn to the genre and I have actively avoided it for years. The original Slay the Spire has been sitting in my Steam library collecting dust since I got it. I never touched it. I had no plans to. So when Slay the Spire 2 launched in Early Access, I almost ignored it completely. What changed my mind was something small but interesting. The developers at Mega Crit moved the game from Unity to Godot after Unity rolled out a controversial new pricing policy that upset a lot of indie developers. That decision caught my attention. It told me something about who these developers are. They cared enough about their craft to rebuild rather than just accept a bad situation. That made me curious. So I downloaded it. [b] I did not expect to enjoy it. I was wrong. [/b] [hr][/hr] [h2] What You Are Getting Into [/h2] Slay the Spire 2 is a roguelike deckbuilder. You pick a character, you fight enemies floor by floor, and you build a deck of cards along the way. Each run is different. You die, you start over, you try again. The goal is to reach the top of the Spire and beat whatever is waiting for you up there. That description made me want to close the game before I even started. It sounds dry on paper. [b] It is not dry at all once you are actually playing it. [/b] The real game is the building. Every card you pick up, every relic you find, every choice you make on the map is pushing your deck toward something. Sometimes you figure out what that something is early and you spend the whole run chasing it. Sometimes a single card you pick up mid-run flips your entire strategy upside down and it works better than anything you planned. That feeling, when a build clicks and you realize what you accidentally created, is what keeps you coming back. [hr][/hr] [h2] Five Characters, Five Completely Different Experiences [/h2] One of the first things that surprised me is how different each character actually plays. This is not just cosmetic variety. Each one has a completely different set of mechanics and a different way of approaching combat. The [b] Ironclad [/b] is the most straightforward. You hit things, you build strength, you hit things harder. For a first run it is the most approachable, and it still has enough depth to keep you busy for a long time figuring out how far you can push it. The other characters open up much stranger and more interesting playstyles. Some are built around specific card interactions that feel almost puzzle-like once you understand them. Finding those synergies is the heart of the game. You are not just playing cards, you are engineering a machine run by run. There are [b] five characters [/b] available in Early Access right now, with more planned. Two of them are brand new to the series. Getting through each one and understanding how they work is already a significant amount of content. [hr][/hr] [h2] It Looks and Feels Better Than It Has Any Right To [/h2] For an Early Access game, Slay the Spire 2 is [i] polished [/i]. The card animations are genuinely nice to watch. The enemies have been redesigned with more personality and visual detail. The UI is cleaner and easier to read than most finished games in this genre. The map has small quality of life improvements that make the experience feel less cluttered. The move to Godot paid off visually. The game does not look like a port or a rushed sequel. It has a clear aesthetic identity and it feels intentional. None of this is flashy. It does not need to be. The presentation serves the gameplay rather than trying to distract from it, which is exactly what a game like this needs. [hr][/hr] [h2] Early Access Means Early Access [/h2] [b] This is the part where I have to be honest with you. [/b] Balance is actively being worked on. Mega Crit runs an opt-in beta branch where they test changes before pushing them to the main game. Shortly after launch, a patch on that branch made sweeping changes to one of the characters and caused significant backlash, including a review bomb that pushed the game down to Mostly Negative for a period. The all-time rating sits at Very Positive, but recent reviews have been rougher because of ongoing balance discussions. My honest take is that [i] this is what Early Access is supposed to look like [/i]. The developers are actively testing, communicating, and adjusting. If you go in expecting a finished, balanced game you will be frustrated. If you go in knowing things will shift and change over the coming months, it is a much better experience. The game is also missing content that is still planned. A true ending, additional game modes, more cards and enemies, and broader language support are all on the roadmap. What is here already is substantial, but it is not the full picture yet. [spoiler] There is also a multiplayer mode for up to four players in private lobbies. It is an interesting addition but it takes real coordination to make work, since the game is built around solo decision-making. If you have friends who also own the game it is worth trying. Just do not expect it to feel like the single-player experience. [/spoiler] [hr][/hr] [h2] What Actually Got Me Hooked [/h2] I want to go back to something I said at the start. I am not interested in deckbuilding games. That was true going in. What I did not expect is that Slay the Spire 2 is [b] less about the cards and more about the thinking [/b]. Every run is a problem you are solving with incomplete information and limited options. You make the best choices you can with what you have. Sometimes you get unlucky and a run falls apart. Sometimes you make a questionable pick early and it ends up being the piece that holds everything together. [b] When you win, you know exactly why you won. [/b] There is no luck to hide behind and no randomness to blame for your success. You built something and it worked. That feeling does not get old. I have come back to it day after day since I started. I think about builds when I am not playing it. I look up synergies between cards I have not tried yet. For a game I was certain I would not enjoy, it has taken up more mental space than almost anything else I have played this year. [hr][/hr] [h2] Should You Buy It Right Now [/h2] [b] If you like deckbuilders already, [/b] yes. This is one of the best the genre has to offer and even in Early Access it delivers more than most finished games in this space. [b] If you are like me and you have never been interested in deckbuilders, [/b] I still think you should consider it. The genre barrier is lower than you expect. The game teaches you what you need to know without being condescending about it. The difficulty will frustrate you. You will lose runs you thought you had won. You will stress out over decisions that feel impossible. But the payoff when everything comes together is [i] worth all of it [/i]. It is [b] $24.99 [/b] right now in Early Access. Given what is already here and the track record of the developers, that is a fair ask for what you are getting. Just go in with the right expectations. This is not a finished game yet. [b] It is, however, a very good one. [/b] [hr][/hr] [i] Reviewed on PC in Early Access. Playtime at time of writing: personal experience across multiple characters and runs. [/i]

There are a few 'feels bad' things from balancing in general here that I may keep a running list of here: - - All enemy damage seems to be balanced around tanky builds (esp. Necro/Osty). It feels like enemies hit really hard compared to how much block and healing most everyone has. It would probably be tuning enemies down a little bit and re-working some of the math for Necrobinder to bring it closer to the other classes.   - Void Form is very very strong. The 'end turn' rider is simply more a cause for frustration than balancing. If you have the energy just simply play your defense or whatever first before playing that card, thus making the 'end turn' rider completely pointless. Some cards and effects allow you to modulate the energy cost of cards, so it is even more possible to play that card and others in the same turn. I popped an exhaust card to reduce all cards in-hand to 1, played Void Form, and then had to sit there and rage while looking at a full hand and overflowing energy, much to my friends' amusement. I don't think this adds anything to the game design and can be easily circumvented by just being careful, so I really do not believe it is worth keeping as-is in the game. Also I think the free plays could be reduced to 1. Or make it generate a colorless card that sets a chosen card to 0 for this turn to add some synergy to other regent build paths. End of the day, it is currently one of those riders that I think a lot of people would be tempted to force-close and reload to recover from as it is simply too good and comes down to making a silly play-order mistake.   - Sand worm boss status cards. I get that it is there to punish players (more than they are punishing themselves) for having too many cards in their deck. That said, even at reasonable deck sizes it is very possible to play every 'frantic escape' you draw and still get eaten by the worm because they all got shuffled to the back of your deck. I like the gimmick and having the card cost increase, I just feel the approach needs to be slightly different. I would like to die to the boss because I misplayed or have a bad/one-dimensional build, not because the game elected that I did not get to receive the status card I needed. Here is a suggestion:        - Change the card type to be exhaust and (maybe) ethereal.        - Instead of shuffling half into your draw and half go to your discard, shuffle all into draw pile.        - Every few rounds the boss buffs a status that corresponds to the cost of new 'frantic escape' cards and hits               you with some more.  Conceptually I love the gimmick of 'status card you need to live/defeat the boss' and hope they come up with a few more bosses and angles that lean into that gimmick as well. Perhaps it already exists but an enemy which is intangible by default but gives you status cards that remove its intangible for a round would be pretty cool. Maybe it is an illusory creature and the status lets you see through the illusion, or it is a ghost of some flavor and you have to curse yourself a little a la DS1 and the transient curses.   - Grasshopper card thief hits like a truck and/or might have a bit too much 'fly.' I think I have killed him still flying every single time I have come across him in a run. He has not escaped me yet. He doesn't do like any blocking whatsoever by my recollection. With the game as it is, still in Early Access, the current public release build is extremely unfair and punishing to players new and old. The Doormaker itself is especially brutal because it punishes people no matter what kind of deck they're using since it can at any point cripple infinite cycling decks, low total card decks, and decks that cannot either use multiple low/free cost cards or do one big play with their mana in one turn. If it was just this alone, the game could get better as patches come along, and the most recent public beta build is trying to address this by replacing Doormaker entirely with the new boss Aeonglass.  However, if that was just the case, this wouldn't be why I'm leaving a negative review. The game in general has enemies and sessions where the game punishes the player for not having a method to outscale incoming damage or methods to offset incoming enemy debuffs. The typical Defend card only gives 5 block, which is fine on lower ascensions, but this ramps up very quickly to where enemies start dealing more than 16 damage per turn **PER ENEMY**, and runs end before even reaching the boss from death by a thousand cuts once the player is trapped in a death spiral caused by increasingly unfavorable conditions that could start as early as in Act 1 during the first few stages.  The game isn't completely unwinnable, but it becomes less a matter of player skill and more of a "pick a God and pray that your build isn't useless against it" as players go up in ascension counts for a character. While it's possible that the game will ease up on its punishing factors, the game is still meant to be difficult, and as it is now, it is not challenging in a fair way to players as every fight encounter feels like the enemy has steroids within reach to use against the player at any time, and the tools the player gets aren't enough without allowing some kind of alteration of the starting deck. If things hopefully change so that the players have more agency on what they can do, i'd be glad to eat my words and change my review to a positive one and edit it to reflect such. But until then, I can't recommend the game as it is now, or in the case that the buyer still wants to get this game, don't buy it at full price and just wait for a sale.

Extremely enjoyable game; seemingly simple at first with fairly complicated and demanding build mechanics behind that facade.  I'll be excited to see where the game goes as it moves through Early Release.    As someone who did not play StS originally, this was all new to me, and so I've spent a lot of time learning basic mechanics and unlearning bad habits from other games.  It has felt really rewarding to start finding the builds that work well, and the randomness helps make the different playthroughs feel different.  As they add more enemies and mechanics it will only get better, and it was well worth the early access price as it already stands.  I'll also add that although at first I wasn't sure about the art style, I've come to appreciate it as a unique entry into the field.  It's a mix of serious and goofy and isn't just a rehash of tired character themes.    For those wondering about the stack of negative reviews on the game, the negative reviews are mostly (though not entirely) due to one of two things:   1) People upset that some of the bosses make certain builds feel bad to play, in a way that can make a whole run feel tainted and un-fun.  This is something they are working to improve; it is an early access game after all.  It's a bit strange that folks feel compelled to review bomb over something like that.  2) There's supposedly been a hire of a controversial figure onto their staff.  I have no idea if this is true or not.  I do not care if it is true or not.  If you care about GamerGate and make your gaming decisions based on that, then sure, take those reviews seriously.  If you're the vast majority of us who couldn't possibly care less, just take the game based on what it actually is.  Which, in my opinion, is good.  There are also negative reviews that are more "legit", I don't want to make it sound like all negative reviews are reactionary whining.  But if you're here for a game that you want to take on it's face value, you're in luck.  This is a good game.

Each run feels like it can go so many different ways between beefed up rewards at the end of bosses, more potent events, and just generally better build archetypes. Concerning the lack of deck freedom, STS2 does feel more restrictive in that common cards aren't really as good as they used to be, and that build will most likely revolve around your uncommon and rares. However, I feel like this is in pursuit of having commons be much more applicable to multiple deck types and keeping your play turn-to-turn more consistent. As evidenced my my playtime, it takes some time to get used to, but it rewards you greatly. It IS a roguelike after all.  From the off chance that someone sees this before buying and is on the fence, it's a good game if you give it a chance.

Anita Sarkeesian being consulted is unacceptable. I never would have bought this if I knew that ahead of time. They should have spent more time trying to actually balance the bosses and fix bugs, instead of simping for a social politics hackjob.   The way the game works is incredibly frustrating. So much of the game is reliant on extremely specific cards being obtained for you to have the slightest chance of making a run work. This isn't as bad in multiplayer (which is WAY more fun than SP) since you have more options with teammates being able to work together and fill in the gaps. But bosses and elites are often just unfair, and it seems like they had very specific ideas in mind for how to fight them. That wouldn't be so bad, except an enemy may be a flat out counter to your build, which doesn't just mean you'll be less effective, it means you basically have a 0% chance of winning. Many enemies have mechanics where they get bonus strength every turn (so basically +1 damage), which is very lame because it essentially means you either get your powers and damage setup in the first couple of turns, or your run ends. Add in that they also start limiting your cards and it just isn't very fun. You can get hard countered by a mechanic like that, and it means that often the game just doesn't have a strategic element to it.   I find the best enemies are those who get stunned or can be weakened over the course of the fight. This lets you put more thought into how to approach the enemy, and it leads to more interesting interactions. This is another reason why multiplayer is so much better, and basically the only reason why you should ever even consider buying the game. There are so many more ways to approach a fight, and some multiplayer only cards that let you do things like grant armor to allies or buff their damage. But in singleplayer, it's just enemies buffing themselves each turn and you hoping you'll actually draw the cards that let you have a chance at winning. For some characters, it's basically impossible unless you get a particular card that lets their mechanics function properly. I find that Necrobinder and Silent are much easier than many of the other characters, mostly due to them being able to mix and match cards and still be effective. That's not really an option with the others.   Bugs are to be expected, especially in an Early Access game, but some of them are just ridiculous. The bridge event (where you have to remove a card permanently from your deck, and lose a progressive amount of hp each time you draw a different card to remove) just kept repeatedly choosing the only Bodyguard card I had for Necro, and would be that or a gold card. It did this like 8 times until i had no hp left and it finally grabbed a different card. That's just ridiculous, and I have to believe at that point it's not even random. I believe they're fixing that in the upcoming patch, but they seem to be very slow to make changes, and now they're apparently going to just remove Doormaker entirely since they're giving up on trying to balance him, and realize that the criticisms are right.  **There's also MP disconnect bugs, but as a huge plus, the game does an excellent job of allowing you to start the game back where it crashed, and can invite your friends back in. That was unexpected, but something the dev should be praised for.   A lot of people are just blaming the Chinese for the bad reviews, but I know multiple people that left negative reviews after the most recent patch due to it clearly making the game less fun. From what I can see in the Beta patch notes it doesn't seem like the team knows what they even want to do with the game. There's not even a huge amount of content in the game either, so what's there is already getting a bit stale, but also just less fun and more frustrating. But hey, I'm sure they can throw more money Anita's way and she can tell them how to add a pride flag or something.

Slay the Spire 2 is shaping up to be a genuinely strong sequel, and as someone who loved the first game, I’m impressed by how confidently it builds on the original formula. The single‑player experience is where the game shines brightest: runs feel smooth, the pacing is tight, and the overall balance is surprisingly solid for a game still evolving. Every character has a clear identity, the new mechanics add depth without clutter, and the familiar “one more run” feeling is absolutely still there.  That said, I can’t ignore the elephant in the room: the developers really hit the Defect with some heavy nerfs, and it’s noticeable. The class feels slower, less flexible, and less explosive than in the first game. The signature orb‑based playstyle is still fun, but it doesn’t quite have the same satisfying ramp or creative build variety. It’s not unplayable, but it’s definitely not the powerhouse it used to be. I’m hoping future patches revisit this, because the Defect was one of the most unique and expressive characters in the original.  Where things really fall apart, though, is multiplayer. Right now, it feels like a completely different game — and not in a good way. The balance is all over the place, match flow feels inconsistent, and the overall experience is more frustrating than fun. It’s chaotic without being strategic, competitive without being fair, and experimental without being polished. I genuinely enjoy the single‑player, but multiplayer currently feels like an early prototype that escaped into the wild.  Still, despite the issues, the core of Slay the Spire 2 is strong. The single‑player alone is worth the time, and the foundation is solid enough that I’m optimistic about future updates. If you’re here for the classic roguelike deckbuilding experience, you’ll have a great time. If you’re here for multiplayer, you may want to wait for balance passes and quality‑of‑life improvements.

The first Slay the Spire was one of my favorite games of all time, and for good reason. It helped pioneer, if not lay the foundation for, the roguelike deckbuilding genre and provided an excellent challenge each and every run. Creating synergies with the cards you chose and the relics you earned was fun, and it offered an incredibly replayable experience that others in the genre aspired to reach. While I’ve played lots of other fun deckbuilders that put their own spin on the genre and take it in new directions, none ever got close to surpassing what Slay the Spire achieved in my eyes.  So, when I say the developers at Mega Crit managed to surpass Slay the Spire in practically every perceivable way, I fully mean it.  Slay the Spire 2 combines all the lessons the devs learned from making the original, everything that made the first game memorable, creative new ideas, and even more polish and effort to make what I consider one of the best games on Steam—and maybe even one of the greatest of all time as well.  The three main characters from the original return, all sporting updated designs, refined cards, and new abilities to take advantage of during your ascent. Playing as them again felt incredibly familiar and yet refreshing at the same time. A lot of the combos and techs you could pull off in the first game are still around, and they all have enough new cards and ability archetypes to create new strategies. For example, the Ironclad has new cards based on inflicting the Vulnerable debuff, the Silent has Sly cards which activate when discarded (an evolution of a mechanic that kind of existed in the first), and the Defect has a lot of ways to temporarily boost the strength of their orbs.  And that’s just scratching the surface of the new additions. We’ve also got two new characters to play as: a pompous alien ruler known as the Regent and a vengeful skeleton necromancer called the Necrobinder. That’s five characters compared to the original three, which adds a lot more variety to the mix. While the original StS had a fourth character eventually added, we already have confirmation that 2 is getting a new character added at some point. In other words, players already have a lot to play around with, and we’re getting even more in the future.  There’s also a new enchanting system which allows you to give cards a special buff. It could be as simple as giving a block card two additional block, or as game-changing as lowering the energy cost of an attack and making it easier to play. These enchantments are somewhat rare and sometimes come at a cost like an equivalent exchange, which balances out just how strong they have the potential to be. It’s a great way to spice up the deckbuilding shenanigans without straying from what people loved about the first.  Beyond the gameplay, Slay the Spire 2 is visually a huge step up from the original. Visuals were never a weakness for the first, as they were simple yet just enough to convey what the devs wanted. But now? All enemies have unique animations for attacking, being defeated, and even pulling off special moves. There’s a frog creature in Act 2 that grows thorns on turn one, then shoots them out as an attack on turn two—all of this is shown visually through animation, which adds a lot of character and charm. As a result, the Spire itself feels so much more vivid and alive than it did in the first game. It’s wonderful, and the game still runs just fine on my older laptop.  Speaking of Acts, Slay the Spire 2 already has two different Act 1s: the Overgrowth, which is a jungle-like environment, and the more aquatic Underdocks. Each Act not only has distinct environments and events, but enemies, elites, and bosses to fight. This, as one could expect, adds even more variety and replayability to the game. And the best part? The devs are adding an alternate Act 2 and 3 in the future, meaning that a single run can have even more possible variations on top of the chosen character.  As I’ve alluded to, this game is still in early access as of the time I’m writing this. New Acts, cards, and characters are to be added and illustrations for the Timeline lore are yet to be completed, but the game already feels like a full package that’s surpassed the original despite this. Also, unlike other modern games, it’s reasonably priced and has no microtransaction nonsense to contend with.  Slay the Spire 2 already feels like a full game, has no issues like those plaguing other contemporary titles, and easily stands out among others in and outside of its genre—all of this, and it’s not even complete yet. Originally was going to wait until 1.0 for a review but in light of the multiple review bombs this game has received, i figured I'd throw my hat in the ring sooner rather than later.  Lets get the most important thing out of the way first; this game is EARLY ACCESS. There are very few things in the game currently that are not subject to change. If you are a gamer that doesn't like keeping up with changes, that only wants to play a game after it is done updating, then I'd recommend coming back to this game in 3 years or so. You may expect to find unbalanced cards, enemies, and relics; you may expect to find glitches and bugs, some of which may crash your game or lose you a run. These are expected, and there is an easy way to report them in game; pause, settings, bottom of general settings a button that says leave feedback. You can leave feedback not just for bugs and glitches, but also for balance concerns, or really any concerns about the game you might have. The devs will read it, and while you might not get a response, rest assured your feedback will be considered. I personally left a bug report, and the bug was patched the very next patch.   Speaking of, there are two different versions to play the game on; The Default Public Version and the Public Beta. The Public Beta receives biweekly  updates, and is prone to changing a lot in a short amount of time. It is the best place to leave up-to-date feedback and play the most updated version of the game, The default public version is best to play if you just want only occasional updates that will change the game quite drastically. Keeping up with the changers will be much easier in this version, as many of the changes made in the beta won't have reached the public version, either having been reverted or changed again by the time the public version catches up. Personally, i enjoy keeping up with a growing game with fast paced updates, so i play on public beta.  Now, is the game fun? Yes. This game absolutely lives up to Slay the Spire 1. Even in its unfinished state, there are so many fun things you can do in this game, the art is beautiful, the music is fun and dynamic, the cards and relics are interesting and synergize in cool ways. I have some balance issues, but they really are pretty minor. It is actually shocking how finished this game can sometimes feel despite how far out they are from actually being finished. I've had a blast with singleplayer and multiplayer. The game is hard, but so rewarding.   I will update this review once 1.0 comes out, but even until then, i still really do recommend this game in its current state. In every way already, this game has already proven itself to be a worthy successor to the Slay The Spire name.
