On the spectrum of to buy or not to buy - this is an early access game and it is going to change a lot before it's a finished product. If you'd like to play around with what they have so far buy it. Otherwise Slay the Spire (1) is much more polished in terms of balancing, just get the first game.  My take so far: The three returning characters, Ironclad, Silent, and Defect, mostly feel like more of what they already were. They’re still solid and interesting to play, but right now they feel very close to their original Slay the Spire versions. I’m hoping future updates introduce new ways to play each of them that feel genuinely fresh.  As for Regent and Necromancer, I think both are still undercooked and need more time in the oven.  The Regent’s energy interactions are clever, but for me it ends up feeling too much like a math puzzle rather than a unique or exciting combat style. Conceptually though, he’s fantastic. Great visual design, strong personality, and a fun addition to the cast.  The Necromancer, on the other hand, feels like there’s one “correct” way to play her. Maybe that changes once more content unlocks through levels and epochs, but that’s how she comes across to me right now. I think she could use more mechanics that incentivize letting Osty lose all his HP instead of always focusing on stacking its max HP. For example, her starter relic could give her some kind of bonus whenever Osty breaks, like extra energy next turn, card draw, or another effect that benefits her directly rather than Osty itself. Stuff like that could help shift some of the focus away from “make Osty as tanky as possible” being the main thing you should always build around.  I do have one specific gripe with Defect though. From what I understand, this is supposed to be a different Defect from the first game, so I’d really like the playstyle to reflect that more clearly. Even small things, like how the orbs are arranged above him could help differentiate him. I’d love to see the orb system itself changed up a bit too, maybe with different interactions between the orbs, the player, and enemies compared to the original StS Defect. Just mix it up a little more.  What I’d personally like to see in future updates is more balancing and polishing for the new characters. The older characters could also use some fresh mechanics or archetypes, but right now I’m just not enjoying the new characters nearly as much as I hoped.  Overall though, I really like how Slay the Spire 2 adds more context and storytelling through the Timeline and Epoch system. Having progression tied to specific milestones and moments in the timeline gives the world a much stronger sense of history and continuity compared to the first game. I also really like how the story and lore connect back into the actual gameplay and character design. That’s a fantastic addition to the game.  Long term, I’d honestly love to see characters from the modding community become part of the canon story, or even make it in as official playable characters. There are a lot of modded characters with genuinely clever designs that feel unique to play while still fitting naturally alongside the existing cast.  Characters from the modding community that I personally think would fit really well in StS 2, either directly or as inspiration:  "The Cursed" and "The Dregs" both have really unique playstyles centered around keeping curses in your deck instead of avoiding them. The Dregs also adds lore and context to its existence within the Spire itself, which can add more depth to StS 2. "The Gatherer" has a potion bag containing weaker versions of regular potions, and her gameplay revolves around crafting potions during combat. "The Runesmith", while probably difficult to balance, is conceptually fantastic. She feels like a mix between Regent and Defect, using Runes to activate certain cards and temporarily enhance card values before they revert back. Her playstyle really pushes you to think long-term about resource management and how your deck functions throughout a fight. "Marisa" is proof that sometimes simple but slightly different mechanics are enough to make a character feel fresh and interesting. "Rhythm Girl" and "The Bard" both add another layer to combat decisions. One rewards playing cards in specific orders, while the other has you compose effects using melodies tied to symbols on cards. "The Deathbringer" has really unique and fun gameplay, even if I’m personally not a huge fan of the visual design. "The Hermit" from Downfall is also an obvious standout.  Other mod honorable mentions:  "Replay the Spire" has fantastic artwork and great gameplay additions. "The Servant" is just a fun character overall. "Stuff the Spire" adds two really cool concepts to the game: Archetypes and Blessings. "Oxide's Colorless Booster" has an iconic art style and a lot of fun cards. "Haberdashery" making relics visible on the player is such a simple but great feature. "Chimera Cards" / "Chimera Cards+" makes card rewards more interesting by adding variable effects to existing cards. Funplings’ "The Silent Booster Pack" adds a lot of fun Silent cards. "Relic Combos" is a great idea. Specific relic combinations granting additional bonuses feels very natural for Slay the Spire. "Potent Potables" adds weaker potion variants that passively grant relic-like buffs while sitting in your potion belt. The interesting part is the tradeoff: using them removes the passive benefit, so you’re constantly deciding between keeping a weaker potion for its ongoing value or consuming it for an immediate effect. It’s a really clever way to make potion management more interesting. "Map Marks" already has a somewhat similar feature in StS 2, but I’d still love the ability to manually and clearly mark routes or points of interest on the map. Pretty much all of Kobe’s Booster Pack mods are full of genuinely great ideas implemented well. "SpooderStuff StS" deserves a mention for Combo Strike alone. "Spire Biomes" and "Spire Locations" both add more consideration to pathing and make different routes through the Spire feel more distinct through rewards, events, and environmental variety. Spire Biomes even adds weather effects to certain areas. "HugYouColors" has some really interesting ideas around collaborative cards. Cooperative mechanics already exist through the multiplayer mode in StS 2, but what makes these cards interesting is the idea of adapting them into the regular campaign. It gives small hints that the characters may have fought alongside each other at some point, which fits really nicely with the stronger focus on timeline and worldbuilding in StS 2. "Hubris" is another mod packed with ideas worth taking inspiration from. "Reliquary" proves that more fun relics are always welcome. "Aspiration" is full of great additions too.    If you come across this review and you’ve also played a bunch of StS mods, feel free to mention other mods you’d love to see inspire StS 2 in the comments below.

Slay the Spire 2 is harder. Significantly harder. At first, that sounds like exactly what a sequel should be. StS2 adds more characters, more mechanics, and more moving parts than StS1 ever had. There are genuinely exciting ideas here, and when the systems click together the game can feel fantastic. The problem is that Mega Crit seems to have mistaken “challenging” for “punishing.” StS1 was difficult, but it usually felt fair. Strong strategies existed, and learning how to build around them was part of the fun. In StS2, it often feels like every reliable or player-favored strategy has been preemptively nerfed because the developers considered it “too safe” or “too cheesy.” Enemies hit harder, cards feel weaker, and many of the dependable approaches veterans relied on in StS1 have had their legs cut out from under them.  In the original game, the Act 1 Jaw Worm stood out because it dealt *slightly* more damage than your early defenses comfortably handled. In StS2, nearly every Act 1 enemy creates that same pressure immediately. The result is that runs feel far more dependent on lucking out with the right cards and relics early rather than using skill and practice to build up your deck over the full length of a run. I have hundreds of hours in StS1 and have cleared basically everything the current StS2 Early Access build offers, yet many Elite fights in StS2 feel more oppressive than bosses from the original game. Unless your character happens to draw into a very specific counter strategy, those encounters feel absurdly overdefended or overtuned. Difficulty is good. Feeling consistently stacked against is not.  And then there’s the Anita Sarkeesian issue.  After all the goodwill Mega Crit earned with the first game, seeing Anita Sarkeesian credited as a consultant was incredibly disappointing. I don’t know how much influence she actually had on StS2, and frankly that’s beside the point for me. Her long history of hostility toward gaming culture and her divisive public reputation make her association with the project feel like a slap in the face to the community that helped support this franchise from the beginning.  Had I known she was involved in any capacity before purchase, I would have skipped the game entirely.  There’s still a great foundation here, and I genuinely want StS2 to succeed. I mean, StS1 basically pioneered its own genre! But between the aggressively anti-player balancing philosophy and Mega Crit’s decision to associate with someone as player-toxic as Sarkeesian, I can’t recommend the game in its current state.

Slay the Spire 2 is one of those rare sequels that takes everything you loved about the original and makes it feel brand new. Mega Crit hasn't just built a follow-up — they've crafted what feels like the definitive version of the roguelike deckbuilder genre they essentially invented. Where others might have swung for reinvention, Mega Crit leaned into refinement, honing in on the elements that made the first game so addictive and elevating the deck-building experience to consistently deliver more of those unforgettable "I can't believe I just did that!" moments. And deliver it does — run after run after run.  The game is simple enough for anyone to pick up, yet has enough depth to be genuinely challenging for even the most experienced players. Whether you're a total newcomer or a veteran who's ascended to the highest difficulties, Slay the Spire 2 has something to offer you.  The addition of multiplayer is an absolute revelation. It's fast-paced, strategic, and immensely satisfying whether you're playing solo or with friends — and the first time you truly grasp the bigger picture of what this game is doing, it becomes one of the most memorable gaming moments in recent memory.  Even in Early Access, the framework and content already on display almost surpass what the original achieved. The fact that Mega Crit rebuilt this entirely from scratch on a new engine — after years of setbacks — and still managed to produce something this polished is nothing short of remarkable. Hundreds of thousands of players flooded in within the first days of launch, with over a hundred thousand concurrent players daily since — extraordinary for an indie strategy roguelike.  If you've ever lost sleep to the original Slay the Spire, clear your calendar. ★★★★★ — The Spire Has Never Felt So Alive Mega Crit had an almost impossible task: follow up one of the most influential roguelike deckbuilders ever made. Somehow, they've pulled it off. Slay the Spire 2 takes everything that made the original endlessly replayable and builds something that feels genuinely fresh rather than just "more of the same." The new Alternate Acts system is a revelation. The idea that Act 1 might drop you into the overgrown ruins of the Overgrowth or the murky, creature-infested Underdocks completely changes how you approach deckbuilding from the very first room. No two runs feel alike in the way they once did — the variance is exciting rather than frustrating. The Necrobinder is a fantastic addition to the roster. Learning to pilot a new character with their own distinct mechanical identity scratches that same itch the original classes did, and the skill ceiling feels just as deep. Built from the ground up in Godot, the game runs beautifully and the new visuals give the Spire a dark, painterly atmosphere that's a real step up. Even in Early Access, the polish is evident — this clearly went through real scrutiny before launch. If you loved the original, this will consume you. If you're new to the series, there's never been a better entry point. Mega Crit continue to be one of the most trustworthy studios in the genre. Absolutely essential. Excellent game, having played an ungodly amount of the first game, this is really amazing fresh take on the first one.  I beat ascension 20 multiple times with each character in the first one, to give you an idea of the time I dedicated to trying to play well. Slay the spire is a winning formula and having more of it is wonderful. The polish and love and care that have gone into this game are really evident. All five characters are excellent, with strong themes which really differentiate them. In the previous game, I wasn't a big fan of the watcher as her power level seemed much higher than the others, but in this game they are much more in line with each other. After around 130 hours of this game I am still discovering new cards and relics, and I know I will continue to discover new synergies and strategies between them for hundreds more.   The core thing that keeps me coming back to the Spire time and again is the possibility that my next run could be better, that my next deck could be more efficient, that I could have played a fight better, pathed better and so on. Not to mention those "oh ♥♥♥♥ I'm about to die" moments where you lock in and play perfectly to pull out a win. There are so many variables to consider but they are all fairly simple ones, but the complexities of the game arise from how these simple variables play off of each other. Getting good at Slay the Spire isn't just about knowing the cards and enemies, but building good principles and heuristics to evaluate the game's choices with. And doing this is very very fun and very very satisfying, so the game is fun even if I don't win.   For these reasons I look forward to patch day and play on the beta branch, the regular updates give me a chance to really test the ideas I have about the game and to constantly evaluate and re-evaluate them. I know that not every change will be one that boosts my winrate, but that's fine. Playing the game and having to evaluate all of the variables is hard enough, I can't imagine balancing it would be easy.   The game is hard, especially on higher ascensions. I don't think it should be easy. STS1 ascension 20 still regularly kicks my ass, and I expect no less of STS2 ascension 10. The existence of harder and harder difficulties for players who really want to grapple with the game's machanics and systems is a key draw for players like myself, and there are a lot of us. Don't expect to consistently climb ascensions just because you put in time. You should talk to other players, and really think about your decisions (in the moment and after) if you want to succeed. This isn't a turn off your brain and tune out game, you get out what you put in. This is what has made this game and its predecessor the best value for money I have ever spent. Seriously. Great start! It needs improvements as it progresses beyond early access. Here are some nitpicks:  1. Boss relics that provide energy at the start of each turn are very uncommon. They have done a better job balancing energy in this game, as not receiving an energy relic is much less of a death sentence  now than in the first game. However, their rarity still makes two thirds of runs feel like they are at a major disadvantage.  2. The first game had several enemies that hard-countered certain archetypes to the point of non-viability (e.g. the Time Eater vs. The Silent with a shiv build). They've done a much better job in this game, but it still isn't perfect. The Globe Head will single handedly end a power build on The Defect, for example.  3. Doom suuuuuuuuuuucks on the Necrobinder. It is obviously weaker than the Silent's poison builds, especially when considering the far weaker defensive capability of the Necrobinder relative to the Silent. The fact that Doom kills enemies AFTER they take their turn, and the fact that it does nothing helpful on its own until it reaches a critical point just makes it so awkward. Maybe it's just me, but although I have scraped by using the Doom archetype on low ascensions, I have never ever felt powerful, even with synergies that I suspect are intended to be strong.  4. Just like in the first game, the Defect just destroys most of the other characters in terms of build variability, depth, and fun. The other characters aren't bad by any means, but the Defect raises the bar so far above the rest that they feel flat by comparison. The Defect has even stolen the status card archetype from the Ironclad! I really hope all of the other characters can reach the same level of variability.  5. The Discard archetype for the Silent is much much much better than in the previous game, but it still it still isn't fantastic even when working as intended as far as I can tell.  6. Just like in the first game, several builds across several characters exceed the power of others by such a large margin that runs feel same-y, especially at high ascensions. The Storm/Power-Spam build for the Defect and the Poison + Block build for the Silent still feel wayyyyyyy stronger than other archetypes within those characters, for example. Suppose you're at high ascension on the Silent and the first card reward offers you a shiv-synergy card, a discard-synergy card, and a poison-synergy card. If you play the percentages and you're being honest with yourself, taking anything but the poison-synergy card is basically throwing.  7. I'm a little disappointed by the Necrobinder's summoning/minion buffing mechanics. You buff Osty's health, but aside from that, the necromancy mechanics are relatively limited. Osty's offensive capabilities don't benefit from the amount you've summoned in very many circumstances. More abstractly, it doesn't feel like the role Osty serves in combat varies much between runs.  8. Maybe I've gotten unlucky, but my Success with the Regent has exclusively resulted from Sovereign Blade builds. Anyone else?  9. Where is the Watcher?!?!? ;(  The art is so badass! The animations are so badass! The game is already fun, and I expect it to get better and better with time.

Finally completed everything in the game (A10 on all 5 characters) so I decided its time to leave my review (and to sort of counter balance from all the off topic reviews this game is being bombed with).  TLDR: Essentially perfect game, 9.5/10. Great QOL coming from the first game, interesting builds and characters that have fun interactions with everything in the game. Some characters may have some issues early on and only pick up steam later, but they all end up at about the same power level by the end. Music is great, sound design is fantastic, and so far the visuals are great (with a couple things needing to be added during early access here and there). If you like rouge-likes, you need to play this game NOW!  Game is highly replayable and addictive, there are still some interactions I still have not fully explored within this game not just with the characters but also in certain events. I can say for sure no two runs will never be exactly identical feeling after beating about 60 or so runs. It is hard to fall into the exact same archetype every run which I would say is a good thing, but you cant force a specific playstyle and it comes down to chance.  I think my only major complaints I could justify voicing is that some characters feel pretty awful to play in the early - mid game and only get really good when you get certain cards, while others feel amazing early and stay that way until the end. Regent for example was the character that took me the longest to complete all the way through, yes they are definitely the most advanced character using two unique energy resources - however it takes a while for them to get going and feel like you are using them at max potential. Ironclad similarly to the first game feels incredible early because of his passive after-battle healing and he has huge potential for broken decks simply because he is very simple in concept. Do not get me wrong, I enjoyed my time with each and every character. I just think they need to get them all to a certain threshold so it does not feel like you are putting more effort into one but coming out with less.  Multiplayer is so fun in this game, easily 1/4 of my playtime was messing around with buddies climbing the spire as whatever characters we wanted. You can play multiplayer highly strategic or play it as if you were solo with a little henchmen that helps you and enables your playstyle. As of writing I was never able to get a full room of 4 set up but if the scaling is fine I am sure it is the most fun you can get out of this game.  What really excites me about the game is that this is an alpha and more content is expected. This could mean more cards, more characters, bosses, etc which is awesome to look forward to for this type of game. The possibilities are quite literally endless in what they can add to the game going forward, and we have already been getting a steady stream of balance patches that have addressed issues and refined casual gameplay.  So all in all, even if you have little to no experience with rouge-likes or deck-builders this game is a great starting point. Get a couple buddies and do some silly runs without knowing anything, I bet it will be an absolute blast.

So first and foremost, I want to address the bad reviews that the game is getting. If you click on the actual rating next to recent reviews, it will take you down to the reviews section and at the top, you can see "All Languages Breakdown". If you click this, you will see that its rating is only being really dragged down by Chinese people mass reporting. The lowest non-chinese rating is an 83%, which is in Japanese. I've read through a fair few of these, and most of them are people complaining about one of the bosses that got removed from the game 3 days ago, or about the fact that they cracked down on infinites. All of this is to say: Please don't let these reviews determine whether or not you get the game. Make your own conscious choice.  Now onto the actual review: Slay the Spire 2 is a really good game, just hands down. Honestly, to the point that I prefer it over Slay the Spire 1. In Slay the Spire 2, the dev team put a lot more emphasis on correct decision making and making EVERY build viable, which in my opinion, is a place where StS 1 struggled. They did this by making infinites harder to achieve and by adding lots of unique ways to now tailor your deck, which I'm looking forward to seeing what "additions" are made to those systems.  Truth be told, although the Co-op mode is good, it still needs a bit of work. But it is by no means unplayable or even bad. My main complaint about it is the inability to see what other players have drawn so you can plan your turns more thoughtfully and accordingly. On top of that, animations can be a LITTLE bit slow, but its not much of an issue unless you got a character spamming cards over and over (looking at you Necrobinder and Silent)  Overall though, the game is very enjoyable, but with a few of the obvious quirks of it being an Early Access game. Some things are still being tuned, and will take time to settle. The Doormaker, the boss that got added and then removed, is a good example of that: It was frustrating to play against, and most people did not like playing against it. But they only made the choice of removing it after fiddling with it for a month to see if they could get it to work out, which I commend them for trying but then having the foresight to realize it won't work out and then just scrapping it.  As far as new cards and classes go, all of them are really fun. I'm glad that they added new things to the game, while keeping the "core" of the old game for the main characters. It makes the new game refreshing, and a lot of the styles of play that were weird in the last game are now way better thought out with cards to synergize with them, meaning some really funny or niche builds can really pop off. The new classes are also very enjoyable, though I will always remain a Silent one-trick because she is my bae.  Overall, if you like StS 1, you will enjoy StS 2. Play the game for a couple hours and you'll be more than happy with your purchase, I guarantee it.

Her influence helped normalize the idea that entertainment must pass a political litmus test before it’s allowed to exist.  Now that same person was brought in as a consultant on Slay the Spire 2—a game that didn’t need any of that. A pure mechanics-driven roguelike. A game whose entire appeal was its elegant systems and replayability. The fact that Mega Crit felt the need to pay for her stamp of approval (or “protection,” depending on how cynical you are) tells you everything about how far the rot has spread. Even the most apolitical, gameplay-first indie darling isn’t safe.

I'm a huge fan of the original slay the spire, but you definitely don't need to be to understand the core gameplay loop. The tutorial does a good job of explaining things, although it locks you into Ironclad for it. It does feel like the devs are far more prone to changing things based on initial feedback due to the review bombing. However, they're doing a great job of finding that middle ground between what hardcore fans want and what new players will enjoy playing.  The unlock system is not my favorite, but it doesn't ruin the game. You can very much beat your initial runs without any unlocks and by the ascensions you might need them you'll have them for sure (and even then, need is a strong word I suspect). I think I got everything except max ascension in ~60hrs (as an aside, ascension is not intended to be the progression system, just an additional challenge! A1 is the only one you'll never need for unlocks and anybody who can beat A0 can do it with a little more practice!)  The timeline is nice. The original game didn't really have lore or story to it. This one doesn't either, but they did a good job of giving you bits and pieces if that's important to you.   One thing that hasn't changed is Act 3 feeling relatively nonthreatening, especially once you know the enemies. It was the same way in STS1: if you got to act 3 you'll get to the act 3 boss more often than not and with minimal changes, while that's not the case for the prior acts.  I also don't like how unbalanced the ancient bonuses are compared to each other. There are several ancients, and they are very different thematically. This is generally a great thing, as it increases variety! However, there are a couple of ancients that feel particularly weak, and one of them can appear in both act 2 and 3. This should improve over time as Mega Crit is still balancing the game, and with only 100 hours I have not figured out how to use every ancient bonus optimally, so this criticism is to be taken with a grain of salt.  If you're on the fence about getting this game, my recommendation would be to to either watch others play it and see if it's up your alley (it's much more fun to play than watch, but you'll get the vibes from watching gameplay at least) or get STS1 when it's on a major sale and see if you enjoy the core gameplay loop of that game, as it has remained similar while differentiating it enough.  Of course, it is an early access game. If you want to play a completed game, I recommend waiting a year or two for the full release, and not getting it now then getting upset when your favorite thing is removed.

Slay the Spire 2 really said, “What if we took one of the cleanest roguelike deck-builders ever made and patched it into a psychological endurance test for people who enjoy being audited by the IRS?”  The 1.0 version was fun. Balanced. Addictive. I'd say fair.   Now? The game feels like it was rebalanced by a haunted spreadsheet and three interns who think “difficulty” means removing oxygen from the room.  Every run now feels like:  Turn 1: Take 38 damage. Turn 2: Draw four curses and a coupon for emotional damage. Turn 3: Enemy gains 900 block and starts a podcast. Turn 4: You die, and the game asks if you’d like to leave a positive review.  And somehow, in the middle of all this, they also managed to do business with some radioactive culture-war consultant type who brought the exact energy of “we’re here to improve your game by making everyone argue on Steam.” Truly impressive. Most devs only ruin gameplay OR public trust. These absolute innovators speed ran both.  The Steam reviews are basically a group therapy session now. Half the players are saying the game is unplayable slop, the other half are explaining why getting curb-stomped by Act 1 mushrooms is actually “the intended artistic vision.”  At this point, Slay the Spire 2 doesn’t need balance patches. It needs a priest, a rollback, and maybe a legally binding agreement to never let the vibes department touch numbers again.  I genuinely want this game to succeed, and I encourage people to play it and support the developers. However, leaving a thumbs down is the only meaningful way I have to communicate my concerns about the game's scaling. My hope is that the developers recognize this feedback and consider restoring some of what made the experience so enjoyable in the first place.  I think if they just made it with what they originally had released, along with a portal to switch to this new keyboard pounding version they could satisfy everyone.  _________________________________________________________  ***UPDATE*** To address the concern of AI:  I do use AI to format my grammar and spelling and general formatting that I may overlook, however the review and wording is written by me. I hope this helps clear things up and helps you to decide if this review is relevant to you or not. Game Review: Slay the Spire 2 – A Disappointing Departure from the Original Recommendation: Not Recommended Rating: 4/10  While the original Slay the Spire is widely regarded as the gold standard of the roguelike deck-building genre, its successor, Slay the Spire 2, unfortunately falters by prioritising rigid balancing over player enjoyment and making questionable choices regarding its development consultancy. For those seeking the strategic freedom and "power fantasy" of the first game, this sequel proves to be a frustrating experience.  1. Artificial Difficulty and the Death of Player Agency The most significant grievance lies in the fundamental shift in design philosophy. In the original game, thinning your deck to achieve a high-efficiency "infinite loop" was a hallmark of skill and a rewarding outcome of a successful run. However, the developers of the sequel have taken a heavy-handed approach to "balance" that feels entirely misplaced in a single-player PvE environment.  Systemic Nerfs: There has been a widespread reduction in the efficacy of Energy-gain and Card-draw mechanics. By tightening the "economy" of a turn so drastically, the game effectively kills the creative deck archetypes that made the franchise famous.  Punishing Scaling: While player tools have been weakened, enemy encounters—especially at higher Ascension levels—have been significantly buffed. This creates a "mathematical chokehold" where players are often left with no viable path to victory regardless of their tactical choices, leading to a gameplay loop that feels more like a chore than a challenge.  The Single-Player Fallacy: In a competitive multiplayer game, "infinites" can be toxic. In a solo roguelike, they are a reward for mastering the game's systems. By stripping these away, the developers have removed the "fun factor" in favor of an artificial difficulty curve that feels inherently unfair.  2. Controversial Consultancy and Ideological Friction Beyond the mechanical flaws, many players will find the involvement of Anita Sarkeesian as a consultant to be a major point of contention. Sarkeesian’s history within the gaming industry is marked by polarizing views that many feel are fundamentally at odds with the core gaming community and the artistic integrity of game design.  The decision to bring such a divisive figure into the development process of a beloved franchise is a red flag. For a significant portion of the audience, her involvement signals a shift in focus away from pure gameplay excellence and toward external ideological agendas. Many players believe that a game’s development should remain focused on the mechanics and the community that supported it from the beginning, rather than catering to consultants with a track record of antagonistic relationships with gamers.  Final Verdict Slay the Spire 2 is a classic example of "fixing what wasn't broken." By over-balancing the fun out of the card mechanics and alienating its core base through controversial hiring choices, the game fails to capture the magic of its predecessor.  To my fellow players: Proceed with extreme caution. If you value the freedom to build powerful, game-breaking decks and prefer developers who distance themselves from divisive industry figures, you may find this sequel to be a profound disappointment. It is, in its current state, impossible to recommend.

My first negative review goes to a game I once truly loved. When the game first came out, it transformed what had originally been a rather solitary card-battling experience into something you could fight through together with friends. The many interaction systems between teammates, along with the new relic mechanics, brought far more possibilities and enjoyment to the game. Back then, I absolutely would have left a positive review — though I doubt they were lacking praise at the time.  Then came update after update. I have to admit, the game became increasingly difficult, to the point where it was harder and harder to create a situation in which players could simply enjoy completing a run. By then, opinions had already become divided. There were times when I felt frustrated by the unpleasant sensation that it was no longer me playing the game, but the game playing me. Still, I believed that both the voices of players and the creators’ desire for self-expression were indispensable parts of building a healthy gaming community. I still thought it was a good game, even if the road toward refinement might be a long one.  But then came the recent developer guidance list, along with some newly added tag and elements that, in my opinion, simply do not belong in this game. At that point, it no longer felt like a game that belonged to the players, but a game that belonged solely to the developers — and we players were nothing more than little monsters lurking underground. I could almost see the developers playing card after card, baring their fangs while smiling at the players’ reactions, carefully testing the limits of our patience step by step.  When a game is no longer pure, when both the game and its players become playthings for the developers, then I no longer think it even deserves a place on a gaming platform. It becomes an insult to those who, after a long day of work or study, simply wish to seek some relief and escape through games.  I imagine this game probably does not need one more negative review. But this review is for the development team’s flippant attitude toward updates, and for these bizarre labels. These are not merely labels attached to the game itself — they are unfair labels imposed upon every player who chooses to play it.  I’ll probably create a special category for this game in my library, because I no longer think ordinary game classifications are enough to describe it. I lay awake at night, poring over the game’s compendium again and again. No matter how I turned, I could not sleep. After staring at it for half the night, I finally saw the hidden words between the lines:  “The Insatiable.”

Suddenly, the game is woke and bad, after all those hundreds of hours they've spent with it. And that is pretty cringe and toxic. It is exactly the kind of thing they're critical of.  With that said, Slay the Spire 2 doesn't exactly feel like a sequel to Slay the Spire 1. It feels like a spiritual successor, almost. At its core, there's still the same gameplay, but it just plays so differently, especially due to deliberate decisions made that don't just reward you with more energy after simply beating a boss. The new ancients and their themed relics, card rewards, and other effects are such a wonderful edition to the game. The new characters are absolutely fantastic to play (Common MegaCrit W for adding a Lich into the game. She's amazing!). Multiplayer adds so much fun and chaos here.  It is arguably just like Slay the Spire 1 but with a different focus in terms of balance... but it feels like an all-new experience. You can't just play a hundred hours of StS1 and expect all your runs to be easy wins in StS2. The experience doesn't translate over just like that, which is fine. It's totally okay, in my opinion. I love how it's a fresh new experience, in fact... Much rather, it builds upon StS1 and makes it a much more cruel and challenging experience that rewards you so much more when you win with all odds stacked against you.  Add to that that there are less ascensions now but on more characters, meaning (currently) ten ascension levels that scale harder in difficulty for five different characters... and multiplayer also has separate scaling and separate ascensions. There's a lot to work with here in terms of replayability.  What I'm personally most impressed by, however, is how accessible the lore is and how Mega Crit presents it to us. I loved learning more about the Spire, the Ancients, and the different characters, and it felt pretty meaningful. I love this. It's great. As such, I highly recommend the game to fans of roguelike deckbuilders, especially ones that have played StS1 and want a different experience.

I've never been a fan of deck-builders or rogue-lites. In fact, I've been the opposite, swearing them off entirely. But when I played Slay the Spire, I felt a surge of interest. Combined with playing Inscryption, I suddenly understood the drive of the genre. Once Slay the Spire II released, I immediately purchased it. The UX is greatly improved and I love the polish of the UI. You can see the intention of the first game in the loving hands a studio that has grown.  The multiplayer mode has been game changing. I enjoyed Slay the Spire by myself but after the second game released I managed to convince my boyfriend to play with me. It is seamless and they managed to curate what could have been unbearably chaotic to be extremely fun. I can't understate how great the UX of the multiplayer is. Being able to draw on the map is also invaluable for multiplayer mode. I would love to see more cards geared towards multiplayer.  The characters are good as always. I was overjoyed to see the return of my favourites with a visual upgrade. The Silent was already my favourite but her added visuals were really awesome to see. Necrobinder is my second favourite, although her kit was difficult to grasp at first, I now play her even more than The Silent. The diversity in both character visuals but deck focuses is endlessly engaging. I would love to see more characters but I am also so happy with the game as it is.  Thank you for this game! I thoroughly enjoy it. Maybe one day it could be ported to mobile, I am constantly playing it on my boyfriend's steamdeck and wish I could play it on my phone.

Mostly faithful to StS1. I beat A20+H with all characters in the first game multiple times, and beat A10 with all characters multiple times in this second game.  Multiplayer shines the most in the gameplay, they deepened the mechanics on classic characters, and the current iteration on "boss rewards" are fun. I would rather balance decisions be made on player pick rates, decision value, and thematic cohesion with deck archetypes, rather than on win rates. The Doormaker fiasco is a prime example of this, where the devs rebutted player feedback about major boss changes by citing win rates, and then ultimately dropping the boss altogether after enough backlash.  Many new relics and events are low impact, while normal enemy encounters hit a lot harder this time around, sometimes being as difficult as elite encounters. Enemy encounters are less creative this time around too, with their theme being "deal the same damage or more every turn" with fewer creative mechanics at play. This shows through most in Act 3, where StS1's Act 3 encounters usually have a unique theme/mechanic that fundamentally changes how you approach the encounter, but StS2's Act 3 encounters are less unique.  And lastly, Anita S. hired as a consultant. Stop hiring non-gamer activist parasites to consult on games. I cannot recommend something that has openly paid money to these kinds of people.  Overall, the multiplayer is a great addition to the Slay the Spire formula, but the devs' decisions this time around do not instill faith. They hire activist parasites as consultants and cite win rates for their balancing philosophy, and they are currently trending toward nerfing things to win rate equilibrium. The good faith I had with the devs from the first game has not proven out for this second game.  Buyer beware.

As someone who has put hundreds of hours into Slay the Spire and considers it one of my favourite games ever made, I was extremely excited for Slay the Spire 2. Unfortunately, after playing it, I honestly feel underwhelmed.  The biggest new feature seems to be multiplayer, and personally I think that was the wrong direction for this type of game. Most people who love Slay the Spire enjoy playing solo, taking their time, thinking through builds, and playing at their own pace. It’s not exactly a quick “jump in for 20 minutes with friends” type of game. Runs can go for hours or even across multiple days. Finding another person who both loves the game and has the time to consistently play with you feels unrealistic for a lot of players.  To me, multiplayer feels more like a marketing feature than something the game actually needed.  What I was really hoping for was a genuinely new mode or progression system. Imagine an endless climb where players keep pushing higher and higher levels with increasing difficulty, seeing how far their builds can really go. Or even allowing multiple characters in a single run with combined decks and synergies. When I first heard “multiplayer,” that’s honestly the kind of thing I imagined, and it sounded amazing.  Instead, the sequel feels extremely close to the original game with only small changes here and there. Honestly, it feels more like Slay the Spire 1.2 than a true sequel.  If you already own the first game, I honestly think you’re fine just continuing to play that. And if you do buy the second one, treat it more like DLC than a completely new game.

I love this game and it has enormous potential. However, I unfortunately cannot recommend the game in it's current state. I'll try to make my feelings understood as easily as possible so I will keep the review relatively simple. The Pros: 1) Multiplayer: Easily the biggest draw for me personally. Being able to slay the spire together with friends has been an amazing experience. 2) New characters: The new characters added with this release are fun and unique adding significantly to the game. 3) New graphical design: With the move to a new engine, they have been able to add animations to both the characters and enemies you encounter as well as new and more complex effects. Most of the time I don't hold graphical improvements with much regard, but these are significant and were much needed. 4) New Archetypes: New deck archetypes for returning characters helps make them feel fun and fresh for players of the first game The Cons: The Dev Team. Basically just that. The problem with this is that the dev team affects most of the aspects of the gameplay. I'll list some of the aspects here that I find most egregious. 1) "Fake" Elites: Normal enemy encounters generally follow a certain set of "rules". Their turns usually are different variations of attacks, buffs, or debuffs and with some rare encounters having a unique mechanic like stealing your coins or a card if you can't kill them fast enough. These encounters are fine and enjoyable IMO. HOWEVER, some normal enemy encounters have unique mechanics on par with power levels of elites and some LITERALLY being the same or WORSE than previous/current elites. Mechanics that completely shutdown certain decks, encounters where not only does a normal enemy summon but summons EVERY TURN if you kill the summon, or one which is extremely similar to an elite from the first game except for some reason it is the normal enemy. All of this is already bad enough but when you factor in the fact that normal enemy encounters have a chance of appearing at the random event floors you can attempt to path around an elite to just to encounter something equally dangerous or even more dangerous than said elite. Then assuming you manage to survive you get a normal enemy reward instead of an elite reward. Overall a very unfun experience to have mechanics that disable your deck or just outright damage/health that rivals/exceeds elite combats from normal enemies instead of elites/bosses.  2) Anti Infinite/CardDraw/0-cost builds: The dev team seems extremely biased against any sort of high card play potential/infinite builds within the game. Many normal, elite, and boss enemies have mechanics that soft or HARD counter these builds. They also have made multiple balance changes to cards/relics to once again reduce the efficacy of infinite or high card play builds. You don't want people to get infinites or have high card play potential? Okay, fine. Then why even let people build them in the first place? If you've decided this is not how you want your game to be played I understand. But you still give people all the tools to make these builds only to completely shut them down at encounters later in the run. NOT FUN. Personally I enjoy attempting to make these kind of crazy builds and theory craft what can be done. But if that's not what they want then just completely remove it from the game so people can focus on building something else instead of gambling on wether or not they get a certain encounter. 3) Recurring bugs: I understand there being bugs. It's early access. I get it. I play the beta branch sometimes. I understand there being bugs. But why? WHY? Do the same bugs that you already fixed keep coming back. Controller support and working properly within the game has been fixed just to be broken again multiple times. Multiplayer between Steam Deck/Linux and PC has been broken and then fixed again. Multiple times. I get that it's probably not the same issue behind the scenes each time. But maybe it is. And even if it isn't maybe you think "Huh, this keeps happening each time we update the game. Maybe we should try to find the underlying issue. Or maybe we should double check these issues to make sure they aren't happening because we know it's been a problem in the past." This transitions well into another problem I have which is 4) Bi-Weekly Beta updates: "Game dev is hard owo. we just can't keep up :(" Bruh. The whole point of a beta branch is to receive player feedback and get a better understanding of how the changes you are making affects the game. Doubling the intervals between the beta branch updates greatly reduces the efficacy of this. I can understand not getting new art every week. I can understand not getting new animations or sfx each week. I can definitely understand not getting new features or content every week. But you really can't have a couple dudes play the game, look at player feedback, and move some numbers around once a week? Really? You have made Millions upon Millions of dollars on the first game. And again Millions upon Millions of dollars on this game. Hire some more people. Allocate some OT. Farm the community for balance ideas or reworks. Something besides this. 5) Anita Sarkeesian: Where do I even start with this. This woman has been a plague upon gaming for years. Why? WHY? Why was she involved with the making of this game in the slightest. Very disappointing.   In summary the game has lots of potential. I sincerely believe that the potential is there for this to be one of the greatest games of all time. Unfortunately it's not there yet and with this dev team it may never be. I hope that in the future I can amend this review to something much more positive, but as of now this is where the game stands.

I feel like the game balance and mechanics need some more time in the oven. The reason why the original game worked imo was that the difficulty and RNG elements kept each other in check. Encounters were mostly manageable even if you didn't get all the cards/relics for your build. Occasionally you would get super lucky and end up with a super broken deck but this was infrequent (at least for me) and normally I would end up with something just ok. Other times some RNG you kick you in the teeth but it was ok because the difficulty gave you some breathing room.  We come to Slay the Spire 2 where all the encounters are very over tuned so now you often cant upgrade cards because you are constantly needing to heal. There are fewer and sometimes no "safe turns" anymore because many of the enemies both attack and defend/status or there are so many enemies they you are constantly losing the battle of attrition. this is only exacerbated by the other unavoidable elements of RNG such as which cards you draw and the order in which you draw them. I hope this doesnt come across as "RNG bad" but me wanting more of a balance where I should feel more in control of the game and where possible only be punished for my mistakes. In Slay the Spire 2 it feels like its not even a question of what I do. I get curb stomped because I didnt get offered an aoe card as a reward or I drew all my defends on the same turn the enemy wasn't attacking, leaving none for the other turns. This effect is compounded for every single roll of the die in the game.  When we bring the above into the perspective of the game devs increasing the difficulty my issue is not that the game is harder or that there are many outcomes dictated by RNG but that the current game balance does not give enough room for things to go wrong. If certain things are outside of my control and those things irrecurably destroy my run then I'm going to have a less than fun experience.  I don't think the solution is nessersarily simple. I'd like to see one or a mix of the following changes in varying amounts so that I feel like I win or lose based on my own merits more often than not. - Decrease the difficulty of certain encounters. e.g. Elites are awful to face for very little gain. - Better rewards for defeating Elites/Bosses. As stated above I'll never fight an Elite unless the game makes me. - Re-roll system for rewards. gives a bit of control back to the player. If im required to have a sufficiently powerful deck to progress then make it easier for me to get relevant cards. - Reduce effects that gum up the deck. Don't have to remove but having normal enemies fill your deck with garbage while dishing out huge amounts of damage just adds to the RNG hell. - Better ways to control your deck. removals are costly and scarce. I can understand why this might be hard to balance but thought I would throw it in there. - More friendly difficulty curve. It feels like enemies get more difficult much quicker than in the original game. It doesnt give you much breathing room to get your build in order.  On a side note. I know this game is still in early access but it really does feel like it should have been a expansion for the original game. I heard somewhere that there might have been issues with the publisher for them to do that but still as it stands It doesnt quite feel like its own game yet.  Take all this with a grain of salt. I didn't mind the original game and I enjoyed it somewhat but I was relatively lukewarm on the experience as a whole. Its possible that this game just isn't for me and that the super big fans of the original game might have a different experience.

If you own the original, there's definitely some considering to do before buying this one. If you don't own the first, like myself, I would say it's definitely a must-buy. I watched a lot of Slay the Spire, but never felt the need to buy it myself until 2 came around, mostly because of the addition of multiplayer.   This game is a wonderful refinement of the format, but definitely comes with it's share of issues. It introduces new mechanics alongside some new faces (and a lot of fun/silly moments/mechanics), and runs in many places where the first game walked. It continues the legacy of the first game very well imo, and cements the series as a genre-definer in the world of deck builder roguelikes.  The gameplay feels very fluid and enjoyable. Building decks is satisfying when it plays out the way you'd like, but isn't so kind as to always give you what you want, forcing you to adapt most of the time. There is a huge amount of cards in game to choose from, so don't expect to be able to go for a specific build every time. That being said, sometimes it feels a little too hard to get a build going. I can't complain about this too much, as there is absolutely an incredibly fine line to tread when it comes to balancing this aspect, and I appreciate the variety more than I would appreciate more consistent build potential. When you get a good build going, it builds fast and scales very rapidly, which is great because the enemies scale very rapidly (especially in multiplayer).  As far as game balance goes, it needs some work. It's an early access game, I don't expect perfection, and they seem to be (generally) listening to the community when it comes to balance changes. Each update brings some new balance changes, some new items related to epochs, and makes things a little more interesting with each subsequent run. Overall, the game feels very difficult, both to it's credit and fault. I appreciate that the game doesn't hold your hand or babysit the player, but recent updates have made it feel nearly impossible to get a build going before the end of act 1. I would say 1 in every 10-15 runs feels like a confident build; Most of the time, I feel like I'm struggling just to survive. Maybe it's because I basically only play multiplayer?  On that note, multiplayer feels like it needs the most love, balance wise. Enemies scale alright for the most part, but some enemies, particularly certain bosses and elites, feel like they scale significantly more than they should with each additional player. It sometimes feels far too punishing to play multiplayer. Again, early access so I can't fault them too much for balancing issues, and it could come down to my playstyle anyways so take that with a grain of salt.  The enemies feel good overall. A good handful of them target and counter specific builds, which feels like a nice challenge to come upon. Some enemies counter basically every build in the game, and feel like more of a slog to push through than a fun encounter (screw you mecha knight).  All in all, it's a really good game and I would say it is absolutely worth every penny. Even in it's current state with issues, it is one of the most enjoyable and replayable games in my steam library. Just keep in mind certain localization issues and steam deck issues, based on other reviews.

Controversial take on Slay the Spire 2, it's a fantastic game. Let me talk about why it's great then address why that's controversial. First, this is a game that took a ton of features that were loved from the first game and EXPANDED on them vastly, this is not a cookie cutter copy and paster that we so often get from sequels. There was time, thought, and effort put into story concepts, game mechanics, aesthetics, and maintaining the SOUL of this series. The mods made for the first version of this game showed gaps in the original development that they filled with the second one, there is multiplayer now on a traditionally single player game, there are new characters, new enemies, new cards, new relics, new events, new scenery, new story, so much is new and original concepts yet somehow the game still feels as familiar and comfortable as launching the first Slay the Spire.  I am currently around 214 hours in of play time currently and have little to no complaints. Is it difficult at times? Yes. Will you be frustrated with some runs? I sure hope so, some games are meant to have a challenge, this game is on mildly difficult and it can be tuned as your progress if it's not difficult enough to add even more difficulty. You want a game that an infant can beat? Play something else.   Here's why it's controversial: In a community that keeps review bombing every time something is not exactly the way they like it, it's making it difficult for the developers to make a quality game. From what I've read the publisher or whoever funds the project before release forced the developers to release early as an early access which means we got an unfinished, untested, unreviewed version of the game that the developers never intended for us to experience, changes will have to be made as we go, if that makes it harder than the game was intended to be harder. Don't buy until Anita Sarkeesian is gone from this game. Why?    1. Lack of Game Design Credentials Sarkeesian is a media critic and activist, not a game designer, developer, or writer. Critics argue that consulting on game development requires understanding of mechanics, pacing, and player experience — areas outside her expertise. Her background is in feminist media theory, which may not translate into practical game improvement.  2. Potential for Creative Overreach When consultants are brought in with a specific ideological lens, developers may feel pressure to alter characters, storylines, or mechanics to satisfy that perspective — even when it wasn't the original creative vision. Critics argue this can result in sanitized or less authentic storytelling.  3. Commercial Risk The Slay the Spire 2 situation is a real-world example — a game that launched at 97% positive reviews saw significant backlash simply from her name appearing in the credits. From a pure business standpoint, associating with a polarizing figure carries reputational and commercial risk, regardless of what she actually contributed.  4. Lack of Transparency Mega Crit never disclosed what she was actually consulted on. Critics argue that if her contribution genuinely improved the game, the studio should be able to clearly articulate how. The vagueness fuels the suspicion that the consultation was more performative than practical.  5. She Represents a Divisive Cultural Moment Her association with GamerGate — regardless of who was "right" in that conflict — means her name is a lightning rod. Some argue that bringing her into a project guarantees controversy that distracts from the game itself, making it a poor strategic choice even for developers who agree with her views.  6. Unverifiable Impact Unlike a writer, composer, or designer whose contributions are tangible, a "diversity consultant's" impact on a final product is largely invisible and unverifiable. Critics argue this makes it easy for studios to use such hires as PR signaling rather than genuine creative investment.

I’ll be honest: Slay the Spire 2 is a genuinely great game mechanically. I put 62 hours into it because the gameplay loop is excellent.  But learning about Anita Sarkeesian’s involvement completely changed how I feel about supporting the project financially.  Her approach to gaming criticism helped normalize the idea that games should constantly be analyzed through the lens of sexism, identity politics, representation, and social messaging instead of being appreciated primarily as entertainment, fantasy, escapism, artistic expression, and fun.  A huge part of gaming’s appeal has always been creative freedom, stylized fantasy, exaggerated characters, attractive designs, edgy humor, and making games for the audiences that actually play them. Many players feel that treating those things as social problems to be corrected pushed parts of the industry in a worse direction.  One of the biggest reasons many of us play games in the first place is to escape from the ugliness, stress, politics, and negativity of the real world for a while. We want immersive worlds, fun gameplay, memorable characters, and creative experiences — not constant ideological messaging or activist-driven criticism injected into entertainment.  A lot of modern AAA gaming now feels obsessed with political signaling, activist approval, and culture-war messaging instead of focusing on gameplay, immersion, creativity, and fun. Many players are tired of developers acting embarrassed by traditional gaming culture and redesigning games around ideological trends instead of audience enjoyment.  That is why learning about her involvement was so disappointing to me. The game itself is genuinely very good, but I do not want to support the continued influence of these ideas in gaming and art. If I had known beforehand, I would not have purchased it.

[h1]Slay the Spire (1) Players:[/h1] You know what you're getting, only you're getting more of it, more refined, more options, more characters, relics, mobs and bosses. Oh, and more storyline (yes, I know, what not what you expected from Slay the Spire!).  You're also getting a nice graphics upgrade, smoother UI and a few wonderful QOL improvements.  [h1]Multiplayer[/h1] ...and you're getting multiplayer! Yes, you and your friends can now slay the spire together - and it's great fun! You can mix and match characters as you wish (or all play the same!) into whatever wonderful combinations you want, mutually decide paths and room options, fight with rock/paper/scissors over which relics you all get (or decide in a friendly cooperative way, but where's the fun in that?!)   While the balance is a little different from solo play, it's still excellent fun; and ascension unlocks (but not character/card unlocks, importantly!) are separate (currently!) between solo and multiplayer, so it feels fair enough.  Ascension level in multiplayer is tied to the lowest ascension of all players present, and you have any characters unlocked that you have unlocked on your profile.  Once playing, you take turns simultaneously, queueing up cards you play, taking enemy damage equally between you (so yes, you do have to all block!) and applying damage to enemy's as a team (and the bigger the team, the bigger their health bars). Statuses, however, are applied universally - both enemy and friendly.  [h1]First time players:[/h1] This game is a rogue-lite deck-builder, with immensely satisfying combinations and challenging enemies. It's smooth, has quick play-throughs, enough options and randomness to keep things interesting - and an excellent balance of cards for decks so that you can absolutely specialize - or else scattershot and take a little of everything (though you probably shouldn't if you want to progress a lot!); and the options you get can rapidly make you sing into a another approach - it doesn't last long enough that a particular playstyle gets stale, and when you've got a good build going, it feels so good to trounce the enemies that have flattened you previously.  I would thoroughly recommend this game as a standard in how good this kind of game can be, done well and with excellent developers. It can be a challenge, but overcoming the challenge is oh, so satisfying!

Normally I don't write reviews, but considering that I've had a nagging feeling in the back of my mind as it relates to the design of this game, and that I recently found out that Anita Sarkeesian was a contractor for this game, I feel compelled to make one.   In regards to gameplay, the relatively new-content loop is 7/10 quality. The enemies, elites, and bosses seem a little too difficult in regard to the relics that are available (or in some cases, no longer available) based on winning boss battles. Male characters seem unreasonably debuffed (Defect, Ironclad) while the female characters specifically are given better relics, powers, and features (this was probably done intentionally by Sarkeesian and co.).   In regards to relics, the new content is actually 4/10, frankly. The rewards that are given at the start of each act are actually worse than STS 1, and the existing relic mixtures don't actually really benefit specific playstyles so much as they simply "generally" buff the characters. Furthermore, the events are also less varied and beneficial than the first game. Much of the "randomness" of the first game's events is lost, and the game seems to be carried much more significantly by card choices than events and relics now. While this benefits players who wish to play more strategically and remove "chance" from the experience, it significantly lowers the enjoyment for people who enjoy the "gambling" aspect of the game that STS 1 provided with its much more varied choice of relics and events.   In regards to boss battle, I would call this a 5/10 experience. Bosses themselves leave a lot to be desired. Some bosses are ludicrously easy, others are unduly difficult, and their difficulty remains constant throughout character choices. Further balancing needs to be done.   Design is 6/10. Character designs have taken a turn for the worse. Defect looks significantly less cool than his prior design, while Ironclad and Silent seem to be completely unchanged. Regent design is acceptable, but the Necromancer character seems like an attempt to shoe-horn in a female character without actually allowing any female characteristics. I'm not sure if this was done for a grant or under some other circumstances, but the design choice sticks out like a sore thumb.   Music is quite poor, I always keep it turned off. Not particularly enjoyable, but I won't dock the game for it.   Overall: 6.5/10. Decently acceptable sequel that is pretty-good new content until early access is over. It's still a great way to pass the time, but the game seems marred by otherwise inexplicable design choices that were made regarding characters rather than focusing on gameplay and balancing. In regards to the choice to employ Anita Sarkeesian, however, had I known that she was involved as a contractor, I would not have bought the game.

I liked the first StS and took pleasure in achieving top ascension levels with each character. While higher levels were a grind and pushed railroaded playstyles, it was a good challenge!  StS2 is not there (yet). Each encounter, even at low ascension, feels like a min/maxer rngfest. While random is a natural consequence of deckbuilders, the number of times where draw sequences are nearly (if not literally) worst possible has been cause for me to alt+f4 more than once. Pairing poor draws with fights that feel difficult regardless of visual notation (regular or elite) before taking on strong bosses - that may counter your deck theme - is frustrating.  While I enjoy a challenge, the current state of the game is cause for me to leave most sessions upset. While I appreciate a hard-fought victory, lopsided losses are common to basic enemies, elites are a loaded dice roll, and some bosses may be impossible - depending on your deck.   Regardless, I've put in time to unlock all the content! Now, I have been struggling to find a reason to want to continue playing as my sessions tend to end before seeing the third act despite playing mathematically optimal.  If you like to play casually, be prepared to learn how to min/max and/or build infinite combos to reach higher tiers of play!  Update 7/4/26 - Still frustrated. Trying to play builds that transition well against specific bosses in the 3rd act. Unfortunately, despite an increase in making it to the final fight in act 3 regularly, I am finding myself bamboozled with navigating terrible, awful draws. I feel that "save scumming" is now the only strategy to reasonably win and that is NOT how I want to play. Am looking for amazing, awesome moments where the deck pops off. I've played 130 hours and am still waiting for that moment.   Update Patch v0.108.0 - Still ending my runs frustrated. Been finding success in building my decks designed to succeed against the Floor Bosses then getting punished later in runs for being too tuned against a specific fight. Generic "good stuff" is less viable than original StS. Highly tuned, hyper focused builds have been my only means of success. When attempting a successful, high ascension run, I'm struggling to find fun. However, I do find plenty of frustration and, most recently, I've been able to share and empathize this experience with others thanks to multiplayer!

Love the mechanics introduced but I cannot give a positive score.  Cards have designs to push players into a particular synergy but then random card selection does not really offer cards from that synergy. I think this pushes the game from identifying what your deck needs into hoping you get what you want. Synergies are so strong, but often the correct decision is passing the card....but then this makes the game more RNG rather than strategical. These design pillars seem to fight each other.  As another point of this strategy, I find the acts unbalanced. I feel I rarely lose runs in act 3, because if I built a highly synergized deck its incredibly strong by that point....but it is RNG if these cards are offered. Thus, the earlier acts are dependent on these cards showing up. Basically, the hyper scaling is so strong with the right cards invalidates the challenge, but the skill is in the RNG of getting those cards. This makes the balance feel off because it is fighting RNG as opposed to identifying the best card offered.  I think it is poor design to offer cards that only play well with other cards and yet have them randomly creatable.  Balance for 2 player multiplayer seems off where both players have to block significant damage each turn. This is arguably harder as a game difficulty than single player and is not easily customizable without modding the game to suit the players. The scaling has a warping effect on types of decks that are viable in multiplayer versus single player.

Having an amazing game is often a curse for making a sequel. Having an amazing game that ALSO is very modder-friendly, is a terrible curse for a sequel. Slay the Spire 2 ("StS2") has this issue in spades. StS is very good, and very mod-able. Grab the Marisa hero and the Touhou environments, and you've basically got an entirely new StS-like game right in StS. Grab the villains reverse-run, and you've got StS+plus with new functionality, bosses, and environments, with fun new mechanics.   ...What I'm trying to say is that StS2 is just a mod for StS1. And it's an unfinished mod. Nothing "significant" has changed, from a player-side perspective. Maybe under the hood it has a new engine that will revolutionize the industry, but playing it... is playing StS. Which I've already bought. It has two new characters, one of which is fairly close to the Slime from the StS reversed mod, and the other seems to be quite close to Marisa from the Touhou StS mod, more or less. Of course, not in those skins, they were reskinned. But it's basically just those two VERY popular mod-characters. Just less balanced. Or polished. And looking a lot less pretty than the Touhou witch.   If you're selling a game, and it isn't your first game, and your first game made you millions of dollars... Then you're SELLING A GAME. "Early Access" isn't a Free Parking sign. It's a saleable product being sold at sale, and will be evaluated as such. If it weren't ready at the price point being requested, then give it more dev time first! You're a millionaire, you have the time and money to make sure it's in a good state before selling it.   Unless, of course, you're blowing all your money on generally questionable and controversial consultants who have a 100% perfect unbroken track record of ruining everything they touch for personal profit, realize you ran out of money to give even more to said consultant, and hastily re-spun your existing game and slapped on two or three of the more popular mods on the workshop and called it a new game. That would be ridiculous... right?   TL;DR: Just play Slay The Spire 1, and download the most popular two or three mods. It'll be a better experience. StS2 is fundamentally too similar to StS1, so it's basically an expansion pack, for a game that already has a thousand really good expansion packs in the community modding tab.

Slay the spire 2 is a unique experience that many other developers have tried to replicate but never quite managed to improve. I play this game with my friends and we all enjoy it as a whole, it can be both charming and challenging in all the right ways. While the developers try to make a point of not allowing their views and opinions to bleed into their game with few public statements, not everything is hidden.  A decent run through the game definitely gives away that the writing within has this sort of 'quirkiness' about it that you only really find in places like reddit, the most notable example being the character Orobos. That alone is hardly a thing to make a review for but combined with the patch notes it paints a larger picture, the mentality of the developers is clear and, much more importantly, who they listen to. Reddit as a website is well known to be an echo-chamber for a variety of topics, video games being no different. The trap a lot of people and developers fall in to is treating the reddit opinion as their entire player base's opinion. Slay the spire 2 is a very popular game and only a small fraction will use reddit, let alone contribute to it. However, the devs see it fit to use this site as their primary source of feedback for their game.  While I respect the boldness to simply say 'This isn't working out, let's start over' when it comes to a mechanic, especially in early access, I'm having a hard time believing whether it's Megacrit coming to that solution on their own, or from their fixation on the complaints of a populist third party pseudo-forum. The rework and subsequent removal of the doormaker boss is the inciting reason as to why I'm writing this review. All the thousands of people who enjoyed going vs the doormaker simply stayed silent, while the loud majority cried out on reddit, and of course, we know now that they were taken seriously. I wouldn't ever call a game 'woke' but with ties to Anita Sarkeesian who is at best, a vampire to a game's funding, and at worst an outright negative influence, it gives you a good idea of what Megacrit are willing to do to their title when the correct solution may have been to do nothing at all.  I'll continue to play slay the spire 2, like most, but with questionable and sweeping changes like these becoming the norm, that may change down the line. Hopefully Megacrit will eventually gain the confidence that they should already have in their immensely successful game and not have to try and find it in places like reddit or people like Sarkeesian.

Occasionaly the add would respawn, and you'd go between the phases. The dev team changed this by turning this boss into a turn for buffing, followed by three phases:  First phase exhausted your played cards (removing once played, forcing you to have a more large consistent deck) Second phase makes it so you can't draw more cards during your turn (forcing more consitently strong hands) Third makes you lose one additional mana for each card played. Which is more punishing granted how mana gaining relics are more rare compared to the first game. This boss, which you could not know you'd encounter until the last third of the game. Naturally having friction to specific deck types is not bad by itself, but slay the Spire 1 did this much better. I was initially skeptical about what could justify a sequel, but they really surprised me with this one  Firstly, there are a lot of mechanical additions that probably couldn't overcome the technical debt of StS1. Enchantments, allies, multiplayer, the entirety of the Necrobinder, there are things you simply couldn't add to the original that shine beautifully here  Secondly, there wasn't any stone they left unturned. Some encounters are sequels to StS1 encounters while strongly being their own thing. Some relics in StS1 that had obvious means of exploitation are nerfed to merely being good rather than infinite generators. My favorite build from StS1 is now for Defect rather than Ironclad. Boss Relics have been replaced by Ancients. Everything has been reworked. There isn't an experience you can have with this game that is replicated by StS1, and vice-versa  There's some temporary art and it currently has fewer ascension levels than StS1, but this otherwise feels like a complete game in terms of content, but it seems the devs disagree given that they're still adding things. Occasional technical issues on some hardware is really one of the few signs of it being Early Access (anyone who experiences such issues should press F2 so they can submit a bug report), but I've not experienced anything particularly dramatic myself  At time of writing there's a bunch of negative reviews right now from some gamergaters who tripped and fell into a time vortex. It's kind of difficult to find people talking about legitimate problems even since there's so many nazis and manchildren who were never going to like this kind of game or obviously haven't played any of it (though I've mostly played on other platforms, so steam probably says my playtime isn't that high either). 1/4 playable characters in the first game was a man and for the sequel they've gone up to 2/5. If you're the type to froth at the mouth at the very name of Anita Sarkeesian then surely that's an improvement for you  Overall, I highly recommend it. First，A8FQ To borrow a line from Ratatouille: “In many ways, being a critic is far too easy. We sit up on our high horse with next to zero risk, passing judgment on creators and every bit of work they’ve poured their heart into – and more often than not, we lean into writing negative reviews.” In all fairness, Anita has turned my entire outlook on gaming completely on its head. An absolutely exceptional "dish" came from the most unexpected of hands, forcing me to take a long, hard look at myself – she’s totally upended everything I thought I knew. It isn’t nearly as vile as the knee-jerk crowd make it out to be; on the contrary, it’s got something truly extraordinary about it. And now I finally understand what it’s really getting at: not everyone can be a great artist. When Tom, an American gamer, caught wind of Anita, he booted up his PC straight away, hit "Not Recommended" on Steam, and dropped this line: “I know who Anita is. This game is dead in the water.” On the very same day, Li, a Chinese gamer, spent the whole afternoon grinding away as the Wriggling Hunter. Knackered though he was, he was having an absolute blast. It wasn’t until he was about to head to bed that he realised just how massive the drama around Anita had become for the game itself. His review ended with this: “Recommended. This game doesn’t deserve to be buried under all the off-topic drama outside the game itself.” These negative reviews aren’t down to the game getting worse – they’re down to unfair factors that have nothing to do with the game itself. The off-field noise around STS2 doesn’t matter. What does matter is this: when someone takes their prejudice against a person out on a game, they almost always forget why they started playing in the first place. At the end of the day, the only thing that matters about a game is the game itself – not all the extra noise surrounding it.
